subsubtopic: VIET NAM-U.K. MESSAGE RESPECTING RECONVENING OF GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext: In connection with Viet Nam and the desirability of having a conference of the Geneva powers, is the Secretary of State for External Affairs in a position to advise the house if it is a fact that the British government has sent a message to the Geneva powers asking for their views as to the conditions which should be laid down as a basis for the convening of a conference, and what will Canada's views be in that connection? I have another question that no doubt will be supplementary to the answer.

maintopic: CONCURRENCE IN TWENTIETH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-U.K. MESSAGE RESPECTING RECONVENING OF GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have received, only a short time ago, a note from the British foreign secretary, on behalf of his government, one of the co-chairmen of the Geneva powers, asking Canada, as a member of the international control and supervisory commission, along with its two colleague
states and the original members of the Geneva conference, for a statement as to the views of the government with regard to what conditions we believe should be considered precedent to the calling of a conference on Viet Nam.
I just received the note a short time before coming into the house, and I would not want to give a precise reply until I have had a full opportunity of considering the matter. But I would like to say, without anticipating the details of the reply the government will make, that our views have been stated, beginning with those expressed by the Prime Minister on February 10 when he said the government was of the view that there should be a cease fire on all sides. As I have repeatedly said, we think that military means are not enough to bring about a solution, and that a conference is necessary.
However, I have had to point out that before a conference could be held there would have to be a disposition for this on all sides, and there is no evidence at the moment of any agreement or disposition on the part of North Viet Nam to the holding of such conference.
Perhaps at this juncture I might just throw out what I suggested a week ago, that if there is no agreement with regard to the holding of a conference on Viet Nam, the time may have arrived when we could give consideration to a conference on the problems facing Laos. The members of that conference would be the same member states that would attend a conference on Viet Nam. It might be that the holding of such a conference would afford an opportunity for considering the matter involved in my right hon. friend's question.
speakername: Hon. Paul  Marlin@Secretary of Stale for External Affairs

maintopic: CONCURRENCE IN TWENTIETH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-U.K. MESSAGE RESPECTING RECONVENING OF GENEVA CONFERENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING ACCESS THROUGH ALASKA PANHANDLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on March 19 I directed a question to the right hon. Prime Minister regarding the study relating to the Alaska Panhandle and means of access through it. Again on March 26 I posed a similar question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. On each occasion there was the indication that a statement might be made about this matter. Inasmuch as this looks like the last day of this session, I wonder whether the Prime Minister is in a position to make some comment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING ACCESS THROUGH ALASKA PANHANDLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the hon. gentleman for not answering the question before. I have had the answer on my desk for two or three days and I should have given it to him earlier in the week.
The problems of access through the Alaska Panhandle from the Yukon and northwestern British Columbia have been under consideration by the government with United States

Inquiries of the Ministry officials for some time. As my hon. friend knows, an agreement has been reached with Alaska for the winter maintenance of the Haines road. There is also a study going on of a rail route from the Arctic circle to the Pacific ocean and, as my hon. friend knows, of paving the Alaska highway and an evaluation of the roads to resources program in northern British Columbia.
The discovery in 1964 and the imminent development of mineral and hydroelectric power resources behind the Panhandle underline the importance of the access of this territory to the Pacific ocean, and a departmental committee has been dealing with this particular matter both as to the location of routes and the manner by which agreement might be reached with the United States for free access along those routes. This committee-and it is dealing with a very complicated and important subject, of course- has been asked to have an interim report ready early this summer.

subtopic: NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING ACCESS THROUGH ALASKA PANHANDLE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I wonder whether the Prime Minister would be kind enough to tell us who are on the committee, or at least what departments are involved, as was done in the case of the interdepartmental committee relating to the hunting and fishing rights of Indian people. subtopic: NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING ACCESS THROUGH ALASKA PANHANDLE

That is a change.

Mr. Chairman, some comments are being made, but I do not think I can be accused of holding up the estimates at any time. I have one or two observations I should like to make concerning the civil service commission which I think are rather urgent. First of all, some time ago the Secretary of State, who is the spokesman for the civil service commission in the house, indicated that a statement of policy would be forthcoming concerning bilingualism in the civil service. I bring this matter to his attention again today for this reason. I put forward this reason some time ago, and it still exists to a very large degree.
From first hand information and also information that has been conveyed to me it is my understanding that there is a great deal of uneasiness and uncertainty among many federal servants in all parts of the country concerning their future as civil servants. There are all sorts of rumours, and one can also draw the implication from the wording of civil service competition notices that in some way or other people who do not speak both languages are going to be discriminated against so far as promotion is concerned.
I think the spokesman for the civil service commission in the house should make a clear statement of policy in this regard just as soon as possible, so those who are members of our very large federal civil service will know where they are going and will know positively what the policy of the government and the civil service commission is going to be. As I have already mentioned, there is a great deal of uneasiness and uncertainty as to the future of members of the civil service. They are very worried about the situation. They want to know what the policy is in respect of bilingualism, whether they are going to be frozen in the same jobs they now hold for the rest of their days, whether they are going to have the same chance of promotion or whether their chances are going to be less favourable than they have been.
I think the situation should be made very clear because there is a great deal of uneasiness among civil servants concerning this matter. I have had all sorts of complaints and requests made to me, and I am sure most other hon. members have too. Therefore I believe either the chairman of the civil service commission or the spokesman for the commission in the house, the Secretary of State, should make very clear at the earliest possible date what the policy of the commission is
Supply-Secretary of State going to be with respect to bilingualism, and what chances people have for advancement if they do not speak the two languages. I think that is something that should be made clear so as to remove the great uneasiness and uncertainty that exists at the present time among federal civil servants.
There is another point. The civil service commission is a creation of parliament and not an arm of the government. It seems to me that just as soon as convenient in the the coming session a parliamentary committee should be set up to examine the civil service commission again, and ask questions. This happened a number of years ago when the previous government first took office, and I think it was helpful. Quite a bit of time has elapsed since and in my opinion it is high time, particularly in view of the increasing emphasis on bilingualism by the civil service commission, that the commission should appear before a parliamentary committee again.
May I also say that not only in the federal civil service commission but in all other civil service commissions, whether municipal or provincial, there has been an increase lately in the emphasis on paper qualifications required for people to obtain jobs. Paper qualifications requiring certain levels of education are all very well. Nobody would disagree with that, but it is my feeling that a great many times paper or academic qualifications are stressed to far too great an extent, and other qualifications that are just as important in many civil service positions, such as basic and native intelligence, ability to work hard, integrity and conscientiousness, are almost entirely disregarded. I think it would be a very good thing if a parliamentary committee would look into that matter.
There is also the question of the tests and qualifications drawn up for certain positions. As I have mentioned before in the house, I should like to find out just what are the qualifications of those who draw up the tests and qualifications. I think it would be very helpful to get information on this point, and we could do so if a committee were set up to look into the civil service commission.
There is another matter which I think is very important. I am sure every member of the house is constantly faced with requests and complaints of people between the ages of say 40 and 60 who, because of the educational system in the country in the past, lack the paper or academic qualifications to obtain jobs in industry or elsewhere. Despite the comments that have been made over the

Supply-Secretary of State years by the civil service commission and others, it seems to me that people in the 40 to 60 age group have very little chance of getting jobs through the civil service commission or anywhere else.
This is one of the biggest problems we face in Canada today and it is certainly one of the biggest problems that any individual member faces. I think it would have a very salutary effect if this matter could be examined carefully by a parliamentary committee which could call before it members and senior officials of the civil service commission. If the civil service commission makes no attempt to help in the employment of people in the 40 to 60 age group, they have virtually no other chance of finding employment. This is a very serious matter.
As was mentioned only a few days ago in the house, the Department of Labour and its minister have made a serious attempt, I believe, to encourage employment of older persons. Yet we hear that the Department of Justice has said it will not employ people over a certain age. Employment for people in the 40 to 60 age group is one of the biggest problems we have in Canada at the present time. I am sure every member of the house knows this, and I think the policy of the civil service commission in this regard should be very carefully reviewed.
As I say, recently the Minister of Labour made an attempt to encourage the employment of older workers, but apparently this policy has not worked out. I give him full marks for trying, but it would seem that the methods used were not very satisfactory. This is a matter that goes beyond the civil service commission and will have to be dealt with at another level, but certainly the commission through its policies can do much in this regard. Therefore I strongly request the government that in the coming session of parliament a committee be set up to examine those aspects of the work of the civil service commission I have mentioned, as well as a great many others.

Mr. Chairman, I will try to be very brief but I wish to raise a very important subject. I want to take the opportunity under this supplementary vote to deal with a most serious matter. For many years there has been a confusing conflict with regard to the policy of the government and the civil service commission in respect of the payment of salaries or wages. I have in mind the situation with regard to those who are paid on the basis of current trade

union rates in the particular area and others who are journeymen in other trades and are employed by the same department but are paid on an entirely different basis.
Since I come from the city of Vancouver, I know of one department of government in which certain journeymen are paid what is known as prevailing rates. In other words, six months after a trade union contract is established these journeymen receive whatever increases may be involved. However, in the same department in which these journeymen receive prevailing rates you have other journeymen who do not receive prevailing rates and are paid between $100 and $140 less than the prevailing rates. I have never been able to understand why journeymen in one trade are paid prevailing rates while journeymen in another trade are paid on a different basis.
We have a situation also which has been brought forcefully to the attention of Vancouver members relating to the orderlies in the veterans hospital there. They proved to us at a meeting that they have to accept greater responsibilities as orderlies in Shaughnessy than do the orderlies in Vancouver General, St. Joseph's, St. Paul's or any other hospital. Yet there is no prevailing rate for them. They receive far less, with greater responsibilities, than do the prevailing rates employees in all the other hospitals not only in Vancouver but throughout the province of British Columbia. Year after year this matter has been raised. Less than a year ago I recall we were told by a member of the cabinet that this matter was not only being considered very carefully-I think the present Minister of Transport made the statement-but there would be an extension of the prevailing rate principle.
I completely agree with the prevailing rate principle. I hope we can now have an answer as a result of the study we were told was being undertaken a year ago. I hope we can be told there will be an extension of the prevailing rate principle, and there will not be discrimination between journeymen of one class and journeymen of another.
There is one other point which I believe is of vital importance, which relates to the continuation of what I consider to be a nonsensical practice. I could give an illustration in Vancouver but I should like to go now, if I may, to Victoria and Esquimalt. In certain categories there-let us take the ammunition depot-you have a prevailing rates structure. I agree it is absolutely correct. However, all the supervisory staff who are respon-

sible for the work and the direction of prevailing rates employees receive less money than those who come under their jurisdiction. Surely, sir, one should not have to say very much on this point. When in the name of heaven are you going to correct the situation where your permanent staff at the supervisory level receives less than those whom they supervise? Do not misunderstand me. I want the prevailing rates principle maintained, but something is absolutely unjust when you accept a prevailing rates structure in certain aspects of an operation, yet those responsible for the direction of the prevailing rates employees receive less money.
I am certain that other hon. members from Vancouver will have something to say about this. I have discovered, because I asked for a report, that those under the prevailing rates structure are not temporary employees. They are working steadily and I hope they will continue to do so. Why do those who supervise get less than those whom they supervise?
I said I would try to be brief on a most important question. I sincerely hope that we can have an answer now as to how far you have proceeded with this study, undertaken a year ago, to extend the prevailing rates principle so that all employees of the federal government receive trade union rates established by those in private enterprise. I should like to request also that you change the policy so that those in supervisory capacities will receive at least as much as, if not more than, those they direct, because they have the greater responsibility.

I should like to associate myself with the remarks just made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. He has brought to the attention of the house a situation which I too feel is quite ridiculous, as it applies to the wage scale of those in the supervisory categories who are working in conjunction with men who are being paid at prevailing rates. This is a situation which I did mean to bring up when the national defence supplementary estimates were before the committee, and I shall reserve my substantiating remarks until that time.
Briefly, I should like to say this is a very important matter. I cannot understand how it is that supervisory personnel are being paid less than those persons whom they are to supervise. I will go into specific details when the Department of National Defence estimates are being considered. As the hon. member mentioned, this situation applies also to some
Supply-Secretary of State of the personnel employed at veterans hospitals. In the latter case, I should like to deal with that situation when the supplementary estimates for the Department of Veterans Affairs are before the committee.
Mr. Chairman, may I-

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps I could interrupt the discussion at this point. The situation raised by the hon. member for Oxford is a basic one and would require a rather more thorough answer than I am able to give now. However, the suggestion about the committee will be taken into consideration. I had not, frankly, considered that matter heretofore, but in the light of his remarks it will be taken into consideration by the government.
The other question he raised related to bilingualism in the civil service. That was dealt with in a speech by the Prime Minister. I understood the purport of his remarks to indicate what he regards as the need for a carefully worked out definitive statement on that subject. I will consider that too. It is a matter of basic importance to the service.
The question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Victoria is a problem throughout the public service. In addition to its regular civil service employees, the public service has always had employees who may be journeymen or tradesmen paid at prevailing rates, whose pay is based on comparable pay in the area in which they work. The general condition throughout the country is that nearly all prevailing rates men are seeking to come under the civil service commission in their regular jobs. The civil service positions are based on even rates across the country, with one or two minor exceptions where extra allowances are paid, such as northern allowances. Leaving those aside, the pay is the same across the country, and that is the principle upon which that pay is determined.
The prevailing rates men are paid on a different basis, according to the rate of pay prevailing in their particular trades in the areas in which they work. One of the consequences of this is that on the west coast we have a situation contrary to that in other parts of Canada, because the prevailing rates men there do not want to come under the civil service commission. Their prevailing rate is high in comparison with that prevalent in other areas.
The converse of that has been stated by the two hon. gentlemen who spoke. They expressed it by saying that the average rate paid to civil servants across the country was

Supply-Secretary of State rather low. In any event, that is the nub of the problem, and the matter is now receiving examination by the appropriate personnel staff of the treasury board. As has been stated, it is a matter of great concern to the employees and it is one of some difficulty, but it is under quite active consideration at the moment to see if some basis can be worked out to remove the apparent difficulties which it is considered exist at present.

I want to thank the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon.
member for Victoria (B.C.) as my advance agents on this question. I also thank the President of the Privy Council for his answer, but I would point out that, for instance, the situation in the dockyard has been under investigation for the past two years, and these people in supervisory capacities are entitled to an answer.
One result of not giving an answer soon will be that we will lose some of these people, because there is a great shortage of skilled people in B.C. and no shortage of jobs for them. We have these skilled people getting less money than the men they supervise, and if this continues they will not stay with us much longer and it will be a loss to the civil service if they go. I realize that generally speaking the same salary must be paid for the same classification across the country, but I point out that there is provision for reclassification of positions.
There is another case which is the reverse of that. Some employees now in classified positions are receiving much less money than people on prevailing rates of pay, and they want to transfer to prevailing rate positions in order to get the higher rates of pay. For instance, this is the case with electricians at Patricia Bay airport. These people are entitled to an answer soon.

If I may add one final word, since we are taking up this matter now and not waiting until the department actually concerned is under investigation by the committee, I would like to amplify my brief remarks by pointing out the great danger that exists if this situation is allowed to persist for too long. I support the remarks of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich who said it has gone on long enough, and in fact I say it has gone on far too long.
I am thinking in particular of the supervisory personnel. Since the work they do is obviously of a much more important nature than the work done by the persons they


supervise, inasmuch as a lot of it is highly technical work and technical work must be passed and supervised, we are in grave danger, for example in the Department of National Defence, if we do not have the best supervisory personnel available.
When supervisory personnel leave they must be replaced, and the proper place for replacements to come from is the ranks of the men who are being paid at hourly rates. But since men paid at hourly rates are getting more money than supervisory personnel, naturally they are reluctant to step forward, and as a result we are not getting proper numbers of people coming forward to take over supervisory jobs. If we do not correct this situation our standards will suffer, and this will affect the efficiency of the departments concerned.

The matter brought before the committee by the hon. member for Oxford is one that deserves an answer in greater detail than was given by the President of the Privy Council. The President of the Privy Council is thoroughly acquainted with the problem of the civil service of Canada. For 25 years he has represented a constituency in which there are many civil servants. I say he must have found that in the last year or so there has been a feeling of fear and frustration in the civil service.
The morale of the civil service is greatly subject to a feeling that all is not well, and this is due to the uncertainty of the utterances of the Prime Minister and other ministers in connection with the subject of bilingualism. No one has any argument to raise as to the necessity for the preservation of the principle of bilingualism in every regard, but surely those in the civil service today have the right to know what is the attitude of the government, and who in the government speaks with authority.
We have had a number of trumpets played by representatives of the government, all more or less with an uncertain sound. Is it intended that all civil servants desiring promotion shall have a full knowledge of both languages? The minister has stated that the Prime Minister made a speech somewhere, but speeches made outside the House of Commons do not answer the legitimate desire of civil servants to know what the situation is.
Is it the intention of the government that promotions are to be denied to civil servants, who for years have been giving of their best, because they are not bilingual? I mention

civil servants in Ottawa, but what of civil servants in other parts of the country? What are the rules that are applied to them? I know something of the civil service. My father was a federal civil servant for 25 years, and I know at first hand something of the difficulties of those who serve, and also of that spirit of dedication that has characterized Canada's civil servants throughout the years.
Certainly in the last two years there has been expressed by many of those who have been 10, 15 or 20 years in the service a feeling of trepidation, of uncertainty. I feel the minister should give a fuller answer than the concise but uncertain one he has just given to the committee. The suggestion by the hon. member for Oxford that a committee of the house should be set up to examine this problem fully is one which deserves the support of hon. members on all sides. I recall one of the committees presided over before I came into the house by Mr. Pouliot, now a distinguished member of the other place, and the benefits which followed the discussions and hearings of that committee.
I should like to ask the minister to let the civil servants know frankly what the situation is. It is no answer to say that the Prime Minister spoke somewhere; that is merely passing off a serious question, one which is exorcising the hearts and souls of civil servants everywhere. What is to be the attitude? What determination, if any, has been made, first as to bilingualism in Ottawa and, second, as it affects civil servants in other parts of the country? Knowing the capacity of the President of the Privy Council for giving lucid and complete information I would ask him to be a little more generous in providing the committee with information than he was a few moments ago. Let him not leave this matter in a state of uncertainty. Uncertainty breeds a lessening of morale. Fear denies that high rate of efficiency which our civil service enjoys.
I ask the minister, one who is sincerely interested in the civil service, to rise now and give an explanation to the house which will dissipate the fears being expressed in the civil service, and will give to those who serve a degree of certainly which at the moment they do not possess.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition has questioned my earlier answer on this important subject. I believe there should be a carefully worked out definitive answer placed on the record. The
Supply-Secretary of State hon. member for Oxford did raise what I felt was an important issue, that is the wisdom or the possibility of setting up a committee of the House of Commons or of parliament, as the case may be, to examine the whole matter of the civil service. The Leader of the Opposition supported his hon. friend in making such a suggestion. I stated by way of reply that this had not received consideration by the government but that I thought this was a very important matter and would see that it did receive consideration by the government.
As to the question of the fears of the civil servants, I have been of the impression that those fears were allayed by the speech which the Prime Minister made a few weeks ago to one of the associations, the professional institute of the civil service of Canada. This is the kind of speech which is published in the official publications of the civil service. After all, it was a speech by the head of the government and it has been my impression, for what it is worth, that it has allayed-
Can the minister epitomize it?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would prefer not to attempt to do so, because I do not have the text here. I should like to put a definitive and carefully worked out statement on the record if it is felt this should be done.
There is one point with which I should like to deal now, because I think the manner in which the Leader of the Opposition has raised the issue may possibly create fears, though I am sure this was not the intention. It has to do with promotions and the possible inference from the right hon. gentleman's remarks that the right of promotion is to be denied civil servants who are not bilingual.
What I suggested was that many civil servants fear this.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is correct. I wish to make it clear that such fears are not justified. What is being sought is to provide that in those areas of the country where the people dealing with civil servants are bilingual, or may be speaking either language, the civil servants with whom they are in contact shall also, as far as possible, be able to speak the two languages. I might add that we have set up language schools which have turned out to be very well received by the civil servants. Such positions as I have mentioned would be filled as far as possible by bilingual civil servants, but this should not arouse any concern or fear with regard to promotions

Supply-Secretary of State in those groups of civil servants of which the Leader of the Opposition spoke.
The right hon. gentleman may think I am cautious, but I do not believe I should go much further on supplementary estimates in trying to set out a definitive statement. However, I should be very glad to try to have an authoritative statement made on this subject in a way which would make perfectly clear to all hon. members what the policy of the government is in regard to this important matter, and also would serve as a statement upon which employees of the government could rely.

I wonder whether the minister is aware that certain people in Canada's military service today have been notified that as of recent date men in the lower ranks cannot expect to be promoted unless they are completely bilingual. I know of one or two cases, particularly in western Canada, where junior officers have been told they can expect no further promotion unless they are completely bilingual. As a matter of fact they have letters to this effect, although I cannot produce them at the moment.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I am not aware of that. I will look into it immediately.

I have a couple of
thoughts on this matter, and as usual I will try to express them with laconic brevity. The question raised by our colleagues from the west prompts me to reiterate a point of view which has been in my mind for some time, namely that some thought might be given to the prevailing wage rate differential. I have never yet found convincing reasons why someone working on a government building in Prince Edward Island should receive 25, 35 or 40 cents less per hour than a similar employee working on a similar project for the same government department in the city of Toronto or the city of Vancouver. Certainly there is no differential in the cost of living which these men have to face, a cost of living which is rising painfully and rapidly. The point brought out by the hon. member for Oxford is, I think, of tremendous importance. It certainly cannot be dealt with in the heel of the session, which we are led to believe this is.
Of course the administration of the national government must reflect the bilingual fact of parliament, if parliament is in fact bilingual; but I think a most careful study should be undertaken before putting this concept into practice, which concept could be not only harmful but extremely painful and,


in the long run, detrimental to efficiency. I mentioned a couple of years ago-and I am not old enough or important enough to be quoting myself-that I thought then there was a danger of a situation developing wherein linguistic ability would transcend other abilities in the governmental service and this would be a most unfortunate development, as important and as cherished as is the knowledge of languages. No one envies more than I do the people who have that ability. But let this not be raised to become the most important factor in the over-all spectrum of a man's ability if he is working in the government service.
The last matter that I have in mind, Mr. Chairman-and it is a matter of some urgency-is this. I believe we have all received an appeal from the employees of the nation's penitentiaries taking bitter exception to the extent of the recent increase in their wage scale. They point out that 16.2 per cent of the penitentiary service employees of Canada received no increase at all in the latest raise; that more than one third received less than $200 a year. These people, quite rightly, are coming to Ottawa to protest about this injustice, and I think all sympathy and understanding should be given to them.
We are living, unfortunately, in an age when there is a great tendency to snap your fingers at authority, and I suppose the Rivard and Banks episodes dramatize and symbolize that very unfortunate development. These men who work in penitentiaries have a most difficult job, which is becoming more difficult. The hours are long, the anxiety is great, the conditions are not always the best. I hope when these people come to meet the cabinet or the responsible minister these facts will be borne in mind. They are going to come to Ottawa before Easter, and I hope some measure of sympathy and consideration will be meted out to these long suffering employees. They have plenty of troubles in prisons. There are problems in building the prisons, and keeping people in them, and so on; but surely those who are bearing the heavy burden, the wardens and guards, should not be thrown the small crumbs that were given to them in the recent pay increase.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I should deal at once with the point raised about penitentiary staffs. The group the hon. member was speaking about does not include the custodial staffs. They were well satisfied- and their organizations have expressed this satisfaction-with their pay adjustments. The dissatisfaction with the pay adjustments is in

the smaller proportion of the total penitentiary staffs. When they wrote expressing themselves I immediately offered to set up a meeting with them and tried to have it last Monday. They were not able to keep that date and indicated that the earliest they could be available was, I think, Monday, April 12. There is a meeting arranged for that date. I can assure the hon. member that the points raised will receive careful attention from the government.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take the opportunity afforded by consideration of supplementary estimates D to make a few remarks.
However, since this session is to be closed soon, I am sorry that we have to rush a discussion which is most important, because it is closely related to the Laurendeau-Dunton commission, as well as the whole stated policy of this government, with respect to this understanding which should exist, to the representation of French Canadians in the civil service commission, and especially to the equal treatment which should be given to the French speaking employees in the civil service commission.
On several occasions the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) stated that his government would seek to give priority to bilingualism, the theme of the Liberal policy.
Unfortunately, after two years of Liberal administration, and despite the fact that many representations have been made to the government, the only result which has been obtained is that the taxpayers must pay for a national inquiry on biculturalism and bilingualism, which, incidentally, has brought no practical results so far.
In fact, the results have so little practical value that not long ago in spite of the promises of the Secretary of State, the civil service commission, in application notices for candidates to higher positions in hospital administration, especially in nursing and in the medical field, mentioned among the qualities required of applicants, that candidates had to be able to understand and speak English. However, contrary to what I think and in contradiction with the spirit of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission, it was also mentioned that a knowledge of French was desirable but not essential.
Mr. Chairman, these are quite important positions since the salaries attached to them vary between $14,000 and $17,000. Now, for these appointments to higher positions, to
Supply-Secretary of State executive positions even, the government does not require the candidates to be bilingual.
This attitude is contrary to the principle it has already stated in connection with its policy program. The government did not deem it necessary to require the candidates to these new positions that have just been created, to be entirely bilingual, even though this is obviously necessary.
I wonder how the Secretary of State and the President of the Privy Council can reconcile all they said in favour of bilingualism with the practical recognition of French at the higher levels of administration of the civil service commission.
Mr. Chairman, surely the ministers are aware of what is going on in their departments. If not, they are incompetent to hold such important positions. I think we should receive a clear answer. Would the ministers concerned tell us whether the publicity to the effect that they really are standard-bearers of total bilingualism in the country is but political propaganda or whether they are really sincere when they say they are tackling the bilingualism problem in the federal administration?
Of course other questions of particular interest to post office and penitentiary employees could be asked, as my colleague mentioned earlier.
The deplorable conditions under which St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary guards are working, for instance, are well known. Those employees are exposed to all kinds of ill treatment and reprisal by prisoners under their custody, and they are risking their lives for starvation salaries.
I wonder if the President of the Privy Council would consider with his colleagues this unfair situation and pay salaries commensurate with the risks to which penitentiary guards in the country are exposed.
Also, Mr. Chairman, the Liberal party has promised a long time ago that if they came into office they would see to it that the salaries of post office employees across Canada are adjusted. In several cases, postal employees get ridiculously low salaries. Those people have to work long hours under trying conditions, and I wonder why the Liberal party does not consider the many requests it has received from them, for those employees are still waiting for results.
Mr. Chairman, if the government does not want us to feel that it has thrown away the $1.5 million which the commission on bilingualism and biculturalism has cost so far, it will have to announce today, before a new

Supply-Defence Production session begins, whether it truly intends to implement complete bilingualism within its departments. Then, and only then, will we believe in its good intentions.
I feel that the Secretary of State and the President of the Privy Council should require all candidates to senior positions within the civil service to be bilingual. Indeed, complete bilingualism should first be practised within government departments, and especially at the higher levels.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the vote carry?

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. Before you call the next item I should like to know whether the minister intends to correct a situation, which is illogical, regarding the superior officers in the administration department, employed by the civil service, and bilingualism.

Following the representations already made to me by the hon. member in that connection, I inquired from the civil service commission and was told that the main reason why French was not considered essential for those positions is that the program was in no way applicable to the province of Quebec.
The hon. member stated that we were not progressing fast enough in the field of bilingualism. I think he should have listened more carefully to the remarks made by the hon. member for Oxford with regard to the fears which seem to exist within the civil service. In accordance with our undertakings we are gradually taking steps toward increasing bilingualism in the civil service. I believe this is desirable, provided vested rights are protected.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the vote carry?
Item agreed to.
40cL. Canadian Arsenals Limited-Administration and operation, $437,000.

['Let me remind the committee of that old saying, that every man has his price. In view of the fact the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has cut me short I am quite willing to admit that in this particular case I would be willing to throw my principles overboard in return for that kind of legislation through a $1 item.\nMy colleague says I am beginning to talk like a Liberal. If that is the case, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should sit down and let you report to the house.\nResolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.']

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to make a statement; rather I want to pose a question, because I am sure that others, like myself, are a little confused as to the position in respect of Canadian Arsenals Limited. May we be informed whether Canadian Arsenals Limited has been sold? If it has not been sold, will the minister give some indication as to government policy in this regard; and if it
[Mr. Valade. 1
has been sold will the minister tell us why it was sold?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the plant at
Valleyfield has been sold and the plant at Long Branch has been closed. I believe it has been sold also, but I am subject to correction in this regard. In any event, the operations there have been cut down. The plant at Val Rose, Quebec, has not been sold but it has been advertised for sale and negotiations are pending.
Will the minister answer the last part of my question?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What was the last part?

Canadian Arsenals Limited is a crown corporation with a magnificent history during times of war and peace, and I should like to know why the government has decided to wipe out this crown corporation by selling it to private enterprise, which would only purchase it for the purpose of making a profit.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This decision was taken in order to save money. The crown was paying a good deal of money each year to maintain facilities which were considered to be no longer necessary because they were being used only at a portion of their total capacity to produce defence requirements. The sales were made in such a way as to make sure that a source of supply would be maintained, so it seemed only reasonable to sell these crown assets.
It was felt that these sales would increase employment in the areas of these plants which would be used to capacity. The machinery, equipment and tools can be used to full capacity for other items of production, and it was felt that if the sales were made additional employment would be created. For that reason also it was considered desirable to attempt to dispose of these plants.
Item agreed to.

Id. Administration, operation and maintenance including grants as detailed in the estimates-to extend the purposes of external affairs vote 1 of the main estimates for 1964-65 to provide, notwithstanding article XI of the agreement set out in the schedule to the Roosevelt Campobello International Park Commission Act, for the total cost o£ developing, operating and maintaining the Roosevelt Campobello international park (one half thereof recoverable from the United States government) and to provide a further amount of, $726,350.

Mr. Chairman, it has been a long time since we have had a full scale debate in this house on foreign affairs. This is something that has been requested by many members on many occasions. I realize that there is very strong disposition in the house to complete the present session of parliament today, so I do not expect we will have a full dress foreign affairs debate at this time. I hope the President of the Privy Council will not suggest to me that I can debate this important subject during the throne speech debate or in relation to some other debate, because I do feel that at an early date in the next session one or perhaps two days should be set aside for this purpose.
In spite of the fact that we are limited in our time today, many of us hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will give us at least a truncated statement particularly with reference to Viet Nam. Many questions have been asked in this house regarding the situation which exists there. Certainly there is a great deal of justified apprehension, worry and concern in Canada about the situation which does exist in Viet Nam. I think the Canadian people as a whole are greatly disturbed, perhaps even more so than in respect of any other event which has taken place for some considerable time. Although I did not hear the minister, it is my understanding that he said in a broadcast an evening or two ago that he felt the situation in Viet Nam is the most dangerous which has developed since the end of world war II.
I do not wish to make things any easier for the minister-I say that somewhat facetiously-but there are more members who on other occasions have held jobs related to that of the minister and who realize some of the difficulties the minister is facing. The minister has told us on various occasions that the Canadian government has been making strong representations to the United States and to a number of other countries to try to work out some kind of negotiated settlement, or at least to start negotiations. Only a few moments ago the minister mentioned one or two ideas he had on the matter, a conference on Laos and the like. I am sure all of us in the house would agree that negotiations should be started as soon as possible and that a negotiated settlement is the ideal thing. I do not think there is any argument about that but it takes two to get negotiations going.
Quite frankly, however, I have been rather surprised at the remarks of some members
Supply-External Affairs of the house, not to mention some commentaries in the public press. One would honestly think the United States was our enemy rather than the people of China and their allies in Southeast Asia like North Viet Nam. Some of the publicity given some groups in Canada, including some members of the house, in the public news media seems very shortsighted. One would wonder who was the enemy.
It is quite true that we may disagree with some of the methods and procedures used by our close friends the United States and others. We may disagree with some details of procedure, but I think we must realize that whatever happens to the United States ultimately happens to us. We are part of the same continent, and what is basically their interest is in many ways basically our interest as well. Whether or not we like it, those are the simple, unvarnished facts of life. Where we have strong views as to methods of attaining objectives, I think we should do everything we can to press those viewpoints. The minister has told us that, directly and indirectly, he has tried to press the Canadian viewpoint, and I hope he has.
There is another matter. The minister has told us that he will give us a full statement as soon as conditions are appropriate. I think any reasonable person might gather that at the moment conditions are perhaps not appropriate for a full statement; but while the minister cannot give us the whole loaf of bread at this time I would request him to give us a slice or two so we may have some idea of what is going on. I hope he will avail himself of this opportunity.
There are other aspects of foreign policy in addition to Viet Nam, although it is perhaps holding public interest at the moment in that it is of world importance. However, there are other matters which I think the minister could clear up this morning and I see no reason why he cannot do so. One is the question of aid to Tanzania. I believe that last summer the government of Tanzania requested Canadian officers to train their army. This request was turned down for reasons which never have been made entirely clear, but some officers were sent by Canada to train the officer corps.
As soon as Tanzania found out that officers to train her army were not available from Canada she immediately approached red China and got the officers from there. You can bet your bottom dollar that the officers sent by red China to train the Tanzanian army were not there for purely technical, military

Supply-External Affairs purposes. I would imagine that their skill in propaganda was probably the principal qualification when they were sent to Tanzania.
Because of the difficulties that have arisen between West Germany and other states in Africa, there is an opportunity again at this time to provide training for the Tanzanian air force. It is my understanding that this would cost approximately $10 million. The minister has told us that he is giving the matter careful consideration and that the government is thinking about it. I think it would be a very good idea, and I hope the minister is in a position to tell us that the government has thought about it enough to make a decision because, if not, the next thing we know Tanzania will have red Chinese officers training its air force.
At the moment Tanzania is probably the leading and most important country in east Africa. If that country keeps coming to us first for such help and we continue to turn a deaf ear to their requests and give them the cold shoulder, resulting in their turning over the training of their armed forces to the most militant communist countries, I wonder what will be the eventual outcome with regard not only to Tanzania but perhaps all east Africa. While at the moment this matter may be on the back pages of the newspapers, it may well be on the front pages before very long unless some decision is made.
There is also the question of military aid to Malaysia. I understand we have provided them with six Caribou aircraft and spare parts to last for a year plus 250 motorcycles. The minister has told us recently-I hope he has not had occasion to change his mind-that the wheat flour authorized to be sent to Indonesia, which I am told is used in military ration packs, has not been sent. I am very glad to hear that, and I hope it is not sent. These are some of the things on which I hope the minister can enlighten us.
There are broader questions like our relationship with the organization of American states, but in view of the shortness of time I will not go into that question now. If the minister would provide us with a one or two day debate, preferably two days, in the very near future after the new session starts, it would be a good idea.
Apart from general observations there is one question I should like to ask. One of the items in the supplementary estimates is for telephones and telegrams in respect of our mission in Indochina, in the amount of $200,000. This is in addition to what has already been appropriated. It seems to me this


must represent a terrific number of telephone calls and telegrams. I realize that our mission in Indochina is probably providing us with a great deal of information of one kind or another, but it seems to me that a supplementary vote in the amount of $200,000 for communication services in respect of Indochina requires some explanation by the minister.
I do not see how we can allow this item to pass until we receive some reasonable explanation, because the amount does seem a bit large. If there is a hot line between the minister and Viet Nam and this amount represents the rental charge for that service, all well and good, but the figure is so extraordinary that we would like to know what it represents. When I first looked at it I thought it was a misprint. I hope the minister will have a very good explanation for it.
There is one more observation I would like to make of a more general nature. As has been said, a great many reasons have been given for the position of the United States government with regard to Viet Nam, but in my opinion a number of those reasons have been rather obscure. Certainly I think no very strong reason has been given to the public at large. I think this is perhaps the fault of the United States public relations department because, of course, there are reasons or the United States would not be there. There may be a number of reasons.
I think one might make the observation that there are other places in the world besides Viet Nam where the same kind of problem is either occurring or can potentially occur. It is the old story. We thought we had learned our lesson in 1939 and 1940 when we saw a similar kind of thing, although at that time it was not the communists but the nazis and fascists in Europe. It is the old salami business; a slice here, have a conference, settle the matter, and certain things have been gained by the aggressor powers. There is a very close analogy in this case. If Viet Nam goes communist, next will be Thailand and then the Philippines and Malaysia. We have got to call a halt somewhere.
There may well be other reasons, but that is certainly one that is very important. If we continually permit the aggressive and militant powers of the communist world to move into certain areas by methods of subversion, and say all right, let them go, it is a long way off, it does not matter, then the next step will be taken into another country and another country and so on. Eventually a halt has to be called before we find that the

next step will be into our own country. 1 realize that you have to use moderation and try to get a sense of balance in assessing these things. Certainly this is one aspect of which no one should lose sight when trying to assess the situations that arise as a result of communist aggression in some fairly remote part of the world.

Let me first of all congratulate you on your temporary elevation to the chair, Mr. Chairman. While we have agreed to limit debate on these supplementary estimates, we simply cannot allow this item to pass without some comment on the tragic situation that exists in Viet Nam. I am going to confine my remarks on external affairs to that particular issue. As the previous speaker said, we have asked on occasion for the opportunity to discuss this situation and related subjects in external affairs, but to date we have not had that opportunity.
I have often heard it said that there are no votes involved in foreign affairs policy. I can say this, however, that if I believe in something I believe in standing up for it whether or not there are any votes involved. There are a good many people concerned with the Canadian government's policy in Viet Nam. I must say I have found a great deal of encouragement in talking to young people. I have talked to students at Queen's University, Toronto university, Montreal university and other universities. While possibly some of our older people are not so aware, shall I say, of the developing situation in the world today, I find that our young people are very concerned and are very anxious that our government take a stand in these circumstances of which they can be proud.
We have had numerous occasions in Canadian history when the Canadian government has shown a lack of courage in international affairs. I am not going to take the time to refer to them now, but I recall the failure to back up our delegation in Geneva when the question of sanctions against Italy was proposed. We are told that United States forces are fighting for freedom and democracy; it is supposed to be a Christian war. I want to bring to the attention of the house the real reason for the presence of United States troops in Viet Nam. President Eisenhower, at a state governors' conference on August 4, 1953, inadvertently let the cat out of the bag. This is what he said on that occasion:
Now, let us assume we lost Indochina. II Indochina goes, several things happen right away. The peninsula, the last bit of land hanging on down there, would be scarcely defensible. The tin
Supply-External Affairs and tungsten that we so greatly value from that area would cease coming...
From what is the hon. member quoting?

I will give the citation at the end of the quotation.
So when the United States votes $400 million to help that war, we are not voting a giveaway program. We are voting for the cheapest way we can to prevent the occurrence of something that would be of a most terrible significance to the United States of America, our security, our power and ability to get certain things we need from the richest of the Indochina territory and from southeast Asia.
I am quoting these statements from a book "War and Atrocity in Viet Nam", written by Russell D. Stetler, Jr., and these statements appear on page 27. These statements were referred to in a press release at that time and have never been officially denied to date. Reference is made to the fact that state department officials were horrified on that occasion at the complete frankness of the President of the United States. Now, that is the real reason the United States defence forces are in Viet Nam, the real reason behind this fight for freedom and Christian civilization. In some instances it has been called a Christian war.
I should like to quote briefly from the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 27, 1965.
Why don't you quote from April 2?

Because I wish to quote from this issue. The article refers to the United States use of gas, and says:
The gas was described by state department officials as a type of tear gas that disables the enemy temporarily. It causes coughing, vomiting and chest pains.
I have had a bit of experience with tear gas myself, and it causes a lot more than that. I continue:
Newspapers around the world commented editorially that the use of gas had a peculiar horror associated with it, even when it was not deadly. ''Whatever the arguments of legality and humanity, this new development looks foolish to the point of dementia," said the Liberal British newspaper the Guardian. "How many battalions will those two gas attacks be worth to the communist world?"
In Asia, Japan's newspapers in particular were bitterly critical. "The United States has been experimenting on the Vietnamese people as a guinea pig," said the influential Tokyo daily Yomiuri. "It obviously represents Americans contempt for Asia."
This is the unfortunate world reaction to this use of gas by the United States in Viet Nam. Then I should like to refer briefly to the Montreal Gazette for April 2, 1965. The

Supply-External Affairs article is headed "Rainfall Washes Out Defoliation Effort." I quote:
A thunderstorm washed out the U.S. air force's massive scorched earth operation against the Viet Cong in the 19,000 acre Boi Loi forest, 55 miles northwest of Saigon.
Later the article reads:
The thunderstorm had put out fires from tons of napalm, phosphorous bombs and fuel oil that 70 U.S. planes dumped on tinder dry trees and jungle growth Wednesday.
The elements thus intervened in a three month campaign that Major General Joseph H. Moore, the U.S. air force commander in Viet Nam, had hoped would leave the woods burning for some time. Spokesmen declined to say whether the air force will try again.
Here is a frightful effort to destroy the natural resources of a country which will be sadly needed in the days ahead. Then the Montreal Gazette of April 2 carries this article from which I quote briefly:
In Paris, George Ball, United States under secretary of state, was reported as telling the NATO council Thursday that a negotiated settlement of the Viet Nam fighting now is an "academic question".
I am sure even our government does not think it is an academic question at this time. This indicates the attitude of these people toward a situation which, I am quite sure, in many cases they do not fully appreciate so far as the political implications are concerned.
I should like to congratulate the conference of the heads of state of the non-aligned countries held in Cairo in October, 1964 for their concern with this very important and vital problem and for their final declaration, a copy of which I have here but to which I do not intend to refer. I do hope, anyway, that our Secretary of State for External Affairs will do all he can toward giving effect to the objectives these people are seeking in their declaration. I congratulate them upon giving leadership to all governments interested in maintaining world peace by inviting those governments to assert themselves as soon as possible.
I wish to say I think it is time we had a new approach to this very serious and complicated question, and I do urge it is not possible to deal with these problems by treating them all as black and white under present circumstances in the world. They are not as simple as that.
Let us be clear in our interpretation of the situation in Viet Nam. What is at issue is not how to defend a nation against attack or subversion, but what to do when nothing will prevent a nation from adopting a communist


economic and social system except the forced installation of an oppressively anti-communist regime. This is the situation these poor people are faced with, and I am quite sure the majority hardly know what it is about.
I maintain that the latter alternative is completely indefensible. Morally it leaves nothing to choose between militant anti-communism and the worst aspects of militant communism; and practically it confirms that communist view of the western nations which is the greatest threat to our own security, the belief that we will destroy them if they are weak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Is it the desire of the committee that I should call it one o'clock?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

When we adjourned shortly after one o'clock to obtain some bodily sustenance and get the holes in our heads repaired I was dealing with suggestions with respect to approaching this problem presented by the situation in Viet Nam from a somewhat different angle.
While I was putting forward those suggestions let me say that those communists who questioned the inevitability of attack by the west and supported the possibility of peaceful coexistence had been discredited by the United States attack on North Viet Nam. Some people claim that a withdrawal of South Viet Nam would destroy faith in America's resolve to uphold her commitments to other anti-communist regimes dependant on massive United States support. This is true. The United States must accept the debacle in South Viet Nam as a defeat for this policy wherever it occurs, in Latin America, Korea or even Taiwan, and it must be flexible enough to find more effective and constructive means of confronting communism as an ideology or as a group of allied states.
The first thing necessary is to accept this sort of distinction. The adoption of communism by the Vietnamese, is in no way analogous to the forced imposition and maintenance of communist regimes in eastern Europe. In the latter case, all historians con-

cede that Russia was largely motivated by the fear of being ringed by hostile bases right on her borders in countries which had joined the Nazis in invading her territory. An analogous situation would be China's imposition of a pro-Chinese puppet in some southeast Asian country if she were to decide there was a strong possibility of the United States establishing military bases in the country otherwise. Obviously, the bombing of North Viet Nam can only heighten the insecurity that is a source of the major part of the danger communism presents to us. Guaranteed military neutralization of the area would be a constructive alternative. In saying this I am not underestimating the difficulties and complications surrounding this question.
The second type of communist expansion, ideological conversion of populations, is a completely different matter. For one thing, it represents no intrinsic threat. People who feel communist economic and social methods will increase their well-being are not necessarily going to be hostile to the west unless we ourselves meet them with an implacable hostility. If we are prepared to accept diversity of social systems and help alleviate the suffering arising from underdevelopment, there is no reason why we cannot coexist with these people. The only alternative in the long run is war. And if we fear emulation, the constructive solution is to out-do them not attack them. The proven ability of the American military might is the major barrier in the world today to communist ideological expansion. If the United States were to support progressive, non-communist governments with a fraction of the money and manpower she has sent into Viet Nam, and demonstrated that non-communist methods of economic development were superior, communism would be defeated, not martyred as in the present circumstances.
In this connection I wish to quote briefly from the London Times of February 26. This is an article reprinted under the heading: "The Freedom We Defend in South Viet Nam Does Not Include Freedom to Ask for Peace".
Slightly unnerving to the Americans was today's petition for peace. The police dispersed a gathering of 50 people who wished to hold a press conference to launch the appeal. Their resolution calls on both the government and the national liberation front to agree to an immediate cease fire. Dated February 16 and distributed in Vietnamese, French and English, it considers that the war, increasing in intensity, threatens to exterminate the Vietnamese race and to ignite a
Supply-External Affairs world war on its national territory. It further states that the whole population demands a cease fire.
That is the wish of the people. The dispatch continues:
The resolution is signed by an author and two doctors. Vietnamese journalists claim that more than 400 "leading personalities and intellectuals" have also signed None of the original three was available at home today and one is said to have been arrested.
A later dispatch in the Times of the following day says:
This is the first such peace effort to have dared come into the open.. I met today someone who had signed the resolution. The police action, though drawing a request for anonymity, had not silenced him, and the charges of communism were scornfully dismissed.. .My informant was convinced that everyone was fed up with the war... All that the people wanted was their independence: let Vietnamese talk to Vietnamese without interference. It was not a matter of 'isms'...For the man in the street-and my informant was not one-the only thing that mattered was peace.
That is a dispatch from Saigon by the correspondent of the Times to his paper on February 27.
In conclusion I wish to emphasize that while the Canadian government talks in terms of action when the tensions in Viet Nam lessen, the people of Viet Nam continue to suffer and be slaughtered; United States forces are now attempting to destroy invaluable forests, the natural resources of the country. As we read in the press only today, some 18,000 square miles of forest territory were threatened, but fortunately saved by a providential rain. Therefore I urge the government to join with all those other nations which have met together on various occasions in an effort to find the solution to this most dangerous situation and to join forces with the powerful voices in the United States which are opposed to United States policy in Viet Nam, a policy which at the present time is identical to the policy announced by the defeated candidate for the presidency, Mr. Goldwater. These voices have been raised in the United States senate as well as in the house of representatives, and by other leading people across that nation. Let us join forces with them.
I was talking recently to one of those persons in the United States who are much concerned with this question. He expressed amazement that Canada had not taken a stronger stand as a friend of the United States against the present policy, while at the same time dissociating herself publicly from the use of such nefarious weapons as gas and napalm bombs, the employment of

Supply-External Affairs which has had such a disastrous effect on world opinion, particularly on Asiatic opinion.
Surely it is possible for the nations concerned in this matter to arrange for a cease fire, bring the belligerents to the conference table and do all we can to bring peace to this portion of the world. As I said before, Mr. Chairman, I realize the difficulties and I know the heart of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in the right place in this grave matter; but we do urge the government to take a stronger and more courageous stand in line with the other nations which have already given the lead.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be short and to the point as they relate to the items of supplementary estimates that are before us in connection with external affairs. I would commend the minister for the stand he has taken with regard to the situation in Viet Nam. We have just heard an appeal to the minister to be courageous in taking more definite action with regard to that situation. I do not know what courage means here. If it means to surrender our responsibilities to a nation that is being attacked by a communist nation that apparently has no intention but to take over that nation, then I do not think it is courage that is needed; it is just a little bit of common sense. I am sure that all of us are interested in peace and realize that any escalation to all-out war would be disastrous at this time; but, Mr. Chairman, I can find no evidence in history that supports the idea that appeasement will ever result in peace. It has not. Aggression must be blocked. While doing this we must understand that the needs of all parties must be met. However, we cannot, and dare not, appease and allow one nation or one idea to make a slave of another. I think we have that responsibility today in the world as never before.
I was rather impressed by the remarks of the foreign minister of Thailand, a neighbouring country to Viet Nam, who when asked the other day if a negotiated peace was possible in South Viet Nam said, "Who is asking for negotiations? South Viet Nam has not asked for talks. Red China and North Viet Nam are not interested. Their position is perfectly clear. They want control of South Viet Nam and complete and unconditional withdrawal by the United States. What do you negotiate? Complete surrender of South Viet Nam to the communists? If that is your intention, then do not waste money and time negotiating. When one is willing
[Mr. Herridge.l

to surrender, then surrender. It is very easy". Then he went on to say that the United States must continue to support South Viet Nam or withdraw, because talk of a negotiated peace is impossible until both sides are willing to deal honourably with each other in such negotiation.
Some peacemongers at work in the world today are actually running the risk of bringing tragedy to the world. Therefore I believe that the policy the government has been following these past weeks is the only logical policy that one can follow; although I would encourage the minister to take the initiative in the two developing opportunities that seem to be before us at the present time. Just today the government of Great Britain called for the views of 11 other nations who are directly interested in the situation in Viet Nam. I think that here is an excellent opportunity, Mr. Chairman, for Canada to express itself clearly on the principle that appeasement settles nothing, but that every possible attempt should be made toward negotiation. I am convinced that red China is going to have to face up-and North Viet Nam as well- to the fact that there is a point beyond which they cannot go in their ambitions to take over more territory, bringing it under their sphere of influence. As they realize this, there is going to be more opportunity for negotiation, particularly if there is pressure from influential nations of the world. I think the call of Great Britain is an opportunity. It is to be noted here that the socialist government of Great Britain have been very careful to assess the situation in Viet Nam and have expressed their support for what is going on there at the present time, as it relates to the aggressive intentions of North Viet Nam, albeit they are willing and intend to do everything to bring about an honourable negotiation, not just an appeasement.
I would think, also, that the suggestion that has come today from the United States itself, with regard to the avenue of the United Nations and using the secretary general himself in personal diplomacy, should be explored and I would hope that Canada would encourage U Thant to take such action if there is any possibility of its bringing any degree of honourable negotiation. This is something for which many people seem to have lost hope for since the 1954 Geneva conference, because certainly there has not been very much honour in keeping those commitments which related to the respect of the territorial boundaries of South Viet Nam. So, Mr. Chairman, without prolonging this

point at all I would say that I believe the minister is taking the right stand. I would encourage him to move forward and use Canada's initiative and good will to do whatever is possible to bring about a satisfactory settlement of this problem before it does reach a proportion where it is completely out of hand and cannot be controlled.
There is another point as it relates to the supplementary estimates that are before us. I refer to Africa. I think it is opportune to take a few minutes at this time to mention this matter. The situation in Africa is far from calm and settled. There are many critical areas, even though Africa has not been so much in the news these last few weeks as it was earlier in the year. But I am concerned, as I look over the estimates themselves and as they relate to the two twelfths approval that these supplementary estimates are intended to give, that there has been no provision for the expansion of our own diplomatic representation in some very vital areas of Africa.
I am speaking particularly now of the country of Ethiopia, although I am not thinking only of the nation of Ethiopia itself, but also of those pan-African organizations which have their headquarters in Addis Ababa. There are three very important organizations today in Africa which are going to be concerned most vitally in the future with the political and economic development of that continent. The first is the organization of African unity, now having 35 members representing the independent African states. The responsibility of this organization in bringing about a peaceful solution to the political problems of Africa cannot be emphasized too much. In addition to this there is the United Nations agency, the economic commission for Africa, also located in Addis Ababa. This organization having been in existence now for a number of years is doing a very commendable job in trying to bring about coordination in the economic development of this vast continent.
In addition to this there is the new organization, the African development bank, which has its temporary headquarters in Addis Ababa, later to be established in West Africa at Abadan. The presence of these three panAfrican organizations presents not only a responsibility to us and the country of Ethiopia, but also an opportunity for us in our own interest in that continent. Canada is doing a very commendable job in many areas of the continent. We understand that our resources are not such that we can have an
Supply-External Affairs aid program of the size which would reach across to meet even a small part of the overall needs of that continent; nevertheless, Canada does have a very important role.
It is necessary that priorities be established quickly so that we can meet those opportunities in a most effective way, in light of the resources we have, through our external aid program. This means that the planning for the future development of the present programs must be co-ordinated with these various organizations in order to obtain the maximum effect from them.
To do this I think it is necessary for our Department of External Affairs, and specifically the department of external aid, to have direct and constant liaison with these organizations, particularly as they plan for the future and as they attempt to establish areas of the greatest priority need.
It seems to me that one of the immediate projects the government should consider in their external aid expansion program is the establishment of direct diplomatic relationships with Ethiopia on the basis that our representative there would be able to provide that liaison I am speaking about, with this very important pan-African organization.
One of the main things we do not have in our aid program in an area like Africa is over-all supervision and co-ordination between the various aspects. Again this would be a logical area for that kind of supervision, when thinking of the necessary liaison and co-ordination which should exist with these pan-African organizations.
