I was interested when looking at the estimates to see that in respect of a small country like the Cameroons, where we have a total staff I think of 13 including both the national and Canadian staff, the cost of the mission there is about six times the value of the trade that takes place between our countries. I am not suggesting there should not be diplomatic representation with a country like the Cameroons, but it does seem that we are not putting our priorities in the right order when, investing that kind of money in a small country, we neglect any representation at all with a very large country such as Ethiopia, which is at the very hub or centre of the political and economical picture of Africa. These various pan-African organizations are located in such a position, and I suggest to the minister that one of the first things that should be done as far as this year's external aid program is concerned is to extend diplomatic recognition to that country, because our representatives there

Supply-External Affairs would be performing an important twofold purpose. Not only would they be developing the traditional ties of friendship that have existed between the countries, they would also be able to provide that liaison with the O.A.U. and the E.C.A. which is necessary, and at the same time assist in over-all coordination and supervision of our aid programs on that continent.
I speak on this subject now because its importance is such that we should not wait to act on it until we are further along in next session's business. Certainly I would agree with the hon. member for Oxford that general world conditions are such that we require at least a day early in the next session to have a full-scale debate. On the other hand, it is also important that the government move ahead with some of those priority things which are before us. It is very easy to get lost in the pressures of our responsibilities to the United Nations, the peacekeeping operations, in the difficult situations that are developing, and in the planning that is inherent in our association with NATO, not to mention those areas of Cyprus and Viet Nam. But we must not let the immensity of these tasks prevent us from carrying on our other responsibilities in respect of such areas as Africa.
Mr. Chairman, I will not speak any further at this time, but again I should like to say 1 do appreciate the policy which the government has been following in regard to both the situation in Cyprus and the situation in Viet Nam, in recognition of the fact that we must, while following this policy, do everything possible to bring about an honourable settlement, keeping in mind that our purpose is not just to combat communism from a negative standpoint but to show the emerging countries that Canada in its privileged position is interested in doing something to meet the needs of people whether or not they are behind the iron curtain or the bamboo curtain. We realize our responsibilities to each other as human beings and must use our influence to assist in bringing about peaceful settlements to the problems that are now before us.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to the second last item of vote Id, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs what kind of wedding gift has been offered to Queen Anne Marie of Greece for which $1,500 has been allocated?
Is the hon. member waiting for the minister to reply?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands would make his contribution to this debate while the minister is looking for the material in answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes.
Mr. Chairman, while I am waiting for an answer from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I am pleased to let the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) begin his remarks.

I will not take up too much time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, as I do not propose to delve into the political background of the situation in Viet Nam, or attempt to assess blame, particularly in light of developments which have taken place in the last two days-and I refer to the presentation of the unaligned nations by the ministers of Yugoslavia and the United Arab Republic, and the request by the British government for some assistance from Canada and the ten other nations in respect of possible grounds for negotiating a settlement, using the offices of the secretary general of the United Nations.
This might lead one to hope that we may now move toward negotiating a settlement in this area, but I do think there is one other important thing before us which involves a moral question. In spite of these rather hopeful and encouraging signs we are appalled by these events which are continuing in North Viet Nam, including the use of the napalm bomb, the phosphorus bomb, that particularly hellish new invention which scatters thousands of razor-sharp pieces of metal, and the burning of the large forests. These things are still taking place and it seems to me that Canada's voice should be raised in opposition to and in rebuke of this kind of behaviour. I cannot think of any conditions or any political aim that could possibly justify the frying of human beings with napalm, the burning of human beings with phosphorus and the bombing of human beings with high explosives in order to obtain an ideological advantage. This seems to me to involve a supreme moral question.
I am quite sure that the Secretary of State for External Affairs joins with the many hundreds of thousands of Canadians in the

shame and horror we feel in respect of these events which are taking place in southeast Asia. I know he will tell us that he is obliged to adopted his present cautious stand because our friends are involved, and that we must not do anything that would in any way embarrass that friend and neighbour, the United States. This strikes me as being a very strange concept of friendship. To me, a friend is a man who will tell me when he thinks I am wrong, who is prepared to rebuke me if he thinks I am in error, and is still my friend. I know of no occasion when a lickspittle was ever able to be a worth-while friend, and with all due respect to the Secretary of State for External Affairs there are many Canadians today who feel with dismay that our government is presenting Canada and Canadians to the United States in the light of lickspittles instead of a real friend of our neighbours to the south of us.
I think we have an obligation to the millions of decent, honourable Americans who are today dismayed at what is being done in their name in southeast Asia, and it does seem to me they have the right to expect from Canada a voice of warning and caution about the continued use of these particularly damnable weapons against a largely unarmed people, with men, women and children being destroyed in this evil and savage war. I think this can be done not only without detracting from our friendship with the United States but rather it could very well reinforce it because the United States would then realize that they had a real friend, a friend that is not afraid to speak out when it becomes obvious that the authorities in the United States, or some of them, are outraging the conscience of the world in this particular endeavour in southeast Asia. I would hope that if these negotiations are long delayed and if these savage attacks are continued by the United States, Canadians may have the satisfaction of seeing the spokesmen of their government have the courage to stand up and speak out against these inhuman atrocities.

I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question? I have heard his remarks today and I have also heard reports of the remarks made by the leader of his party the night before last in which he said to the United States: Brother, you are wrong. What I should like to know is whether the hon. member thinks the United States is wrong in continuing the resistance against aggression, or is it merely wrong in the methods it is using? I would appreciate
Supply-External Affairs it very much if the hon. member would clear that up.

I would be very glad to. As I said, I did not intend to go into the question of the political aspects, but if one looks into the matter he finds that the scale of retaliation, if you wish to call it that, against North Vietnamese aggression, which no one denies -it has been an aggression of infiltration, not of very large magnitude, into South Viet Nam-is out of all proportion and totally unnecessary to hold the situation in southeast Asia, and for that reason I say it should be condemned.

Mr. Chairman, I realize that all of us are anxious to terminate this session, but the fact remains that a debate on this question should have taken place days ago. We in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition have frequently asked the government to set aside a day to discuss this very important matter, because it is one upon which I would have thought the government would have welcomed the views of members generally. However, that was not to be. Request after request for a debate on the subject has been met by qualified promises and nebulous affirmations.
I rise merely for the purpose of saying that I should not like the views of the gallant and hon. member for Kootenay West or of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands to go forth as the general view of the members of this house. So far as the hon. member for Kootenay West is concerned, he is one of those to whom I listen at all times with great respect. He is a man of fearless speech. His courage is known to all of us. But those qualities do not always assure complete objectivity in the conclusions reached by those possessing such qualities.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands who used some very strong language. He never expresses himself with uncertainty. He always uses language that will secure headlines. Such words can easily be found in books of antonyms and synonyms. His expression a few moments ago about the United States and the conduct of that nation was not such as to earn for him the description of a frank and fearless friend. Through the years I have contended that Canada ought not to be the tail on the American kite, but those who express themselves in such extravagant language do not contribute to a solution of a serious prob-

Supply-External Affairs lem, one that merits the objective consideration of members no matter what their party.
Through the years I have tried to come to a general consensus of agreement with the government of the day on those things that affect the nation internationally. I said a moment ago that I was not one who accepted stands taken by the United States regardless of their merit. Often it was made clear to me when I was prime minister that stands Canada was taking were not acceptable to the administration in the United States, and I made it perfectly clear that Canada would take the course that in Canada's opinion was the right one. We were criticized for that. We suffered the importation from the United States of extraterritorial assistance to the Liberal party in two elections as a result of our stand.
But the fact that I contended over and over again for a policy for Canada in keeping with Canada's position and responsibilities does not mean that I would resort to grandiloquent and vituperative language to describe the conduct of the United States. It stands in southeast Asia today in a position which no other nation in the world would like to occupy. They are suffering the casualties and pouring out their blood and treasure.
I have not got notes of the adjectival recriminations that the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands used with regard to the stand of the United States, but he did use strong words such as "inhuman", "outrageous" and "savage". These words always hit the headlines. He said Canada should speak as a good friend of the United States; that it should condemn what is taking place. I ask him, why is it that the socialist government of Great Britain, with all the experience that Britain has had in hundreds of years of diplomacy, is not speaking the way this socialist party in the House of Commons is? Do you think Britain would not speak out if the descriptive words used by the hon. gentleman were based on other than oratorical affectation?
No one likes the situation that prevails there. When he was asked a question by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, he rather softened his position. He said he believed that the scale of retaliation was out of all proportion. This is an argument that one can understand, an argument that appeals. I tell you quite frankly that I believe the United States made a psychological error in the use of lachrymal gas. I cannot understand that. I say that it is a rather strange thing that the use of gas took place without the knowledge of the President of the United States, the commander in chief of the armed


forces. This frightens me, for if military commanders in the field can do this, what is to stop them from going farther and using atomic or nuclear weapons? I still believe in the adage that war is too important for generals; in other words, that governments have a responsibility to watch the progress that is made and the recommendations made by those in the armed forces.
We have not been able to find out what Canada has done. We have been told that the matter is receiving close and careful consideration. Mention was made of what the United Nations might do. The United Nations cannot do very much. The United Nations, in consequence of the adjournment by reason of the failure of several of the nations to discharge their responsibilities under the charter, is today an emasculated body in international affairs. If the United Nations were sitting today, something might be done. I am not suggesting this as a means, but it has been suggested that the United Nations might make South Viet Nam a United Nations trust territory for a limited period of seven to ten years. This would certainly give an opportunity for the cooling off of passions.
However, it cannot be done today. The United Nations can do nothing. It adjourned, not because it did not have anything to do but because it knew it could not do it without a vote, and to have a vote would have meant a confrontation between the nations in the United Nations. So far as the secretary general is concerned, whatever the benefit of his services may be, if he goes into southeast Asia he will not have behind him the prestige and authority of a body that might be effective, if it were actually sitting.
Now, it is a popular thing to say how wrong the United States is. One would almost think that the forces in North Viet Nam were all saints; that they have no thought of aggression. They do not realize that they have along that north boundary line eight or more divisions of Chinese communist troops that regularly feed so-called volunteers into North Viet Nam. I think we should look at the record. One of the things that impresses me is the attitude of North Viet Nam. One of the reasons that country has proceeded in the way it has was revealed in May of 1962 when the military forces of the government of Viet Nam captured a number of Viet Cong documents. One of these documents contained instructions from the provincial committee of the Lao Dong party, the communist party, to the party's

district committees concerning formation of the new people's revolutionary party.
It read as follows:
In regard to the foundation of the people's revolutionary party of South Viet Nam, the creation of this party is only a matter of strategy; it needs to be explained within the party; and, to deceive the enemy, it is necessary that the new party be given the outward appearance corresponding to a division of the party (Lao Dong) into two and the foundation of a new party, so that the enemy cannot use it in his propaganda.
Within the party, it is necessary to explain that the founding of the people's revolutionary party has the purpose of isolating the Americans and the Ngo Dinh Diem regime, and to counter their accusations of an invasion of the south by the north. It is a means of supporting our sabotage of the Geneva agreement, of advancing the plan of invasion of the south, and at the same time permitting the front for liberation of the south to recruit new adherents, and to gain the sympathy of non-aligned countries in southeast Asia.
Then, later it reads:
During these explanations, take care to keep this strictly secret, especially in South Viet Nam, so that the enemy does not perceive our purpose ...
Do not put these explanations in party bulletins.
Well, that is what has happened. What should we do? As I say, the United Nations cannot do anything that will be effective. It has been placed in a position in vacuo, as a body for peace by the policy of the U.S.S.R., its satellites and one or two other nations who will not pay their just contributions. What is to be done? There remains only the question of negotiation. The United Kingdom today is not following the flamboyantly incendiary ideas of the socialist party in Canada. The United Kingdom has suggested that there should be a reconvening of the Geneva conference provided certain conditions are achieved, and it asks a number of nations to give their views on what those conditions should be. I should like to hear from the minister what condition Canada believes should be imposed as a condition precedent to the convening of the conference. Certainly, the convening of the conference without an agreement in advance of certain conditions will be simply to add chaos to the serious situation that already prevails. All of us desire peace but we will not bring peace about by a campaign of propaganda, of abuse of one nation that stands today in the position that Great Britain stood for so many generations in all parts of the world.
I had no idea of rising to take part in this debate, but having heard the speech of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands I could only say I would have been recreant to my position as member of par-
Supply-External Affairs liament to have sat silent and allowed his message to go out as representative of the general view of parliament.
We want peace. What can be done to that end I have not heard anyone say as yet. If we could get to the negotiating table and there was any hope that negotiation would succeed, then indeed progress would be made; but we cannot get to the negotiating table unless North Viet Nam decides to end its policy of insurrection, attack and infiltration. If North Viet Nam will but give that assurance I am sure there would be little delay in the convening of a conference that all mankind hopes will be convened at the earliest possible date. All of us recognize that if the situation continues as it has for the last few months, in particular during the last two months, such a conference cannot be long delayed, else what is happening will gradually explode into a conflagration that will envelop nations far removed from southeast Asia.
Stand the Americans must, on the basis of the undertakings and commitments they accepted. If they do not stand and simply walk out then, as the hon. member for Oxford asked today, what happens? What happens in Malaysia, our commonwealth ally? What happens to Thailand; what to Burma; what to the Philippines?
It is so easy to sit here and criticize, and say what is being done is wrong, but the great problem that faces world statesmen today is what can be done. All I see Canada can do at this time is to make her voice known to the freedom loving nations of the world, calling upon them to negotiate and, at the same time, exerting whatever influence she can on the U.S.S.R., and also on France, to do their respective parts to secure approval by the Hanoi administration of a discontinuance of its belligerent activities. That done, we at least have a basis upon which to go forward. Undone, we face an accelerating position of grave danger, not only in Asia but generally throughout the world.

Mr. Chairman, I think the last hour or two demonstrates the great unwisdom of not having a debate on external affairs at this vital time. I am just going to mention a couple of items, one of them complimentary to the minister and one critical.
We are a little concerned in Canada that foreign policy has lost the elan, dash and momentum it used to have in earlier days, and we wonder why. I am personally dis-

Supply-External Affairs appointed in the minister's seeming inability to carry through his once obvious interest in the Latin American region. I had thought we would see the day when he as minister, and his chief as Prime Minister, would lead this country into the organization of American states. I have had my speech of congratulation ready for two years on that subject. I am not going to destroy it, but I am putting it further and further back into my files because I do not expect to be using it now.
Under both the minister's predecessors great things were done in the Latin American region, and great appreciation was obvious in Latin America for what Canada was doing. Now I feel the momentum has been lost, particularly in the region which was formerly the British West Indies islands, in which I feel we have a great opportunity and tremendous responsibility. If we get to another session I am going to make a more prolonged plea to the minister to take initiative there, and for Canada to take initiative there.
I would also like to say that I am reminded of what took place in 1940 in the British house of commons when, in an era of appeasement, the leader of the opposition was called upon to speak for England. I believe that on the question that was discussed in this chamber during the last three quarters of an hour the Leader of the Opposition spoke for Canada. He spoke for many, many more Canadians than those members of the New Democratic party, who made their remarks before he expressed his cogent, reasonable and tremendously pertinent views. This is another reason why we should have had debate.
It is all very well to say the voice of Canada should be raised, but the voices I have been hearing of late have been those voices that are quite ready to sit in righteous judgment upon the United States for their internal policies, and especially for their external policies. There always seems to be an open season upon the United States in certain quarters in this country. I remember the people of the left wing in Canada who used to talk about these gentle agrarian reformers sweeping down from north China. Always the more tender support is shown to those of the north in Asia. But one essential fact we must never forget is that we in Canada gain nothing when the United States is embarrassed, and certainly we are not furthering Canadian foreign policy by irresponsible utterances which make the United States' great task all the more difficult.


I do not think the government or the minister-and here is where I am going to speak on his side-has shown through the Viet Nam crisis any tendency to portray our country as a lickspittle. He has shown himself a friend of the greatest friend of peace the world has, namely the United States of America, and we should remind ourselves occasionally of the tremendous burdens which the American people bear.
No country in the world has ever undertaken, for so long a period, the burdens of maintaining peace in such a far flung world. To put it in the area which is much less important than the human area, one thinks of the tremendous burdens on the American taxpayers, year after year after year, bearing burdens in all parts of the world, and quite often the only gratitude is, "Yank, go home," or the occasional self-righteous criticism of those who should be their friends.
As the Leader of the Opposition mentioned, far more important is the human suffering. Who bore the greatest burden in Korea? Who is bearing the burden in South Viet Nam? Who is always called upon to man the ramparts when freedom is assailed-and freedom is always assailed? These "gentle" people in North Viet Nam are those who precipitated these difficulties. Putting it very simply, if they would refrain from incursions upon their southern neighbours-and in this context I recall North Korea and South Korea-these problems would not arise.
I do not know how I or any of my colleagues can judge with too great finiteness the use of gas. I notice that a member of the United Kingdom house of commons asked yesterday: Is it worse to make your enemy cry or die? I think perhaps we do not have sufficient information. No party in this house has a monopoly of virtue or concern for human life, no matter how strenuous are the efforts to carve out such a monopoly. I feel that reckless criticism of the United States ill serves our foreign policy and ill serves the cause of peace. In this connection I commend the minister's constant retraint, often in the face of provocation. Knowing that he represents people who are deeply devoted to peaceful processes, he has never attempted to gain momentary publicity by striking out recklessly at the United States upon whose exertions the cause of freedom so largely depends. On this I congratulate him.

The remarks I had intended to make, Mr. Chairman, have been much better

phrased by the Leader of the Opposition and by my hon. friend from Queens. The reason I put a question to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was this: I wanted to find out what was the real attitude and policy of the New Democratic party with regard to this situation. Listening to reports of the speech made by the leader of that party in Toronto on Wednesday night I came to the conclusion that he was assailing the United States and in favour of the communist forces of the north. If this is what the leader of the New Democratic party intended to say, and if this is the attitude supported by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands I think the people should know, because that is not the general feeling of people in this country. If it is not what he intended to say, then I think he should correct it, and that right quickly.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I could deal with a number of questions which have been asked before addressing myself to the main subject we have been discussing.

In answer to the question put by the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Drouin), Canada presented Queen Anne Marie with a mink stole.

The hon. member for Oxford asked me a number of questions. One of them concerned government policy with regard to the suggestion that Canada assume responsibility for the operation and maintenance of the air force of Tanzania. This question has been before the government for a few days. We have sent a communication to President Nyerere. Our ambassador has advised us that the president will not be back in his country until Monday. I hope we will soon be in receipt of a reply from him regarding the matter. We would then be able to announce our policy, I would hope, before the middle of next week.
With regard to Indonesia, the situation still stands. We have not sent any wheat flour to that country although we are continuing, as the hon. member knows, our aid under the technical assistance program to some 40 students from that country who are studying in Canada.
With regard to the $200,000 for telegrams, telephones and travel on the part of the supervisory commission in Viet Nam, the explanation is that we have provided $100,000 in our main estimates. Our expenditures to December 31 amounted to $223,000. The sup-20220-829

External Affairs plementary estimate is intended to replace the $100,000 borrowed to take care of telegram costs to December 31 and to provide $100,000 for costs to March 31, 1965.
Most of these costs are recoverable, of course, as the hon. member knows, from the international commission itself. There has naturally been an increase because of events in Indochina during the past few months; we have been anxious to be fully informed on the important developments taking place there.

Would the hon. gentleman permit one question in this regard? The figure of $200,000 is mentioned under the heading of the supervisory commission for Indochina but there is another $200,000 under "departmental administration". Altogether this makes more than $400,000. Is it all the same thing, really? It seems more than a coincidence that the items should be identical.

These are estimates, of course. They cannot be anything other than estimates.
The hon. member for Kootenay West spoke today about the problem which is of concern not only to Canada but to all countries at the present time-the situation in Viet Nam. He said I should not look at this question as being black and white. I fully agree with him. This important question does not lend itself to simplification and cannot be looked at as if the issues involved were black and white. But the hon. member will, I hope, pardon me if I say that the position which he and his party have taken on this matter does suggest that, in their minds, the position may be resolved by looking at it as if it were either black or white.
The leader of the New Democratic party said the other day in this house, and outside, that we in Canada had taken a one-sided position-that we appeared to be protagonists of the United States, and that our true role should be one of objective assessment and that we should have the courage to take a position regarding this highly dangerous situation in the light of our friendship with the United States, as he put it, and pursuant to a desire to bring about peace in the area. I cannot agree that we have taken anything but a balanced position on this question. I do not quarrel with the statement which the right hon. gentleman, the leader of the official opposition made today on Viet Nam. I agree with his interpretation of the situation in Viet Nam as he described it a few moments ago. That, too, was a balanced position. I

Supply-External Affairs am glad to know, too, that the hon. member for Queens is also of the opinion that the Canadian government has adopted a balanced position, taking into account not only the circumstances in Indochina at the moment but the circumstances as they have evolved since the Geneva conference was held in 1954. I agree with the right hon. gentleman and others that a matter of this sort does warrant discussion in this house.
It is not without significance that the first debate on this question in the British house of commons took place only yesterday and that there was a discussion this week in the Storthing in Norway, and only a few days ago in Denmark and in Holland as well. I would ask those who criticize what I call the balanced position the Canadian government is taking, which seemingly is supported by the great majority of the members of this house, to remember that it is consistent, as the hon. gentleman observed a few moments ago, with the position taken by a socialist government in the United Kingdom. It is worth recalling some of the things that were said yesterday by Mr. Stewart in his first statement as foreign secretary of Great Britain. Speaking of Viet Nam, he said, and I am now quoting from page 4 of today's New York Times:
Some people, he said, keep suggesting that the Viet Nam problem could be solved if the United States just withdrew.
"That solution has the merit of simplicity", Mr. Stewart said, but it would reward "aggression from the north" and "would be regarded with profound alarm by all the non-communist countries in that part of the world".
He rejected any thought that the United States was pressing the war too far by bombing the north.
I would point out, by way of parenthesis, that at no time have I ever made a statement that went as far as this:
It is too much to ask people to sit and be attacked without any recourse, he said, and he mentioned some restrained words by President Johnson.
"On the evidence in the record", he said, "I think it would be quite wrong to argue that the action of the United States is the action of a country engaged in reckless escalation of warfare".
Nor is it permissible, Mr. Stewart said, to speak of "cruelties" by the anti-communist side alone.
He said the Viet Cong had killed innocent civilians in South Viet Nam at the rate of more than 2,000 a year.
Whether one agrees with this position, the fact is that the government of Great Britain, a socialist government, has in the light of its consultations and the information available to it taken a position that is generally consistent with the position which we take here, which has been taken in Australia, in New

Zealand and which, interestingly enough, is being taken in the Scandinavian countries as well. I have before me a statement made the day before yesterday by Mr. Halvard Lange, the foreign minister of Norway, a country not looked upon as warranting the suggestion that it blindly follows the foreign policy of our great neighbour. The position taken by Mr. Lange is along the lines we have taken. It is consistent with the policy enunciated by the prime minister of Denmark and by the foreign minister of Holland as well.
No one for a moment thinks that this is an easy situation. No one can help but be filled with dismay every time we hear of bombing in Viet Nam. None of us likes war. We are all convinced now that war is an anachronism. We know perfectly well that a war, certainly of the dimensions of warfare today, is not calculated to achieve the kind of victory which at an earlier period it was assumed warfare could bring about. This situation has to be understood in the light of events that have brought the United States into South Viet Nam.
We have before us, on our table, the majority report of the commission of 1962, a report supported by Canada and by India. We have the minority report of Canada of February 13 last which, in the words of Mr. Wilson, the prime minister of Great Britain, presents a balanced view of the facts in that divided country. We have got to recall the circumstances which brought the United States into South Viet Nam. In 1954 the Geneva powers determined that until such time as there could be free elections, until such time as there could be unification of North and South Viet Nam, each territory would be regarded as having the attributes of sovereignty. From 1954 up until about two years ago there was one form of government there. Whether we agree with its totalitarian or quasi totalitarian methods is beside the question. There was a government in control of the situation in South Viet Nam; a government that had harboured over one million refugees, whom I visited in 1956, who had come from the north. This government, in its effort to resist infiltration and aggression from the north, called upon the United States to give it defence support. No one can suggest that the intervention of the United States in these circumstances is illegal. This kind of assistance is pursuant to article 52 of the charter of the United Nations. Successive governments in South Viet Nam have asked the United States to continue to assist them to meet agression, infiltration

from the north, and armed resistance by the Viet Cong in the south.
News of bombings of course is disturbing; but so, I would remind my hon. friends who take issue with the government's position, is the chronicle of communist murder and armed attacks against innocent civilians which form the pattern of activity of what is called a "liberation" struggle. Our own observers have established the fact of North Vietnamese interference in South Viet Nam. It is not just an internal rebellion plain and simple. It contains, certainly, domestic South Vietnamese elements, but without North Vietnamese encouragement, supply and direction, it would not have had the same strength. The division of Viet Nam into communist and non-communist halves results from native political forces; this I admit. However, this difficulty is not a creation of the west; its continued existence represents the conviction of those Vietnamese who were concerned that a communist Viet Nam under Ho Chi Minh would be little more than a province of China, a fate which the Vietnamese people have feared and rejected throughout their history. At Geneva in 1954 both North and South Viet Nam had separate representation. The South Vietnamese at that time refused to accept the political aspects of the Geneva settlement as inimical to the interests of the Vietnamese people. Violations of the Geneva accord were begun following aggression by the north in the early part of 1955. This is the conclusion of the majority and the minority reports of the commission of 1962 and of February 13 last.
When it became clear that the south was not going to fall under northern control as the result of elections which would not have been fairly carried out, the north decided that a more aggressive policy would be needed to accomplish its ends, and whether we like to admit it or not, the fact is that through terrorization of villages and the deliberate assassination of local administrators the Viet Cong established control over wide areas of the countryside. Local support of guerrillas obtained in this way is scarcely the same as spontaneous expression by electoral choice.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot understand the attitude that suggests in this situation that the United States, our neighbour, a country with whom Canada must have and has such close association, must be assumed to be regarded as the villain in the piece. Hon. gentlemen assumed right from the beginning that the fault lay on the doorstep of the United States. I suggest there was no objective assessment made of the contemporary history of this situation. Had there been I am sure this conclusion could not have been reached.
The United States is, as the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) observed, bearing a heavy responsibility. It is not only assisting South Viet Nam in this struggle, but because of its armed superiority, because of the pre-eminent position as one of the five great powers, sharing with the Soviet union at the moment pre-eminence in the field of arms, it is defending the free world to an extent greater than any other country. When I say it is defending the free world and defending freedom I am speaking of Canada as well as Asia.
It is easy for us to brand the United States action as imperialism of a U.S. type, but I suggest that it is as the result of United States strength in the military field that many millions of people in the world today, in the light of events since the end of the second world war, are able to enjoy the freedom they now possess.
I am not suggesting that United States policy in this situation is right in every particular. As the right hon. gentleman said, speaking as a former prime minister, we have taken issue-his government and this government-with the United States on important matters of foreign policy. We took issue with them in the matter of trade with China, we took issue with them on a number of other matters. We do not fully agree with every aspect of their policy in this particular situation; but I suggest that one of the responsibilities of a government, in charge of the affairs of a country so closely related geographically and otherwise to the United States, is to consider and exercise care over any disagreement with the United States in a matter of such importance, in the light of our own national interest. This is an elementary principle in the foreign policy of any country. If my hon. friends were sitting here on Mr. Speaker's right, they would take the

Supply-External Affairs same position we, and the present government of Great Britain, are taking.
Great Britain is taking this position not only because of the general reasons applicable to United States foreign policy in Indochina, but because it is part and parcel of Britain's own interest to examine very carefully any situation which would cause a breach between Britain and the United States.
Mr. Chairman, Viet Nam is a test case; I suggest that if the North Vietnamese aggression with Chinese connivance succeeds, it will only be a matter of time before the next victim is selected. The issue then concerns the security, integrity and independence of small nations not only in Asia but all over the world. If the United States were to leave Viet Nam at the present time, what would happen to that country? What would happen to Burma? What would happen to India, a commonwealth country? What would happen to Malaysia, a commonwealth country? What would happen to the Philippines, and what would happen to those island countries of Australia and New Zealand? What would be the position of Japan? These are considerations that must be borne in mind by anyone who simplifies the problem in the way that my friend, the hon. member for Kootenay West, has sought to simplify this complicated problem.
An exclusive military response to the challenge that faces the United States is, of course, admittedly dangerous and inadequate. I suggest that we have never been able to successfully dispute how dangerous it would be to surrender to communist aggression. But surely a middle course can be charted.
Our first objective in Canada is to continue appealing for a cease fire by all concerned. We have done that right from the beginning. Second, we must find a way to bring about negotiations, and this requires a will to negotiate on both sides. The President of the United States, in the most recent statement that I have had made available to me, said that he and his officials would do anything that any honourable man could do to negotiate. I am not aware of any similar statement or any statement along those lines having been made by those in charge of operations in the north, or by those who direct the fighting that is going on by the Viet Cong in the south. There is no evidence, I repeat, of any disposition on the part of Hanoi to stop their aggression, to stop their infiltration or to agree to a cease fire, and to give consideration to what conditions might be discussed in order to bring about a con-
IMr. Martin (Essex East).]
ference which might lead to a peace in Viet Nam.
My hon. friend said that we must have peace. I agree we must have peace; but to get peace in this situation requires more than one party. Negotiation requires at least two sides, and it takes a manifest willingness to avoid provocation, and a desire to reach compromise. I ask my hon. friends what alternative they have offered. Do they suggest that the government of South Viet Nam should lay down arms, that the government of the United States should withdraw its forces and that they should leave the situation in Viet Nam entirely to the Viet Cong? If that is the course they propose, and that is the only alternative apparent from the position they take, then they do render insecure those friendly countries with whom we have close ties in Asia, as well as other countries with whom we maintain satisfactory relations.
Would the minister allow a question? Will he tell the house the conditions precedent that he thinks should be applied?

As far as Canada is concerned, Mr. Chairman, we have said that we ask for a cease fire and evidence that a cease fire will be observed. In the appeal that has been made to Canada and other countries by the Belgrade powers, the suggestion is that there should be no preconditions posed by any one of the belligerents. We are not imposing any preconditions at present.
I have seen a suggestion that the United States takes the position that not only must there be a cease fire but there must be a withdrawal of the Viet Cong from the south and evidence of a willingness on the part of the north to avoid aggression and infiltration. I am not aware from anything I know that this is the official position taken by the United States, but we have had no indication whatsoever of any kind from the north as to what conditions it would impose before laying down its arms.
Mr. Gromyko, the foreign minister of the Soviet union representing one of the cochairmen, met the other day in London with Mr. Stewart, the British foreign secretary representing the other co-chairman, and refused-I am not critizing the Soviet union for this refusal for certain reasons-to join with Great Britain in an appeal to all parties to agree to a cease fire. I suspect that one of the reasons for this refusal is the knowledge that such action could not be expected to come from the north at this particular time.

I am satisfied that if Hanoi were to show any willingness to desist from provocative acts and to cease its aggression against South Viet Nam the United States would respond in kind. Unfortunately there have been no signs that the Hanoi authorities and their friends in Peking are prepared to talk in preference to fighting. They have repeatedly rejected the idea of negotiations, demanding instead a unilateral United States withdrawal. More flexibility than this would be required if negotiations are to take place.
We have been asked what we are doing in this situation. This is a fair question to ask. We have a responsibility, not only arising out of our membership on the international control and supervisory commission but because, like any civilized community, we abhor war and wish to make our contribution toward reducing its possibilities and its existence. We have been engaged in the fullest possible diplomatic negotiations with the United States, with Great Britain and with other countries. We would have liked to be able to have direct contact with the other side so that we could express the same views we have expressed to our friends in private, in the kind of negotiation essential to achieve results.
I said the other day that our representative on the commission, because of the fact that he is on the commission, has access both to the authorities in Saigon and in Hanoi. Within the past six or seven weeks he has had two contacts with Hanoi as well as a continuing contact with Saigon. We have made our views known as well to the secretary general of the United Nations. We have discussed with him ways and means of trying to bring about a cease fire under conditions, however, that are not going to leave the people of South Viet Nam to a merciless fate. That we cannot agree to for the reasons I have already stated. To give in under those circumstances would be merely to postpone a similar experience, when the situation facing the people of South Viet Nam would erupt elsewhere, perhaps in Thailand or in some other country in southeast Asia.
Our approach to the problem of a peaceful settlement has had a threefold objective. The first has been to contribute wherever possible to creating conditions for negotiation. For example, it might be possible to balance off the preconditions stipulated by the two sides as a basis for settlement. It might also be possible, as I suggested this morning, to take advantage of a conference on Laos, if
Supply-External Affairs one is convened, to help to keep the channels of communication open.
Second, in whatever negotiations come about every effort must be bent toward securing a fair and final settlement. There can be no surrender of the basic principle of the right of any people to choose freely the path they wish to follow in their political and economic development.
Third, a negotiated settlement must provide for an adequate degree of control to ensure that these provisions will not be upset by aggression from outside. We had a conference in 1954 and a division was made of Viet Nam into two parts. A separate, new, sovereign state of Cambodia was set up, and we thought in	1954 we	had	set up	thesovereign state	of Laos.	We	will not besettling this problem, as the right hon. gentleman suggested, if we approach a peace conference ill prepared or if we reach conclusions that are	bound to	be	ignored	andviolated before	almost at	once. This	was
done in 1954. The agreement had no sooner been signed than aggression began from the north. Those are the facts and no one who has studied those facts or has read the reports of the commission can come to any other conclusion.
Canada favours a settlement of this problem that would set up an independent or neutral Viet Nam or, if the country cannot be unified, a neutral South Viet Nam and a neutral North Viet Nam. But in order to give substance to this objective of a neutral or independent community we have to envisage the kind of guarantees that would guarantee such independence or neutrality. The Prime Minister has made the suggestion that there is to be found in the international community a responsibility to provide for the guarantee which I am sure would be insisted upon by the United States and by South Viet Nam.
What would that guarantee consist of? We would like to see the United Nations used for this purpose. The peacekeeping machinery of the United Nations has been used on other occasions. It has kept the peace in the Gaza strip for over 10 years. Cyprus is another such situation where peacekeeping operations under the auspices of the United Nations have been established.
But we have to look at the realities facing the United Nations at this time. It is not practical to suggest in the face of differences over article 19 that have divided east and west, an agreement could be reached that would now permit the establishment of a United Nations force in Viet Nam.

In any event, would not the establishment of a force of sufficient size to patrol South Viet Nam and North Viet Nam, with the communist hordes immediately to the north, mean a force so large there could be no hope of recruiting it under the United Nations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would say in response that undoubtedly the fact that China is not a member of the United Nations, that China is such a powerful country and so heavily populated, does present obstacles to this suggestion.
In any event, we all know that no matter how strong a force is provided in a situation like this, the success of such a force depends in the final analysis on the willingness of all parties concerned to give the force an opportunity to carry out its mandate. There could never be established a force that would be comparable, numerically, to the populations that are available to the heavily populated countries of Asia, particularly China.
We have had peacekeeping operations that have been successful. When we think of the situation in the Gaza strip where 4,000 to 5,000 men have kept the peace for ten years, we find in that a precedent and a model, but only because both the United Arab Republic and Israel have been prepared to co-operate with this force which they now recognize as an indispensable factor in the preservation of peace in that area.
If the United Nations is not available, for the reasons I have given, the Canadian suggestion involves a consideration of the contribution that might be made by the international community. This international community might be made up of the countries represented at the Geneva conferences of 1954 and 1962. It may be that this would not be possible. It may be that only a force or a presence made up of Asian countries, would be acceptable to the parties. In any event, what is important is the substance of the suggestion itself. A conference such as we are talking about, such as we hope will take place, could only succeed in its objective if a step were taken to guarantee whatever settlement is made. I am sure that will be insisted upon both by the United States and by South Viet Nam. I would hope it would be supported by China, by North Viet Nam, by the Soviet union and by the other countries whose influence must be considered.

I should like to conclude this statement by saying that we will
continue to use the normal techniques and channels available to us. This we are doing. Our membership in the commission makes Canada an independent witness, and this role we must continue to exercise objectively and impartially. We must insure that our judgments and those of the commission are balanced and equitable. Although there are difficulties in the way of the United Nations playing the role we would like, I do agree that the office of the secretary general is so prestigious it could be used at this time to co-ordinate the efforts that are being made on a wide front.
Finally, I would want the house to know that we, too, on this side realize there is a danger point in this situation. I am satisfied that the government of the United States, with its heavy responsibilities, is equally aware of the danger point. I only hope that our combined efforts will see no violation of the rights of self-determination in the south and, that we will be able to embark on courses that will bring about a settlement in this disturbed area, thereby localizing any possibility of the expansion of a situation that could not only engulf Asia, but if it were allowed to spread could engulf the world.
I wonder if the minister would allow me to ask him a couple of questions in relation to the remarks he has been making?

Let me point out how wonderfully this plan has been evolved. It has all the appearances of bureaucratic short cuts because, after all, bureaucrats do not like parliament.
I hope that having become ministers, they do not carry with them some of the instincts of bureaucracy which they possessed when they occupied high positions in the administration of this country. The point at issue is the attempt to effect legislation by items in the supplementary estimates.
Over the years we have been accustomed to the use of $1 items for various purposes, but that was not the point raised this afternoon. The point raised was the attempt to legislate by the use of supplementary estimates. The President of the Privy Council did not give us instances in the past to support his argument. There have been occasions from time to time when legislation has been modified by a supplementary estimate, and the most recent occurred just last November. When the government finally got around to increasing the payment to disability pensioners and war veterans allowances last November, the house agreed that could go through in the form in which it was presented to us, namely by means of a supplementary estimate, but it should have been by way of amendments to the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act.
But consider the circumstances then. Time was very pressing. We ourselves requested that if the government was going to take this action which had been announced by the Minister of Veterans Affairs it should be done promptly so that the veterans would have their cheques before Christmas. The only time in which to get the action approved by way of a supplementary estimate was during that period of seven days which at my suggestion had been set as a time limit for the consideration of estimates for the year that still remained to be considered. The supplementary estimates came before us during that last week when we were dealing with estimates. It was under those conditions that the house agreed as a special case to permit a statute to be modified by a supplementary estimate. But that is a rare occurrence.
In the supplementary estimates we have before us now the Leader of the Opposition has drawn attention to at least eight instances where the modification of statutes is contemplated, and it is to this procedure that we are objecting. 19d. To authorize the payment out of the superannuation account, in the current and subsequent fiscal years, of interest in respect of contributions made under section 6 of the Public Service Superannuation Act to the account that
(a)	have been on deposit in the account for at least two years from the date of their receipt, and
(b)	cannot be applied for the purpose for which they were originally paid into the account because the election pursuant to which they were made is void;
such interest to be compounded and to be calculated and paid at such rate and in respect of such period as the governor in council may prescribe, $1.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should explain that in the case of deposits byindividuals to the superannuation fund, if the contributors are found to have no right under the fund or withdraw their contributions, under the act as it is now worded, they cannot get any interest if the payment is made after two years. This is to take care of individual cases where people are caught in this kind of situation; that is, there are cases that arise where a contribution may have been made and it is found that the contributor is not eligible to make that contribution and this is not found out until two years after the contribution has been made. It works a hardship, and is something that would appear not to have been contemplated by the act, if that contributor is denied his interest when the contribution is returned after the two year period.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to items 19d and 21d, in both cases this consists of an amendment to a statute. I am not arguing the merits or the reasons why this change should be made; but there is only one way in which we can amend statutes, and that is the legislative way, through parliament, in the ordinary processes. I am not arguing the legitimate reasons for the amendment that has to be made; I am arguing that it should not be done, and must not be done, under the guise of supplementary estimates.
I could ask the minister the simple question: How does subsection (2) of section 32 now read, the subsection that is being repealed? Would the minister say how it now reads, so that we know what we are repealing? The very fact that the minister is
[The Chairman.]
not in a position to do that is indicative of the position of affairs.
I ask him to take the same kind of reasonable attitude that was taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to this -I was going to call it a novelty, but it is more than a novelty; it is a departure from parliamentary practice. It is something that we cannot accept, no matter how desirous we are of getting this session through. We cannot accept a principle whereby a government can come along in supplementary estimates and amend statutes. Let us be reasonable. Bring this in next week, just as soon as the government can. They can introduce it immediately as an amendment; and if it has all the merits the hon. gentleman says it has [DOT]-and no doubt it has those merits-it can be passed in the regular way.
But what is behind this? Why the haste, for a couple of days? Why take parliamentary practice of many years and throw that procedure out the window because there are one or two cases that deserve an ameliorating amendment? If the amendment has to be made, if we passed a bad section, one that was never intended and ought to be altered, let it be altered and let all such alterations be made in the normal, legislative way.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to develop this subject, but if the right hon. gentleman is concerned about this, I would hope he would not press it. I can read section 6 of the superannuation act; but the point here is rather narrower than that raised in some of the other cases. It has to do with the very few employees who were contributors under the superannuation act and who were found not to be eligible to contribute. When their contributions were returned to them, they were denied the interest because their rights were not defined within the two years, or were wrongly defined. It does seem to be an injustice to the two or three individuals concerned. I wonder if the right hon. gentleman would, in the light of what I have said, reconsider his attitude with regard to item 19d, because it seems to me that, notwithstanding what he said about the question of principle, it is really a matter of a few cases of hardship. It could be argued, but I am not going to do it here, since it is a mere accounting item.
Mr. Chairman, is the minister suggesting that item 19d is not an amending procedure?
That is my suggestion.
And that therefore it is different from the point raised by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. With regard to items 18d and 21d he admits that they are amending, but 19d is not?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would like to deal with each separately, Mr. Chairman, but that is precisely my suggestion with regard to 19d.

I will deal with 19d, Mr. Chairman. Is the minister prepared, then, to drop 18d and also 21d? If he is prepared to drop these, then vote 19d is an authorization which I would be prepared to accept. It is not an amendment to a statute but an authorization to provide for an interest rate.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In respect of vote 18d, I am having a check made before giving a firm commitment to drop it. I want to make sure of certain details of information I have. In respect of vote 19d, I think it would be proper to pass it, notwithstanding what the right hon. gentleman has said. I want to say something about vote 2 Id when we reach it because it falls in a different category again.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two about vote 19d. I am aware of an individual who lives in my riding who was improperly advised by members of a department as a result of which he proceeded along an improper course, under the impression that he had some protection under the superannuation act. This supplementary estimate would bar such an individual from having the whole matter discussed.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is based on the supplementary estimates of 1961-62 in respect of the act, and this practice has been followed continuously since then.

Item agreed to.
21d. To amend subsection (5) of section 20 of chapter 38 of the statutes of Canada, 1960 by (a) striking out the expression "before the time he became a contributor" and substituting therefor the expression "before or after the time he became a contributor"; and
(b)	adding, immediately following the expression "failed to elect under that act within the time prescribed therefor", the expression, "or under clause (F) of subparagraph (iii) of paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 5 of the Public Service Superannuation Act", $1.

speechtext: Let this vote stand.
Vote No. 21d should be allowed to stand.

speechtext:
Yes, perhaps we could allow 21d to stand.

22d. To authorize the treasury board to delete from the accounts certain debts due, and claims by, Her Majesty, each of which is in excess of $1,000, amounting in the aggregate to $1,117,485.77, of which $451,991.49 represents 42 items that have been carried as assets in the statement of assets and liabilities, $451,992.

Would the President of the Privy Council give us some indication of the type of debts that are being written off under this item? Some of them may relate to individuals but it is obvious that others would relate to companies.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
These are normal write-offs each year. Perhaps I could pick out an example and give an explanation which would serve the hon. member's purpose. One involves a debt created by the presentation of an incorrect birth certificate by a man who died while still in the service. The man died, but because the whole matter had been wrongly set up there was a debt shown against him. These matters have to do with accounting procedures rather than anything of substance.
The next one has to do with a court case in respect of which the crown recovered the costs incurred, and the individual was directed to reimburse the crown. It was then found that part of the costs were recovered but that the rest would have to be written off.
That is the sort of item covered by this vote. I might add that all these were examined and approved individually by treasury board before being included. There is no other authority for writing off these claims, even though it would be hopeless to try to collect the debts, and if we did not do it in this way, we would have to carry them on the books long after it became obviously impossible to collect them.

I should like to refer to the mines and technical surveys debts specifically. Under the heading "department" it indicates that this is a debt in respect of mines and technical surveys, and under the heading "number of debts or claims", it is indicated there are three, amounting to $334,549.45.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
These claims represent unpaid balances by certain oil companies. I could give you the names of the companies if you wish. Three companies operated oil wells, the production of which was not sufficient to enable them to pay the charges which had been made by the department, and it became obvious that there was no prospect of collecting the charges. The companies did not have sufficient assets and the wells did not produce to an extent which would enable

Supply-Finance
them to pay. Those charges amounted to $475,000.

speechtext: Does the hon. member want the name of the firm? This represents an unpaid balance of a loan granted under the provisions of the Coal Production Assistance Act. This is authority to write that item off.

speechtext: What is that advice?

speechtext: Thank you very much.

Item agreed to.
23d. To authorize the governor in council to add to part II of schedule A to the Public Service Superannuation Act the members of the staff of the Canadian council of resource ministers-le conseil Canadien des ministres des ressources (hereinafter called "the council") and to provide that forthwith upon the addition thereof
(a)	the council shall be deemed to be a public service corporation for the purposes of section 23 of the Public Service Superannuation Act;
(b)	the Government Employees Compensation Act shall apply to the members of the staff of the council; and for the purposes of that act, such persons shall be deemed to be employees in the service of Her Majesty; and
(c)	for the purposes of any regulation made pursuant to section 5 of the Aeronautics Act, the members of the staff of the council shall be deemed to be employees in the public service of Canada, $1.

Mr. Chairman, the argument I advanced in respect of an earlier vote applies to this vote. We have no information regarding this matter, yet we are asked to authorize the governor in council to add to part II of schedule A to the Public Service Superannuation Act the members of the staff of the Canadian council of resource ministers, and to provide that forthwith upon the addition thereof that council shall be deemed to be a public service corporation, and the Government Employees Compensation Act shall apply to the members of the staff; and for the purposes of any regulation

made pursuant to section 5 of the Aeronautics Act, the members of the staff of the council shall be deemed to be employees in the public service of Canada.
All these sections with which we are dealing under this vote could be covered by one amendment, even though three statutes are involved. I am sure there would be no objection in that regard; but certainly this is not the way to legislate and not the way to designate the application of a statute to an additional group, in this case the members of the staff of the Canadian council of resource ministers. I am not arguing that it may not be proper to have them included, but for the life of me I cannot understand the attitude of the government in attempting to amend acts of parliament in this way. It might be a different situation if there was any haste or rush to make these amendments, but there is no haste or rush. All the government has to do is issue a general amendment to these various acts and bring it before parliament at an early date. What is behind this move on the part of the government? The adoption of this kind of method will simply make a shambles of the House of Commons. We should not amend statutes in this way in order to qualify certain groups for inclusion under any regulations. Those are matters to be dealt with in the ordinary legislative way. They are not involved or difficult. They are not going to take much time, but whether or not they take time this is a method that cannot be accepted by the House of Commons.
Six o'clock.
We agreed to sit later.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This particular item is an unfortunate example of how a part of what is commonly regarded as the public service of Canada, presumably through inadvertence, was not given the kind of legislative treatment that is common to all members of the public service and which the former government thought they had provided. If the right hon. gentleman wants examples, I would point out that this has been the traditional method of dealing with this problem under all governments.
No.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Take item 684 of supplementary estimates (5) for 1960-61.
What does it say?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Supplementary estimates (5) for 1960-61 are a good example. I just do not understand the right hon. gentleman seizing

on this particular item. I should have thought that if he knew the facts he would have been less enthusiastic in attacking the present government than he appears to be at the moment, because what is being done in this particular case is merely to follow the traditional practice under the Public Service Superannuation Act. In this particular case it would normally have been done long ago, and all the evidence I have been able to get leads me to believe that it would have been done by the former government if they had been aware that it was required to be done. This is the unfortunate situation we are in in this case, and if the right hon. gentleman really means to imply that public servants who work for the Canadian council of resource ministers should be denied-
No, no.

Mr. Chairman, that is no way to get co-operation. I am just as anxious that they get their rights as anyone else. The hon. member was a member of the house when this legislation was passed and he did not notice this omission and nobody else did. The proper way to amend legislation is by following the ordinary accepted principle of the presentation of a bill to parliament. I object to this procedure now being suggested. When he says that I should be anxious to see the change made because this group of individuals are entitled to be included, I say that I am not arguing that. I am simply saying: Bring in a bill with all their considerations instead of subterraneously attempting to amend statutes through the guise of supplementary estimates. Bring this in and it will be accepted, but why do it this way? Why should the House of Commons be placed in the position of amending statutes through the medium of supplementary estimates? I am not arguing about the objective in respect of the individuals in question but I am arguing that this whole procedure shows a disregard of parliamentary practice.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to call it six o'clock. I know there is a desire to finish this evening but I would suggest that we call it six o'clock and agree to sit later this day. It seems rather silly to me to sit through the supper hour when members of the house and the staff would find it more convenient not to do so. I suggest that we agree to return at eight o'clock and continue until ten o'clock tonight.
