speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When we adjourned at six o'clock we were considering vote No. 23d of the Department of Finance and votes Nos. 18d and 21d had been allowed to stand.

May I just take one minute to say that I have just been talking to the Prime Minister who is in Philadelphia tonight making a speech at Temple University where he is receiving an award. It has been arranged that the Prime Minister will meet with President Johnson tomorrow around noon at Camp David.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote No. 23d carry?

When you asked if vote No. 23d shall carry, I may say that I wish to participate in this debate that has been going on since we started consideration of the supplemental estimates of external affairs. In paragraph (c) of vote No. 33d-
This is vote No. 23d for the Department of Finance.

I understand that perfectly, my friend. I am not participating in this debate because of some recent conviction or some conclusion reached today. My position was made clear to this house as long ago as last November when this government introduced some supplementary estimates. At that time they sought to legislate by supplemental estimates, and a number of members in this house protested strongly to the members of the cabinet. While it is true that

Supply-Finance
I had occasion to rise twice and say I protest about estimates being introduced in that way, Hansard will not show any discussion on my part. The minister for the department involved stood up and announced that because the legislation he was trying to effect by supplemental estimates involved a contentious matter, he would allow the item to be laid aside.
Now, I do not believe in legislation by supplemental estimates. Certainly, we are getting a prize example of it in these supplemental estimates tonight, which total something around $346 million. I have to agree with the hon. member for Prince Albert when he says it is more like supplemental legislation that is involved in this process, rather than supplemental estimates. I have read every word in these supplemental estimates three times since the noon hour. This vote 23d for the Department of Finance will authorize the governor in council to add to part II of schedule A to the Public Service Superannuation Act the members of the staff of the Canadian council of resource ministers-and to provide that forthwith upon the addition thereof, (a) the council shall be deemed to be a public service corporation, and then paragraph (b) says that "such person shall be deemed", and paragraph (c) also uses the words "shall be deemed". We are legislating by supplemental estimate in the amount of $1.
I ran on the Liberal party ticket in 1962 and 1963. I must say I get a little provoked when I come down here and listen to Liberal cabinet ministers standing up and saying, that is the way you did it so it is all right for us to do it that way. I ran against Conservatives in my riding because I thought we could legislate better; but down here they say: That is the way you did it, and it was wonderful, so we are going to follow your example. In November when I was investigating this question of legislating by supplemental estimate, I went to see three different lawyers. I am not a lawyer; I am a businessman who engages lawyers. I spoke to them about this legislation by supplemental estimate. I was told by the lawyers in whom I have every confidence, and one of them is a highly placed legal officer of the crown, that legislation by supplemental estimate is probably done three times in ten years. I expressed amazement that legislation was possible, and this was at a time when I was opposing the government on the question of community antenna for television. This highly regarded lawyer informed me that every time

we passed a supplemental estimate it came back to us as a printed bill, and the bill was an enactment of this house. When I expressed resentment over the fact that this could be done in this way in the dying hours of a session, I was simply told, "Well, you may resent it, but that is the way it is done about three times in ten years".
Today, we are told that this legislative method was adopted 31 times in 1961. I should like to look at the items. I do not believe it is 31 pieces of legislation. There may have been 31 $1 items, but we are not protesting the $1 items. I am protesting only this method of legislating under the guise of supplemental estimate. I do not know of a single figure in these supplemental estimates in this booklet to which I would object. However, I certainly object to about ten pieces of legislation that the Liberal party has tried to foist on us under the guise of supplemental estimates. I am ashamed that the Liberal party name would be attached to legislation by supplemental estimate. I wish there were more Liberals who felt the same way about it.
I go back to external affairs vote 33d in order to ask two questions. I am going back to external affairs, in case somebody wants to know, at this point in our discussion on vote 23d for the Department of Finance. If they want to call me back to finance, all right, but I am going back to external affairs to state that ten lines in paragraph (c) should be deleted-not three. The fourth line of paragraph (c) says:

notwithstanding section 35 of the Financial Administration Act-
We are setting aside an act of this parliament by a vote in the supplemental estimates. It is not clear in my mind whether or not we have set aside in paragraph (c), three lines or ten. We should have set aside ten. If we have only set aside three lines we have passed legislation under the guise of a $1 supplementary estimate in vote 33d, under external affairs, and I believe the House of Commons should look at that again because we should not be legislating through supplementary estimates. When people stand up and say, "You did it that way; therefore it must be all right," let me say two wrongs do not make a right. There is only one right way to do this. The legislation should be brought in by the government at the proper time, and not under the guise of supplementary estimates.
The first speaker who opposed legislation by supplementary estimates covered the field pretty thoroughly from page 9 to the back

of the book, and some hon. members questioned him for wandering because we were dealing with a particular vote under external affairs. However, he was covering the point that is in dispute and 1 thought that should have been clear to everyone in the chamber. To stand up and say it has been done before, does not justify it. Vote 23d under finance should not be passed because it is changing an act of the House of Commons.
Somebody stood up this afternoon and made a great howd'ye-do about parliament going to rob one poor fellow who was the victim of an error made in some department, and said surely the house would be anxious to correct a mistake. That is governed by vote 59d under national defence, at page 17, and at no time was that vote mentioned. I am the first person to mention it directly.
There are about 10 cases in which the government is trying to pass legislation under the guise of supplementary estimates, and Canada expects more of its government than that type of action. I am opposed to the passage of vote 23d, under the Department of Finance, at page 12.

I am also concerned, but perhaps not in the same high technical detail as some other members, with vote 23d, paragraph (c), which appears to be setting up a new council that was not agreed to in the past, and I think the Minister of Transport should give some indication of what is involved in this.
The previous speaker mentioned the community antenna section that appears to be set up in this manner. I do not have the statute before me and am not familiar with section 5 of the Aeronautics Act, but it would appear that under this vote the staff of a new council is being established. I suggest that the minister responsible should give some explanation of paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) because obviously they do not mean what they say, or at least I presume they do not mean what they say. The item states:
To authorize the governor in council to add to part II of schedule A to the Public Service Superannuation Act the members of the staff of the Canadian council of resource ministers.
I presume this refers to the secretariat that was discussed at great length following the meeting of the resource ministers, and if such a secretariat is being established all hon. members interested in the relationship between provincial governments and the federal government, on the matter of natural resources, should examine it.
Supply-Finance

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would not mind me interrupting to say one thing. This council of resource ministers was created some three years ago under the responsibility of the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle, who was a minister in the previous government.
But is it a statute?
I presume what we are discussing here is the secretariat of that organization.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

Obviously we do not have to pay the ministers. As I recollect it, the secretariat was to be comprised of representatives of the federal and provincial governments. Are we suggesting that the secretariat be a federal agency and, if so, why are we not formally establishing it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for York-Humber talked about two wrongs not making a right. With the greatest respect may I say I have looked at a number of precedents and I thought we were following the right procedure. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition was kind enough to grant me a moment or two before the dinner adjournment and, if I may, I should like to repeat that in adopting this method we were following a method that had been accepted as perfectly legitimate in other years.
I would invite the attention of hon. members to the estimates of 1961-62, vote 520, and I quote:
To authorize the governor in council to add to part I of schedule A to the Public Service Superannuation Act
(a)	such part of the staff of government house as is paid by the governor general from his salary or allowance,
(b)	notwithstanding subsection (2) of section 9 of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation Act, the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, and
(c)	notwithstanding subsection (1) of section 5 of the Government Companies Operation Act, Canadian Arsenals Limited;
and to authorize the governor in council to make regulations respecting the terms and conditions under which any employee of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation or Canadian Arsenals Limited who is, on the addition of those corporations to part I of schedule A, a member of a pension plan to which either corporation contributes in respect of him, may elect not to become a contributor under the Public Service Superannuation Act.
May I say with the greatest respect that the estimates now before the committee falls on all four corners within the method adopted at that time, and I refer particularly to the words, "to add to part I" of the

Supply-Finance
schedule. May I say further that the very purpose of this estimate is to right a wrong inadvertently done to certain members of the secretariat, and it seems to me the prime responsibility resting upon us as members is to do justice to our employees. This is what we are attempting to do.
Rightly or wrongly in the method we have adopted, we will at least do a justice to these people by correcting an oversight so that they can become entitled to pension provisions and compensation, and I would earnestly urge the committee to accept the vote.

The argument is not quite as simple as that; but before advancing it further I would ask the President of the Privy Council whether the Canadian council of resource ministers is provided for in any statute? If so, what is the statute?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry; I cannot answer that. It was set up by the former government. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman himself could tell us.

It has no authority by statute of parliament, as I understand it. It was set up, and what is attempted now is to give an unofficial board certain rights. To accomplish this requires an amendment to the Public Service Superannuation Act, or whatever act applies. It is all very well to say, as did the hon. gentleman who just resumed his place, that the object of parliament is to do justice to employees. That is right-to do justice to employees in accordance with the proper application of law. There is no rush about this. What has happened here? Why this ungodly haste on the part of the government to bring in a series of so-called supplementary estimates making provision for the amendment of these various acts at this time? Why not wait until the new session of parliament and make a general amendment to cover these things, instead of using this abysmal method of having parliament act in a way which is not in keeping with the general tenor of parliamentary procedure? I do not understand why the government should wish to press ahead. One would almost believe there was not going to be another session- that there is to be a dissolution of parliament and the government wants all these things done right away. The Minister of Transport shakes his head in a negative manner. Why not have one amending bill brought in to cover all these acts which seem to require consideration, instead of adopting this subterranean plan-it must be a plan because there

cannot be so many instances of departure from the ordinary rules of parliament without there being a reason.
The Minister of Transport told us there was no possibility of this being done before dissolution. This being so, with a new session about to begin, cannot the government simply allow these items to stand and bring them forward in the form of one amendment in the new session? Whenever injustice has been done there will be support from Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition to ensure a remedy for any omissions which may have taken place. I cannot understand what is behind this. I am never suspicious of actions by the government. I look at anything of this kind in an objective way in the same manner as is characteristic of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, removed completely from political considerations. But the government has not answered this question: Why this unseemly haste?

Why did you do it
before?

Who let the cat out of the
bag on the back seat? I am surprised that one as scrupulous as the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice should be supporting this. I know how careful he is- and in that department there has to be care. In any case, if the government wishes to get on with our business it is not going to get on by trying to browbeat this committee into passing something which it should not pass.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no wish on my part to browbeat anyone, but the committee which is asked to pass these items is no different from the committee which in 1961-62 was asked to authorize the governor general in council to add part I, and so on. I submit that this, too, was legislation by an estimate. It cannot be any clearer. My submission is that if there were no undue haste on that occasion it should not be said there is undue haste on this occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I hate to enter this area of high drama into which the Leader of the Opposition has moved.
Low drama on the part of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I think that when the facts are known concerning this resources council everything will become clear. At least, I hope so. The council of resource ministers is a product of the resources for tomorrow conference which was held in Montreal in 1961,

under the leadership of a predecessor of mine in this office, the present hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I have said in this chamber on other occasions that I hoped the papers covering that particular conference could be made require reading for every Canadian, because nothing has contributed quite so much, in my opinion, to the acknowledgment in other countries of the extent of Canadian resources.
We wanted to develop something out of that conference, as did my predecessor. He was working toward the establishment of a resource ministers council when the government changed and we came to power. We continued along those lines and implemented that policy. The resource ministers council involves the resource ministers of the ten provinces in Canada and myself, a total of 11 ministers. The idea is to endeavour to bring the resources of Canada, wherever they may lie, into a plan for concerted action, a national policy for the good of Canada as a whole. As we developed, we established an office in Montreal, a secretariat which was headed by a very good man. He stayed with us for 18 months and we have now appointed another engineer, Mr. De Laet. I suggest that the secretariat is doing an exceedingly good job.
Nobody is arguing that point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

The secretariat numbers some eight or ten people. They inquired if it were not possible for us to provide the advantages which the civil service of Canada provides for its ordinary employees. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We are not arguing that this provision in vote 23d does not serve a good purpose or that these people should not be added to schedule A of the Public Service Superannuation Act. I think the minister of northern affairs has missed the point entirely.
Supply-Finance
May I point out that included in votes 23d, 21d and 18d are three votes of $1 each, all altering the Public Service Superannuation Act. Our suggestion is that this act be amended by a short bill presented to parliament in the usual way. This is the way to deal with legislative improvements.
May I remind the house that when the house is dealing with matters that are not controversial-and I submit that the amendments here, if brought forward in a proper bill, would not be considered controversial- it acts with the greatest rapidity. On March 4 of this year, if hon. members will look at Hansard, page 11989 and the following page, they will find that within a period of ten minutes this house passed amendments to the Canada Shipping Act, provision for capital expenditures for the C.N.R., and implemented an amendment to an agreement to avoid double taxation with Japan. That is how rapidly the house can act when the proper measures are put in front of it; and that is all we are suggesting. Withdraw these items, bring in a bill, and next week when the speech from the throne is being dealt with, the speech from the throne could be interrupted for ten minutes and a bill could be passed through the house to deal with these matters. That is how simple it is.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to accept that suggestion, but I want to point out to hon. members of this committee, before doing so, exactly what this involves. Leader of the Opposition takes the responsibility for the position he has asserted, I would be very glad to put this into the form of legislation that will be more agreeable to the committee. The same remarks would apply-

the onus on the opposition for denying these rights to individuals, why was not the legislation brought in before, in these cases?

speechtext: I did not mean to do that; but I want to make it clear that I hope hon. members understand exactly the implications involved in entering into what has been referred to as the wrong method of legislating. As long as they do understand, I am quite content and happy to withdraw the three items. That is what I was seeking to make clear, because I must confess that the wording of estimates is not always as clear to me as I would wish it to be and I suspect this is the case with other hon. members in the house. I am quite satisfied to withdraw the three items on the undertaking given by the house leaders of the opposition parties.

Mr. Chairman, all I want to say is this. There is no question of the Leader of the Opposition taking responsibility. I am carrying out my duties as a member of parliament, upholding the rights of parliament. Those rights have now been admitted by the hon. gentleman and I am glad to see that he has decided, after consideration and review of the matter-and this apparently was not clear to him earlier- that this would be a contravention of our practice. I only hope that the amendment is brought in at an early date and these people, including those covered by item 18d, will receive their just due by the proper method, namely an amendment to the legislation in question.

Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue could give us some explanation as to why he wants to transfer this amount and add it to the national debt, because it is rather a significant amount of money.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on March 6, 1964, the Minister of Finance made an announcement concerning this matter of han-
Supply-Finance
dling the public service superannuation fund so that it would be in accordance with the recommendations of the Auditor General. This is an effort to do that. Perhaps I could give more detail, Mr. Chairman, although I do not know how much detail the hon. member wants me to give on it. This amount is to be written off to net debt and it represents the unamortized portion of the deferred charge credited to this account in respect of the deficiencies which had arisen up to December 31, 1962, plus interest, to the date of the crediting of the deferred charge. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to translate that into merchandiseable English.
Or French.

What does it really
mean?

Mr. Chairman, this says that it is to take from the account the unamortized portion of the actuarial deficiency in the public service superannuation account. What does this mean when it refers to "actuarial deficiency"? Does that mean there is a deficiency in the superannuation account, or are there some statistics which have been worked out by actuaries who say that there ought to be so much there, but in fact there is not that much.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.
The hon. gentleman has the right explanation.

Mr. Chairman, this nodding of the head does not appear on Hansard. I would like someone to get up on his feet and explain what this means in language which the right hon. Leader of the Opposition has described as merchandiseable English.

Mr. Chairman, the gentleman has the right answer in this regard. There is an actuarial deficiency in the account. There are one or two items which will be transferred to a special bill, which I am sure will be dealt with by this house in ten minutes, and which will look after the actuarial deficiency in the future to make sure that when civil servants retire there will be the correct amount in the

Supply-Finance
fund required to carry out the purposes of the legislation.

Now that this has been put into merchandiseable English, perhaps it simply means that there has been a mistake made in the provisions of the superannuation fund. This leads to one or two more questions. Is the government taking any steps to see that this type of error will not be repeated? If one looks at the civil service salaries he will find that they are not very high, and will come to the conclusion that the $396 million is a tremendous amount. That is almost $400 million, and I assume that this deficiency has occurred over the past year.
Oh, no.

Perhaps it has not occurred within just one year, but why in hell do you not say so in these supplementary estimates? Why should they be stated in this manner? I am not at all satisfied with this kind of explanation and it seems to me that if the government is in a hurry to pass these supplementary estimates it ought to make clear and satisfactory explanations in respect of these items. My understanding is no less than anyone else's and it always irritates me to hear someone say that they understand these things. I do not believe that they have even thought about them, let alone understand them.
If this type of deficit has been incurred over a period of a year, or over a longer period of time, then I think this fact should be stated, and I think we should be told what steps are being taken to bring about a change in the necessary provisions to ensure that these actuarial deficiencies will not occur in the future. I do not believe that we can expect the Canadian public to accept an expense of this kind to be paid out of the treasury without some kind of an explanation. If these debts are to be paid by the treasury and added to the national debt, there are two ways of doing this. It can be added to the debt or paid out, and it does not seem to make much difference which method is adopted.
I think this sort of thing should be explained in a better way than has been adopted, and I personally intend to keep on asking questions until I am satisfied that I understand the situation thoroughly.

I do not want to fix the blame in respect of this actuarial deficiency on anyone. What has happened over the years, and I would refer my hon. frend to the reports

of the Auditor General from 1958 onwards, is that salary changes have taken place in the civil service without provision having been made for the additional contributions encumbent upon the government to make under the superannuation act. What this provision will do in one step, by a charge to the national debt, is bring the superannuation fund up to the amount required in order to carry out the obligations inherent in the Civil Service Superannuation Act. In addition to that, and this has been mentioned previously, other provisions will make sure that this sort of thing cannot happen in the future. The government will be required to make a charge against revenue in the current year, and over a five-year period, in order to keep the fund in line with salary changes which result in additional obligations under the superannuation act.

That answer has made the situation much more clear. The last question I want to ask is, what have we done to correct this situation in the future? The correcting measures are not contained in this item, obviously, and if they were it would be wrong. It seems to me that there should be some changes made to the public service wage structure so as to automatically provide for changes which will occur to the superannuation fund. Is it the intention of the government to introduce legislation which will correct this situation and bring these things into their proper relationship?

I should point out to my hon. friend that this item will take care of prior accumulated deficiencies, and that item 18d, which has now been dropped and which is to be incorporated in a bill to be presented to parliament, will ensure that this sort of thing will not happen again. I refer my hon. friend to the wording of vote 18d which is designed to prohibit any government from doing the same thing in the future.

It has nothing to do with the new program?

Supply-Fisheries

Estimated amount required to recoup the fishing vessel indemnity account and the lobster trap indemnity account established under vote 540 of the Appropriation Act No. 5, 1955, and vote 527 of the Appropriaiton Act No. 6, 1956, to cover the net operating losses in the said accounts as at March 31, 1965, $81,000.

No, as I have just indicated this is the amount that is required to recoup

speechtext: Is the minister in a position tonight to provide us with the statement of policy on unemployment in the Atlantic provinces that he promised some weeks ago? The hon. member for Cape Breton South and I are interested in what will be done by the government on Cape Breton island, particularly with regard to placing more people in work. It is a big problem, but during the election campaigns of 1962 and 1963, so far as the minister was concerned it did not appear to be insurmountable. As I mentioned in the house the other day, there are presently 78,000 unemployed in the Atlantic provinces, some 13 per cent of the working force, or a total of 5,000 more unemployed this year than at the same time last year.

I wish to associate myself with my three colleagues from the Atlantic region, where it is a shocking situation that unemployment is higher than in the rest of Canada. Great pride is occasioned when the national unemployment figures go down, but it is a serious matter when they rise in the Atlantic provinces, whether because of the government's policies or lack of them.
I did not hear the minister make any election promises on Prince Edward Island in 1962 and 1963. We would have loved to have him with us, but he did not come, and if he had any recipes or formulas at that time I hope he will reproduce them, because we do not want to sink further into the relative pit of unemployment vis-a-vis the rest of the country.
During the last six or seven years, thanks to the great assistance that came from the former government, we in the maritimes were beginning to find our feet, and latterly the initiative of the Stanfield and Shaw governments brought about a new spirit of adventure. However, unemployment is again becoming heavy and I hope the vigorous and intelligent Minister of Labour will do something about it.
I would like to know, is the special services branch the one responsible for the $500 program for winter housebuilding.
Yes.

Has the program been a success and how far has it extended across Canada? Some areas seem to get more ad-
Supply-Labour
vantage from it than others, and my own area has experienced considerable difficulty because houses cannot be painted in winter. Sidings cannot be applied, and when there are three or four feet of frost during the terminating days of the program, it is very hard to instal sewerage.

At this point I do not wish to engage in a provocative debate with hon. members about the question of unemployment. Even if we wished, it is too large a subject to debate tonight, and all I want to say at this time is that I cannot accept in their entirety the views put forward by members of the official opposition.
With respect to additional proposals to meet unemployment, we shall have a speech from the throne early next week, and following that disclosure of plans it will be possible to debate the problem better. Further, in that debate if the opportunity arises I will be glad to discuss the general unemployment situation in Canada, in the Atlantic provinces and on Cape Breton island and, if I am given time to continue beyond the normal span allotted to hon. members, I may outline all the projects that have been developed to meet unemployment, especially in Cape Breton.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Is the minister taking credit for all the projects for which, thank God, we have Bob Stanfield in Nova Scotia, and Industrial Estates, to bring new industries to Nova Scotia?

My hon. friend cannot have it both ways. He cannot thank God for Bob Stanfield and then bemoan the distressed conditions in his province. We believe in co-operating with the provincial government, and some recent developments in Nova Scotia have illustrated the value of sincere co-operation between the two levels of government. We want that co-operation to continue. I am not particularly interested in detracting from the achievements of the premier of Nova Scotia, provided my hon. friend does not detract from the achievements of the federal government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: What I blame you for is the closing down of the Point Edward naval base and places like that.

In reply to the question about the special services fund, this additional amount of $40,000 is required to meet the fees which by law must be paid by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the

Supply-Labour
inspection which is conducted at the beginning of a program, and at the end. Our requirements are greater than anticipated because we expect that inspection payments will be necessary for 35,000 units.
The purpose of the winter housebuilding program is to combat seasonal unemployment and the bonus is given as an encouragement to get the work done in the winter months. It is true it would be easier for those parts of the country where houses can be built more easily because of good fortune in having favourable weather conditions at certain times; I do not know of any way by which we could even out under this program the weather variations which occur from one end of Canada to the other.
The program has been a success; there is no doubt about that. There was a big program last year. It will be the same this year and nobody now suggests that we terminate it. Even the house builders who found it somewhat upsetting at the beginning have concluded that it is a good program and that it has contributed to employment stability.

The Minister of Labour has clearly indicated that he made no promises during the last campaign. However, members of his government did. He and the Minister of Transport took delight in making claims about the wonderful things which had been done in Nova Scotia and Cape Breton in particular. I would ask the minister to take a few short moments and name, if he can, two or three programs which have been initiated for the benefit of Cape Breton by his government. There is no need for him to elaborate on them; I ask him just to name them. If and when he does, I will have something to say, though I do not intend to say it tonight; I shall do that at a more advantageous time and at a later date.
The minister told us earlier of his government's intention to carry on complete cooperation with the Stanfield government, thus supporting what the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria has said. Had it not been for what the Stanfield government and Industrial Estates have done and the establishments they initiated in Nova Scotia, the situation would be a great deal worse even than it is today, because the federal government has done nothing except to give some assistance to joint programs initiated by Industrial Estates and the government of Nova Scotia.
I ask the minister to name quickly two or three projects which have been initiated in Cape Breton by his government. Let him do
[Mr. MacEachen.l
so, since he and the Minister of Transport have taken great delight in laying claim to all the wonderful things they are supposed to have done in Nova Scotia.

Although it may be desirable to complete the work of this session without undue delay, I do not think we should allow the Minister of Labour to shrug off two years of Liberal government and all the promises which have been made on the basis that there will be another speech from the throne next week. Mr. Chairman, we have already had two speeches from the throne and statistics in the Atlantic area show that unemployment is higher now than it was when we started. The Minister of Labour is telling us, in effect: Wait until Monday when we bring in another speech from the throne; unemployment is only 13 per cent now, and it may be 17 per cent next time.
We have waited for two years for this government to bring forward policies which would provide the kind of assistance to the people of the Atlantic area capable of placing them at least in a position where unemployment would be no worse than in any other part of Canada. Instead, unemployment in the Atlantic area today is two or three times as great as it is in the rest of Canada.

In order to relieve the gloomy picture he is painting, will the hon. member not admit that unemployment has decreased substantially in the Atlantic provinces in the past two years and that total employment has increased substantially, as can be verified by referring to figures of the dominion bureau of statistics? Hon. members opposite have made certain statements but they have not supported them by official statistics. These show an improvement in every part of the Atlantic provinces every year.
Hear, hear.
I do not intend, however, to be drawn into a general debate on employment tonight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I suggest to the minister that the hon. member for Cumberland has the floor and perhaps he should be allowed to continue.

I was willing to let the minister rise and make some statement which might possibly be of benefit to the Atlantic area and to the 13 per cent of the people in that area who are unemployed. Instead of that, he gets up and gives me an argument about statistics.

He is a member of a party which has the services of a great expert on statistics, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is no longer in politics; he does not bother with statistics any longer. I am not arguing with the Minister of Labour about statistics. I am talking about the 13 per cent of the labour force which is unemployed, and saying he has done nothing to assist in the two years he has been in office, although he comes from the area concerned. What does he tell us when he rises to address the committee? He says, wait until Monday. Well, we have had a lot of Mondays but we have seen nothing from the Minister of Labour which would indicate to me that he has done very much about the unemployment problem in our region.
When the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport are asked questions about unemployment in the Atlantic area they tell us about all the different projects which have been undertaken to provide assistance to the people there. But let us face the facts. The facts are that all they have done is maintain the legislation which was put on the statute books by the former Diefenbaker administration. While that legislation was excellent, they destroyed the effectiveness of the main vehicle which the Diefenbaker administration proposed to use to eliminate the problems of the Atlantic area, namely the Atlantic development board. They did this by reducing it to the position of a gap filler provided with the insignificant sum of $100 million-
Oh, oh.
Insignificant in the light of government expenditures today.
What's $100 million?
An hon. member asks "What's $100 million?" I will tell him. It is just what we are giving to the C.B.C. in the coming year.
Touche.

That is as much as is available for the four Atlantic provinces, and, remember, this has to serve those provinces over a number of years.
It is available to the C.B.C. for one year, and the president of that corporation says, "Give it to us for at least ten years without asking us any questions as to how we spend it". That is the difference, and that is the reason why I feel we have a right to expect from the Minister of Labour tonight some
Supply-Labour
explanation as to what he thinks can be done for the Atlantic area to eliminate the high degree of unemployment that is in existence there today and with regard to which the people of that area sent us here to try and get them jobs. Let us hear from the Minister of Labour, not next Monday but now, what he is going to do, instead of this business that we are going to hear it in the speech from the throne. Let us hear tonight what he is going to do.

Mr. Chairman, the late coal critic of the former opposition has now turned Minister of Fisheries. This is very confusing. The financial critic is now Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. We don't know where we are going with this outfit. The Minister of Labour was asked a very simple and straightforward question. We know that employment has been increasing over the last two years, but I am not just referring to the last two years; I am referring to possibly the last ten years. Employment is always on the increase, relatively.
The hon. member for Cumberland mentioned this problem and the Minister of Fisheries says that is not true. But he has the statistics from his own department to support the statement. I ask the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Transport, who has taken great delight in jumping up and saying what wonderful things have been done for Cape Breton and Nova Scotia, to get up now and indicate just two or three projects that this government has initiated which have been of any benefit to Cape Breton. If he is stuck, perhaps he will get up and just mention one project.

Mr. Chairman, if the Minister of Labour gets up to do that-I would not tax him with too many statistics, and if he does not have them I will send to my office for them-I would like to know if he will tell me, the committee, and particularly the hon. member for Cumberland what percentage of the labour force, according to his latest statistics, is unemployed in Canada; and what is that percentage in relation to the Atlantic region? Then, in the face of those statistics, would the minister say that things are getting better in the Atlantic region in this field?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I would. It is a fact that unemployment rates in various parts of Canada are higher than in others. One of the highest such rates is in the Atlantic provinces. I admit that. I state it every time I make a speech about

Supply-Labour
unemployment. But I also point out that there has been a very significant decrease in total unemployment in the Atlantic provinces, a very significant decrease. There has been a very significant decrease in total unemployment on Cape Breton island over the past two years; there is no doubt about that. It is quite clear that the unemployment rate, tor example in the province of Ontario, is certainly relatively low, on the prairies it is relatively low and in British Columbia it is certainly relatively low in comparison with the Atlantic provinces. It is clear, also, that the remaining areas of the country which require continuing special measures to reduce further unemployment include the Atlantic provinces and eastern Quebec. This is true, and we hope that in the speech from the throne it will be possible to conduct a more constructive debate on this question, in the light of proposals that may be made in that document, to reduce further unemployment in these areas.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is unfair to the committee really to expect a general debate on supplementary estimates on the question of unemployment, when we are dealing with three or four items in the general administration that do not raise the question at all. I am ready to debate the question on the speech from the throne, and there we will all have a chance to put our position before the house. However, I do not think it is fair to ask the committee to deal with the question on this particular vote, which deals with grants to the international institute for labour studies, legal fees, and so on.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may just say a word or two with regard to what the minister has been saying. I come from British Columbia and admit that we do have a very much better employment picture than the Atlantic provinces; but as a Canadian, and coming from British Columbia, I would like to see in other parts of this country the same level of employment and the same lack of unemployment as we have in British Columbia. The minister has suggested that perhaps in the speech from the throne he will be able to answer all these questions. I put it straight to the minister now: How is he going to answer all these questions? He is going to get on his feet perhaps once, not subject to questioning at all, and he is going to give almost the same wonderful, rosy picture of everything that he has given in the past. The minister and the Minister of Transport will get to their feet and give the same wonderful, rosy picture that was handed out prior to the
[Mr. MacEachen.l
last election as to what they were going to do in the province of Nova Scotia and in the other Atlantic provinces. They said, "We are going to cure unemployment. We are going to make employment as good as elsewhere in Canada". The minister's own statistics, which he knows so well, show a figure of 13 per cent unemployment in the Atlantic provinces, which is much higher than elsewhere in this country, where it is 6 per cent. It is bad enough in the rest of Canada, but they said they were going to cure this situation.
Mr. Chairman, I would point out that the statistics the hon. member has given relate to the situation three years ago in the Atlantic provinces.

Don't worry about what it was three years ago; merely say to yourself, "Am 1 carrying out my promises that were given prior to the election in these rosy speeches made by myself and the Minister of Transport as to what we were going to do to solve the unemployment situation?" The minister has been asked to answer this question tonight, not in a debate starting on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday next. He has been asked to stick on the record one, two or three special things which he and his government have done for the Atlantic provinces in order to cure unemployment. I am not asking for just those specific things which were instituted by the last government and carried on by this government, but we want the special programs which have been brought in by this government for the advantage of and to reduce unemployment in the Atlantic provinces.
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friends have assured me that they would be satisfied with at least three such policies.
Yes.

So I will give them three. One is the $100 million that has been put aside for the disposal of the Atlantic development board. That is a very important, new policy. Second, the present government has contributed 90 per cent of the cost of completing the trans-Canada highway in the Atlantic provinces.
Oh, oh.
Yes, 90 per cent.
Is that a brand new one?

This is a new policy which is having very substantial effects in the province of Newfoundland, in the province

of Nova Scotia and elsewhere. The third is a new designated area tax policy which has made it possible to establish in eastern Nova Scotia at least three plants which, in the absence of this tax policy, would never locate in that area of Nova Scotia. I refer to the heavy water plant, to Canadian Motor Industries Limited and to Clairtone in Pictou, Nova Scotia. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I discharge the request by indicating three new policies that are contributing to improved employment conditions in the Atlantic provinces, and especially in Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would agree with the minister that we do not want to get into any extended debate by any means. I know that on that side of the house they do not want to hear anything about unemployment. I would also agree with him that employment has increased and unemployment has decreased somewhat throughout the country. I think the hon. member for Queens asked the minister for the figures for mid-February with regard to the Atlantic provinces, which he has not yet produced.
The minister keeps saying these figures are a little lower than they were two or three years ago. Would he also agree with me that the economy of this country started to improve early in 1961? Naturally as a result we would hope that unemployment would decrease and employment would increase.
After a lot of pressuring and coaxing by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and others, the minister finally mentioned three magnificent steps, as he called them, that have been taken by this government, including the establishment of the Atlantic development board. Let me remind the minister that the Atlantic development board was initiated by the former administration.
I did not take credit for the establishment of the Atlantic development board.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
One of the faults of the minister is that he is a bachelor and does not have patience. A married man must have patience.
The Atlantic development board was initiated by the previous administration and the viewpoint of that administration was that funds should be made available. There was no amount set, as has been set by this government. The amount decided upon now is $100 million, but the province of Nova Scotia has not been able to get very much out of
Supply-Labour
that fund up to the present. The Minister of Transport apparently does not want to assist that province. It is true that he can point to the 90 per cent share in respect of the trans-Canada highway, raised from 50 per cent, but that only means-
I hear the Minister of Fisheries, while sitting on his brains as usual, whispering "trans-Canada highway, trans-Canada highway", but it took some time for the Minister of Transport to catch on. Let me ask the Minister of Transport how many people will be given permanent jobs which will last for years to come as a result of this increase in the share?
The minister has mentioned designated areas. I have asked the minister on several occasions if any special consideration was given to Canadian Motor Industries to move to these designated areas which would not be given in respect of any other part of the country. I suggest that C.M.I. could have settled in Brantford, or anywhere else in Canada which was classified as a designated area.
Or Windsor.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Or Windsor, as the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs has suggested. They could have easily settled there. They decided on Nova Scotia as a result of the efforts of Industrial Estates Limited which enticed these companies to establish there. The same applies to the establishment of the heavy water plant. The minister knows that that industry received the advantages of a designated area circumstance, but that could easily have been established somewhere else because they are not receiving anything more in our island than they would get in any other designated area in Canada.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: I am always glad to hear from the Minister of Transport.
Would the hon. gentleman tell us what government awarded the contract for the production of heavy water?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I am only too pleased to inform the minister that the contract was awarded by an outfit by the name of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, or some such similar name.

Supply-Labour
That is exactly correct. In other words, it was awarded by the government of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Would the minister tell me whether this company received the contract because it tendered the lowest bid per pound of water, or was it awarded the contract because the government of Canada like that company? Was it not given on the basis of dollars and cents?

May I ask the hon. member a question? Would the hon. member tell me who provided the financing for Deuterium Company of Canada Limited, and who also provided the financing for the Clairtone Company which established a plant in Pictou county. Was it the federal government?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: It certainly was not financed by the federal government. I think we are all aware that it was financed through Industrial Estates Limited of the province of Nova Scotia. I do not understand the attitude of the Minister of Transport, who is always jumping up on his feet, flying all over the place, telling us this was done, that was done and everything else was done. Why does he not get on his feet and calmly tell us in reality what has been done.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We want to prorogue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I ask the Minister of Transport to tell me how many people are going to be provided with work as a result of this government action, and how many are going to be put out of work in the town of North Sydney? The international longshoremen's union has suggested that there will be 600 stevedores put out of work by the Minister of Transport as a result of his action as indicated by the famous joke he made at a board of trade meeting to the effect that he would do more for Newfoundland than for anywhere else. It looks as though that is what he is doing, because North Sydney is certainly going to be pushed downhill. The figures I give are not mine, but those provided by the union.
I have asked myself on many occasions when the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport are going to meet with these people. Surely the time has come when the Minister of Transport should meet with them and explain to them how they are going to find work. If the minister should make a trip for that purpose I hope he will call a meeting of the former employees of

the naval base, which was closed down. I understand there are about 400 of them who would like to know how they are going to meet their mortgages, feed their children and earn a living in the future. It was the motorcycle kid, the Minister of National Defence, who closed that naval base and put these people out of work. They have nowhere to go for employment now, and that is a direct result of more foolishness on the part of this government.
I would be pleased to hear the Minister of Transport tell the house how he is going to re-employ these stevedores who have been put out of work. Both he and the Minister of Labour are always facetious when answering questions I have asked in this regard. They shrug their shoulders and say, maybe everybody will die; perhaps there will be an atomic bomb drop and nobody will have to work again. Both ministers are facetious about this very important and vital subject, particularly when answering questions in the house.
I would ask the Minister of Transport to relax, and not to get cross or excited, not to lose his temper, but to get to his feet calmly and tell us what he intends to do. I see that he is now going out to tell somebody else some answers. Perhaps he is going out to call Mr. Rivard.
Oh, oh.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: In any event, I trust the Minister of Labour-
What a nasty sense of humour.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I do not intend to deal with you tonight, but I promise I will deal with you on another occasion.
The Minister of Labour did make some statement regarding the heavy water plant which was established in Nova Scotia. A contract was awarded to Deuterium of Canada. Will the minister inform the committee whether this contract was awarded because this company tendered the lowest bid, or was it awarded out of the goodness and kindness of the government's heart-out of the milk of human kindness because these poor people needed some assistance?

Let me say that the heavy water contract was awarded in large part because the plant was to be located on Cape Breton island and in view of the economic advantages that would flow to the area from that location.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: If it were not for the fact that my rheumatism is bothering me, I would get down on my knees to thank him.
You get down on your knees to Bob Stanfield.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Would the minister tell us whether or not it is correct that this contract was awarded to Deuterium of Canada because the figure they quoted was $20.50 a ton, which was lower than any other bid, or was the Minister of Industry kidding someone when he gave those figures in this house? Would the minister answer that question?

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. I am sure that the problem which has been raised by the hon. members for Cape Breton is a very important one, but I do not see anything to which it could be related under vote Id. Surely we cannot properly have a full-scale debate on this vote.
Sit down.

It seems to me that we are straying a long way from the subject when we are discussing contracts awarded for the production of heavy water and other things. I would apreciate Your Honour considering the vote with which we are now dealing in order to ascertain whether this discussion can be related to it.
Was the hon. member speaking to a point of order?
Yes, I rose on a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, this item deals with general administration and I am sure that anything in relation to the general administration of the Department of Labour is relevant, and for that reason I do not believe the hon. member was out of order.
On the same point of order, Mr. Chairman, it is my understanding that on vote Id we are provided with the only opportunity this session to discuss matters relevant to the Department of Labour.
What about the throne speech debate on Monday?

I am prepared to stay here for some time tonight in order to deal with those matters which I feel should be considered. I suggest to the hon. member for Medicine Hat that if he wants to defend the Liberals he should sit on the other side of the house. We have had enough of that 20220-832
Supply-Labour
kind of nonsense. These questions must be answered.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Has the hon. member concluded this remarks?
No, Mr. Chairman. I thought you were calling me to order. I simply say that there are questions before the house that should be answered.

Mr. Chairman, I put a question to the Minister of Labour, and while I was behind the curtain for a moment he began his answer in which he listed three items and said he had fulfilled his obligation. Since then the matter has been pretty well hashed over but I should like to review for a moment what he called new policies. I emphasize the word "policies". He maintained they were new policies. He began with the Atlantic development board. That is not a new policy. The amounts of money available have been changed and I am afraid they have been changed to the detriment of the province of Nova Scotia.
He also referred to the 90 per cent federal share of the trans-Canada highway as a new policy. This again is not a new policy. There is nothing new about it. He also referred to the tax incentive to industry to establish in designated areas. I would point out to the Minister of Labour that industries establishing in Nova Scotia today are not doing so because of any advantages made available to them by the federal government's tax incentive program. As other members on this side have pointed out, there is nothing special about this tax incentive so far as Nova Scotia is concerned. It is available to every designated area throughout the country.
Those are three of the policies which he referred to as being new and as being helpful to Nova Scotia, and they are anything but helpful. They are not policies to the advantage of Nova Scotia at all. I asked him to get up and name two or three projects which the government had initiated to the advantage of Nova Scotia and he has not fulfilled his obligation because he has not given one example of any kind of program that this government has initiated or had any responsibility for initiating.
He also referred to the heavy water plant. For a long while the people around Glace Bay were calling it the hot water plant because this government was playing around with the matter. They played around with the requirements of the atomic energy commission when the plant was first established in Nova Scotia. They said there was only

Supply-Labour
going to be a requirement for so much heavy water in Canada, but suddenly the amount needed has doubled in a few short months.
The Minister of Labour as the minister from Nova Scotia should be primarily interested in this development in Cape Breton and I ask him this question. How is it that the government has announced another successful tenderer when the minister in charge of the atomic energy commission, the Minister of Industry, has stated in the house that Western Deuterium's process for the manufacture of heavy water has not been approved? How is it that we have such a situation? It is true that in Cape Breton we do have a heavy water plant under construction and we understood it was a plant that would manufacture the full requirements. But suddenly in a few short months the requirements have doubled and, according to the Minister of Transport, the government has now permitted a contract to be awarded to Western Deuterium, even though the Minister of Industry has stated in the house that their process for manufacturing heavy water has not yet been approved by the atomic energy commission.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I do not want to interrupt the hon. member but it seems to me that when he discusses an atomic energy plant he is not dealing with a matter which is within the four comers of vote No. Id. It may be a matter which is of interest to the hon. member's particular area but I suggest it is still outside the confines of vote No. Id. Perhaps the hon. member will want to return to a consideration of this particular item.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy you have seen fit to call my attention to the fact that I should not be discussing heavy water, but I would point out quite clearly to the Chair and to the house that the subject of heavy water was first brought up by the Minister of Labour. I never mentioned the heavy water plant and was not going to say anything about it until the Minister of Labour tried to imply that it was established in Nova Scotia because of the activities and the initiative of the government, which he knows is not the case. I am sorry, sir, but heavy water was brought into the discussion by the Minister of Labour who once again is making wild claims as to what the government is doing for the Cape Breton area.
Again I say to the Minister of Labour that as a representative from Nova Scotia he should be vitally interested in that province. I do not agree with what the Minister of

Transport said, that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. If the Minister of Transport can stand up in public and say that if it comes to a choice between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland he is going to favour Newfoundland, I think the Minister of Labour should get up and take the same stand on behalf of Nova Scotia. Let him get up and say that if there is a choice between provinces he is going to be primarily concerned with his own province. Let him do what other ministers are doing. Let him get up and fight for Nova Scotia.
Oh, oh.
Again we hear from the former coal critic turned Minister of Fisheries. Once again he is yapping from his seat.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think this debate is getting entirely out of control. I would suggest to the hon. member that he should co-operate with the Chair. It seems to me that vote No. Id is not concerned with the present general situation in Nova Scotia, although I am sure this is a matter of interest to all members, but is related to the administration of the Department of Labour. Again, I am not trying to restrict the hon. member but I do feel that his speech should be restricted strictly to the labour aspect in so far as it affects the hon. member's province, if this is what he wants to discuss.

I will be glad to go along with that and co-operate with the Chair. I would only ask that the Chair co-operate with members of the opposition so far as the attitude and behaviour of other members of the house are concerned, particularly the Minister of Fisheries who as usual interrupts from his seat. With regard to what I was saying about labour and employment conditions in Cape Breton, it is not my fault that the Minister of Labour who comes from Nova Scotia is not responsible enough to get up and make representations and fight on matters that concern Nova Scotia in the same way that other ministers in the government fight for their own provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I have a matter I want to bring up other than the one that has been under discussion. It has to do with unemployment insurance for farm labourers. With regard to the question that has been brought up by members from Nova Scotia and the maritimes, the minister said a few minutes ago that we should wait until Monday, and I think this would perhaps be a good time to remind him of one of the

pledges made by the Liberal party during the last election campaign regarding the introduction of legislation to give farm labourers the benefit of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I can assure the minister that in agricultural areas today there is a shortage of skilled farm labour. The situation is becoming more serious with every passing month. Perhaps the most important contributing factor is the fact that people with unemployment insurance books cannot secure stamps when they take employment on farms. 1 know this is an involved problem and I should like to see the government bring forward legislation to permit anyone with a book to be able to secure stamps if he takes a job on a farm. This, in itself, would not I believe create those abuses some people imagine might arise if the door were opened wide. It would be a step in the right direction and would be very beneficial, not only to those employing labour on the farms but also to those who wish to work on the farms.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Before we go on, may I extend an appeal to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, the hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member from Prince Edward Island, to assist-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please; the hon. member can put forward his own views on the matter that is before the committee now, but I do not believe he can reflect on the views or the participation of other members in the committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: I speak to the point of order, sir. I do not understand how you knew what I was going to say because I did not say anything about the views of any member. I just happened to mention several members. You could check Hansard for a precedent and you will find that this has taken place previously when members on the other side have made this suggestion. I am only asking if they would stand with us on this side and impress upon the Minister of Labour the serious unemployment situation in the Atlantic provinces, and assist us in this manner?

It would appear the minister is either unwilling or unable, and I am going to assume he is unable, to provide this committee with the information as to policies this government has that will in any way correct the very serious problem of chronic unemployment in the Atlantic area. We have asked the minister to enunciate new 20220-832J
Supply-Labour
programs that have been initiated by this government in the past two years that have been specifically advantageous to the Atlantic area.
Now, I will agree that there have been extensions to existing programs that have been of some benefit. I certainly want to dissociate myself from the minister's statement that giving the Atlantic development board a fund of $100 million has been of advantage to the Atlantic area, especially in view of the fact the $100 million has almost disappeared. It would seem to me that it becomes more and more evident just how much of a disadvantage this action by the present government was. However, I will say that the extension from 50 per cent to 90 per cent on the payment of construction costs of the trans-Canada highway was a real advantage and will continue to be an advantage until that highway is completed in the Atlantic area.
What we are looking for, what we were led to believe in the Atlantic area by the present governments during the election campaign of April, 1963, was that there would be new policies of specific benefit to our area that would eliminate the high unemployment that has been with us for many years. This unemployment was attacked and reduced, and would have continued to be reduced if there had been no change of government. Indeed, let me say that would have been reduced at a far faster rate all over this nation than is presently the case, because of the policies of the former government, many of which are still in effect.
It would seem to me that while the Minister of Labour might have created a favourable image in this nation as a result of his performance in the House of Commons, he has been a complete failure so far as producing any new labour policies that have been of material assistance to the unemployed of this nation, especially in the Atlantic area. Certainly the present figure of 13 per cent unemployed in the Atlantic area is an indication of the justification for the statement that he has been a failure. If he has new policies ready on Monday that will be of benefit to the area, then I will be the first to congratulate him. They will be the first new policies that have been produced by this government that have any application to the Atlantic area.
The people of the Atlantic provinces were sold down the river by the pie-in-the-sky talk of members like the Minister of Labour during the election campaign of 1963. They have produced nothing but high sounding

Supply-Labour
words and small, insignificant deeds for the people of that area. Let me tell the Minister of Labour that if he thinks he is getting a lot of letters complaining about his performance in his constituency, it is nothing to what he is going to get in the way of adverse votes from his constituents, as are Liberal candidates in the other constituencies in the Atlantic area, unless this government smartens up and smartens up fast so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned.

I should like to say another word or two. I suppose one should allow Cape Bretoners to have the last word. I was disappointed that the minister should look with pride on putting a ceiling on the Atlantic development board. This is not something in which he should take pride.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You did not have ten cents in it.
We had no limitation. At the time we said that $100 million was not sufficient to redress the ancient wrongs of the Atlantic region.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You had nothing but form, no substance.

Perhaps the hon. lady will tell me what she is going to do for the Atlantic region. I think her truth squad ended there.
I should like to say that not only has there been a failure to take new, constructive steps but very definite contributors to unemployment have occurred since this government took office. I see no remedial measures taken whatever. A few years ago in the city of Charlottetown, under the leadership of Hon. Raymond O'Hurley, a fine aircraft industry was established. It employed many people and was a great boost to our economy. It has been closed in recent months, but nothing has been done. I suppose these men are going to Upper Canada on the subsidy of the Minister of Finance. Then, we had the Queen Charlotte naval establishment closed, and no provision made for that. Now, the minister speaks about the many things he will tell us in the speech from the throne. I am prepared to listen to the minister when he speaks in the throne speech debate. In fact I always listen to him whether he speaks in English or in Gaelic, but he said it would not be fair to carry on a full scale discussion tonight. I represent part of the country where 13 per cent of the work force is unemployed and I make no apology for discussing it.
Would the member tell the committee the percentage of unemployment there, when his government was in office, when unemployment reached its peak? The actual figure was 20 per cent.

Considering how difficult it is to pry figures from the minister, may I tell him I can go to my office and get him the figures for the last two years. I can make comparisons with the rest of the country to show that we in the maritimes are sinking down in an absolute and relative scale.
Has the minister assessed the impact on unemployment of the 11 per cent sales tax, on building materials and production equipment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It may be very important but the hon. member will admit there is some question whether this is relevant to vote Id. We are ranging far afield when going into the matter of sales tax during discussion of this vote.

On the contrary, with respect I submit it is relevant with regard to the general field of labour and employment. If you will hear my question out, I wish to point out that we are dependant upon full employment, and as a nation must produce for our exports and internal consumption. The government has placed this tax on building materials and on production machinery. Has this bothered the minister? Has he taken it up with his cabinet colleagues? Has he said to them "I have figures in my department which show this 11 per cent tax is an iniquitous one"? Has he assessed its impact on unemployment?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
Would the minister say what that assessment is?
I reported the fact that despite the dire prophecies made by my hon. friends opposite, construction activity increased substantially.
