5d. Payments to carry out the purposes of the Vocational Rehabilitation of Disabled Persons Act and agreements made thereunder, including undischarged commitments under previous agreements; payments in accordance with terms and conditions approved by the governor in council to employers of 50 per cent of monthly wage paid or $75 per month, whichever is less, on behalf of each full time worker 45 years of age or over engaged during the period November 1, 1963 to March 31 1964, and who is otherwise eligible under the older worker employment and training incentive program-To authorize payment in the 1965-66 fiscal year of amounts, not exceeding in the aggregate the unspent balance remaining at the conclusion of the 1964-65 fiscal year in labour vote 5, main estimates, 1964-65, to meet undischarged commitments under the older worker employment and training incentive program that might otherwise have been paid pursuant to the appropriation based on the said vote during the 1964-65 fiscal year if they had come in course of payment, $1.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Would the minister briefly explain this vote?

I presume this relates to the program for older and disabled workers, and I find it refers to "undischarged commitments under previous agreements." It goes on to say:
To authorize payment in the 1965-66 fiscal year of amounts, not exceeding in the aggregate the unspent balance remaining at the conclusion of the 1964-65 fiscal year in labour vote 5, main estimates, 1964-65, to meet undischarged commitments-
By this item are we extending this program for another year, and will the same amount of money be made available? I do
Supply-Labour
not want to get into another maritime squabble about how it has been distributed, but I would like to know how successful the scheme has been.
I can only speak for the people I know who have made application under it. There have been so many forms to fill in that most employers will not complete the applications that have to be made. I think the minister might operate it under the unemployment insurance commission, which would provide a method of giving faster consideration to the applications that are made. In some cases seven months have passed before applications were processed. I know good results have been obtained after all the rigmarole of red tape has been gone through, and the program has provided employment in new fields for workers who would otherwise have difficulty getting employment. But the red tape should be curtailed.
If the government is going to continue this program is it intended to step it up so that it can be enjoyed by more than the limited number already in it? Can he say how many have taken advantage of it to date?

The purpose of the vote is merely to extend into the present fiscal year authority to pay some bills and to spend some money that had been voted in the last fiscal year. The main estimates provided $3 million for this program. There are some claims. This amount has not been expended because the program has cost less than a million dollars. The purpose of this item is to allow us to pay in this fiscal year bills or claims falling due and to use the unexpended balance of the vote.
The present older workers program has applied to about 800 workers. As originally announced, it was intended to be an experimental program. I regard it as a moderate success. It provided us with a good deal of information upon which to base further development in providing opportunities for older workers. It is my intention very soon to announce a further stage in this older worker program. This particular program has been terminated but it will be followed by another based on the experience we have gained in this experiment
In the complaints I made about red tape, I did not realize that only 100 people were involved.
Oh, oh.

I am not being critical for that reason. But three or four cases came to my

Supply-Labour
attention and in each there was an unholy amount of red tape involved. I am not asking for any information with regard to the minister's forthcoming proposal, but would it not be possible for these questions to be settled in future at least on a regional basis or even on a local basis rather than be handled from the provincial headquarters as I understand has been the case up to now? This has involved long delays and a great waste of time. In one case with which I am familiar two or three unemployment insurance areas were concerned, and should the head office of a company happen to be in another province, additional delay results. Would it not be possible to consider the use of local unemployment offices and to give them a bit more autonomy in assessing the job placement potential and other factors involved? I recall one case where over six months elapsed before a satisfactory conclusion was reached. At no time did departmental officials indicate that the application would not be successful. But the company got tired with the red tape involved and the prospective employee became disillusioned with the assistance he was getting. This seems to me to be the biggest weakness in the program. Even so, I thought it had a limited success.

Perhaps I could begin by making a slight correction. The figure I used -800 workers-was the number employed in the last month of the program. The period the hon. member mentioned for dealing with an application was obviously outrageously long and I hope that in the continuance of our efforts we would get ahead more quickly.
I agree we ought to consider giving room for more local initiative so that consideration could be made and approval given quickly. The form of the new program will be announced reasonably soon and we shall have a chance to take our experience into account, as well as the views expressed by the hon. member.
I understand from the minister that $2 million is available for these purposes. If the operation is extended, how long is it expected the program could continue on the basis of these funds?

We do not intend to continue the present program. We have a further program in mind. The amount which will be authorized by the continuing authority granted last year will be relatively small, something of the order of $50,000. The remainder will lapse.

I was interested to hear the minister say he proposes at an early date to replace the present program. I rise to express the hope that any new plan he brings forward will make it impossible for employers to take advantage of this legislation as a means of securing cheap labour. I think the hon. gentleman will find in his office a communication from the British Columbia federation of labour citing examples of how the old project was subject to abuse of this kind. I know of one case in my area where quite obviously this has been done. An employer was able under these provisions to secure an employee at a rate of pay which barely complied with the minimum wage standard of the province. We should relate this to the fact that he was being repaid to the extent of $75 a month, which meant he was getting the services of an employee for a very low outlay indeed. It was obvious to me that there was no question of training or retraining an employee in this case.
I do not know whether the minister has instances of similar practices in other parts of the country, but I should like some indication whether this was one of the problems presented by the old program and one of the reasons it was wound up.

We had the view that we ought to provide for a greater amount of training than we had insisted upon in the earlier program. I took the view that the return to work of a person who had been chronically unemployed for a considerable length of time might in itself constitute work reorientation that would be tantamount to training, especially on-the-job training. But I think we have to go beyond that and provide some training, and this is one of the problems that we encountered in the program. We attempted to guard against exploitation, or employers taking advantage of the program, by insisting that this bonus would be applicable only to new jobs or jobs that had been created subsequent to the program or because of the program, otherwise individuals could be laid off and others brought on and $75 a month would be paid as a bonus. We guarded against that, I think successfully.

Mr. Chairman, I have one last question on this plan. Would the minister indicate how much money was spent on advertising this program, and second, what is the percentage figure of the administration costs to benefits in this particular program?

Mr. Chairman, I have not with me the exact advertising costs. They have

been made available in answer to questions in the house, and I will get them for my hon. friend. I have no way of segregating the administrative costs of the program as administered by the special services division. The total amount, as I recollect, that was expended last year was close to $1 million. This $1 item authorizes us to spend in the new fiscal year part of the amount authorized last year, which will amount, we think, to about $50,000.

Item agreed to.
30d. Unemployment insurance commission-Administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act including the transfer of labour to places where employment is available and expenses incidental thereto in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $320,000.

Mr. Chairman, on vote 30d I have a "beef" which will take only a few minutes, but it is one of those things that keeps cropping up all the time with regard to the unemployment insurance administration. I am referring to appeals from an insurance officer to the board of referees. Time and again I get letters from constituents who have had their appeals heard in their absence by the board of referees, and when I write to find out why they did not appear at the hearing they send me a form letter that comes from the unemployment insurance commission. I do not have one with me, but it says in effect, "You don't have to appear at this hearing. The board will consider whatever you send them in writing and they will let you know what they did with your appeal". The letter in effect says, "Don't bother appearing; we will look after you". They do look after them; they generally throw their appeals out because there is nobody there to present them.
There are two reasons for this. One is, as I just mentioned, that by the letter from the commission they are encouraged not to attend the hearing, and second, there are people who are unemployed, who have been disqualified for some reason or another, and they do not have the money to travel maybe as much as 100 miles to the hearing place of the board of referees. I know that from many communities in my district they have to travel 75 to 100 miles, and the same distance back, and sometimes it is an overnight trip.
The two things I would like to bring to the attention of the minister are these: First, that he ask the unemployment insurance commission to encourage people to go to the board of referees and put their case forward. The hearing is completed, their case has been
Supply-Labour
thrown out, and then they write back and say, "Where can I get a hearing?" and they think that maybe their member of parliament can do something for them. If they were only encouraged to go, they would feel they had presented their case and put forward everything that could be put forward, and had received a fair hearing. If this were done I think a good many of the complaints with regard to the unemployment insurance appeals system would be alleviated. Perhaps also their appeals would be allowed; because it is very difficult to obtain any further appeal to the umpire.
The second thing I would like to suggest is that if there is an appeal these persons be given a mileage allowance to appear before the board of referees, if they so desire. I believe this would be only fair to those people who are unemployed and have been cut off benefit, some of them retroactively, and in some cases unjustly. The insurance officers are not infallible, but if these people do not get a chance to present their case because of a letter which they have received, I do not think this is right. They are not encouraged in any way to appear and present their case. I would like the minister to direct the unemployment insurance commission to change this form and to encourage people to go to the board of referees for their appeals, and also to provide some sort of mileage allowance so they will be encouraged to do this. This will effectively improve the administration of justice in the unemployment insurance commission, and it may result in more appeals being allowed, to the benefit of those people who really need this assistance.

Mr. Chairman, I want to reply briefly to the hon. member and put forward one or two points in this connection. First of all, as the hon. member realizes, the unemployment insurance commission operates as an independent body under the authority of parliament and is not subject, in its administration, to the direction of the minister. But I will be glad to draw these problems to the attention of the commission for their consideration because I think it is, where possible, appropriate that persons go before the boards of referees to present their case. It should be remembered that the board of referees is composed of a chairman expected to be an impartial person, another person nominated by the employers and a third person nominated by the workers, so that employers and employees have on the board

Supply-Labour
persons who are appointed to put forward the appropriate representations. However, Mr. Chairman, I do agree that where possible the persons directly affected should have a chance to go before the board.

Mr. Chairman, I have raised this matter with the unemployment insurance commission on several occasions. The chief commissioner has been quite good in this connection and on three or four occasions has directed a rehearing on the basis of the fact that the people misunderstood their rights because of the letter that was sent out. But they are still sending the letter out. I do not know who can direct them to change it, but the same type of letter is still going out, certainly from the Toronto office.
We will look at that letter, Mr. Chairman, and see if we cannot get it changed.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister, when he is drawing the request of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka to the attention of the commission, would also draw to the attention of the umpire a recent case in which he made a decision in Cape Breton during a mine tie-up, when a group of railway workers were disqualified from collecting benefit because of his particular ruling. Would the minister point out to the commissioner that these men were operating under a constitution which stated that they did not have to cross a picket line? This is the reason they were disqualified, namely because they did not cross the picket line.
The constitution does not require them to cross any picket line; in fact it emphatically states that it is not necessary for them to do so. Would the minister also point out the fact that the company, in calling these railway-men to work, placed a condition on their employment for that particular shift which was contrary to the labour laws of Nova Scotia. That being the case the umpire and the board of referees have gone astray and are obviously wrong in the decision which was handed down. I ask the Minister of Industry on behalf of these Cape Breton railway workers to bring this situation to the attention of the umpire and the board of referees. Would he do that?

My hon. friend will realize that, under the law even the commission itself has no authority over an insurance officer who has given a judgment. The judgment of the insurance officer is subject to an appeal to the board of referees. The judgment of that

board can be taken before an umpire, who in this case is Mr. Justice Kearney of the exchequer court. That is the apex of the situation. I do not know whether it would do very much good to bring this case to his attention, or whether it would even be proper, but I will consider this and if I decide that it is a proper course I will then consider taking that action.
Will the minister tell us who appoints the board of referees?

The chairman of the board is appointed by the governor in council, and the representatives of the employee and employer are appointed by nomination of the employer association and the employee associations.

Since there is no connection between the minister's office and the appointment of these referees, does he not consider it proper to call the circumstances of this case to the attention of the board of referees, pointing out that they were entirely wrong in deciding to deny railway workers that which they allowed miners under similar circumstances? The minister must be aware of the fact that these men are operating under a constitution which states that they are not required to cross a picket line, and for that reason this ruling was wrong.
I should also like to point out to the minister that if he reads the Nova Scotia labour laws he will realize that no company is allowed to impose the conditions of employment, which in this case were imposed on these railway workers, calling them out to work and asking them, before they went on shift, whether they would cross a picket line. I suggest in that way a condition of employment contrary to the law was imposed on these men. I am sure the minister has the authority to pass on to the referees the information in respect of this case, and I think he should pass it on in very strong terms.

I think any minister of labour would be subject to a great deal of justifiable criticism if he attempted to impose or express his opinion on a board of referees which is set up by law for a definite purpose, namely that it shall be completely independent in reaching decisions. I am sure my hon. friend would not want me to do something that is contrary to the purposes of the law.

All I am asking the minister to do is have this matter re-examined. We can

exchange very high-toned statements back and forth across this house during a debate, but the minister is well aware of the fact that there have been exchanges between himself and other people in responsible positions. He is not fooling anyone in this house if he denies that fact.

Mr. Chairman, I simply want to state, on a matter of privilege, that since I became the Minister of Labour I have not had any communication of any kind with any board of referees, or others, in any part of Canada.
I am quite sure that the Minister of Labour is fully aware of the fact that-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I did recognize the hon. member for Skeena, but if he will relinquish the floor I will allow the hon. member for Cape Breton South to continue.

Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to ask the Minister of Labour whether he would care to amend his last statement to the effect that he has never been in touch with any chairman of any of these boards, because he is aware of the fact that he has been in touch with at least one, although perhaps at a social level.

Mr. Chairman, some things are changed only as a result of repetition and as the result of being brought continually to the attention of this house and the ministers here. I should like again to raise a matter that has been brought to the attention of this house on many occasions in the past. This matter has been raised publicly, in the House of Commons, in its committees, and by way of correspondence. I refer to what I consider to be the rigid interpretation of a section of the act which disqualifies people from benefit, and as a result treats them unfairly. The section in question is section 54(2)(a), if my memory serves me correctly, and relates to the interpretation of availability for work- that is, whether or not an individual is available for work.
The rigid interpretations which have been placed on that section are compounded and made worse by leading questions that insurance officers ask claimants. The result of the answers given to these leading questions usually means the diqualification of these claimants. This is the kind of thing that happens. An insurance officer will interview a claimant and, after obtaining his or her name, and other relevant information, will ask whether he or she will accept work for
Supply-Labour
the same wages they received in former positions. Naturally the claimants answer in the affirmative.
Another type of leading question advanced has reference to the category of employment. One particular case that comes to mind relates to a woman who had worked in a hospital. She was asked by an insurance officer whether she would be prepared to accept employment in a similar position in a hospital, and she naturally answered in the affirmative. These people who were led into giving answers in the affirmative to this type of question were disqualified on the basis that they were willing to accept employment at approximately the same wage or in a similar category, thereby limiting their availability for work, and were, therefore, not available for employment under the meaning of section 54 (2) (a).
Decisions arrived at on the basis of these answers have been appealed, but unfortunately the claimants always come up against decisions made by umpires which, under the act, conclude the cases. The commission has no authority to hear an appeal or reverse the decisions. The minister has no authority to change a decision made by the umpire.
At one stage of my naivety I wrote to the minister and the commission about these matters, and always received a lengthy page and a half explanatory letter substantiating the decision of the insurance officer or the decision made by the umpire. It was only after I discovered that the commission and the minister did not have the authority to change the decisions that I realized I was wasting my time.
One other situation which is unfair to claimants, particularly in areas such as the one 1 represent, which is fairly large geographically, is the remoteness of communities from larger centres. The unfairness to claimants in these areas is that they are deemed to be not available for work because the area in which they live does not provide an opportunity for work in the particular category in which they were working before. If they have been snared into answering the insurance officer's leading question in the affirmative, thus restricting themselves unknowingly to a particular type of work, they find themselves disqualified.
I have explained to some of these people the full complexities of the situation, and what is occurring is that this sort of rigidity in the interpretation of the law and the leading question approach of some insurance officers are resulting in claimants probably lying in their answers by saying that they

Supply-Labour
are willing to accept employment anywhere at any wage rate and in any capacity, thus getting away from the strictness of application of that particular section. I submit that once this sort of attitude toward the law becomes prevalent, and it is becoming more and more so as people become more conversant with what is taking place with regard to the interpretation of the section, the law falls into disrepute and people are led into dishonesty in order to get the benefits that they consider are legitimately theirs under the act. They do not see anything wrong in doing that sort of thing. Persons in large metropolitan areas such as Vancouver, Toronto or Winnipeg are in areas where there are great employment opportunities in a variety of trades and jobs and these other people do not see why an individual, merely because he happens to live in a large metropolitan area, should be able to receive benefits when they who have been living in the north or in some other remote area have been denied benefits. They do not see anything wrong about being expansive in their remarks to the insurance officer and saying that they are willing to work anywhere at any time and for any wage rate.
I realize this is something which can only be dealt with by an amendment to the statute because the interpretation of the present section has been so narrow and confined as to not permit of any broadening, and the only way we can break out of this rigidity is by changing the law itself. I point out again to the minister, as has been pointed out before, that this situation is working an undue hardship on many claimants. Because of the rigidity of the section and the leading nature of the questions asked, there is an unfair and unjust application of the law to many claimants who apply for benefits. I think the only solution open to us is for the minister to introduce an amendment to the section so that it can be applied in a broader manner than it has been in the past few years.
I do not know if the minister wants to make any comments pro or con. I have refrained from mentioning the names of individuals because it is not the thing to do, especially when there are quite a number of cases that revolve around this point, but I am sure the individuals who are interested as claimants would be interested in having the minister at least give this matter sympathetic consideration. If the minister would care to make any comment it would be helpful.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure almost all members of the house have representations from claimants and one of the most important subjects in those representations has to do with the application of the availability for work provision, because it is of the essence of qualification for benefits. As the hon. member for Skeena has said, the commission is powerless. I am quite ready to give a clear undertaking that this matter will be considered in the light of amendments we hope to introduce to the insurance system as quickly as we can. We will consider this question.
Item agreed to.
5d. The Senate-general administration, $107,600.

Mr. Chairman, before you put the question on this particular item I should like to make a few comments. It applies to the operation of what is politely or impolitely, depending upon the mood of the individual, referred to as the other place. This has always seemed to me to be a strange way to refer to it and I would prefer to refer to it as the Senate because that is what it is, and it is almost always referred to in that way.
The program of the New Democratic party, as was the case with our predecessor, the C.C.F., includes the abolition of the Senate. As that is one of the things we would like to see accomplished I cannot in conscience lend my support to the item before us for the simple reason that by so doing we would be running counter to our belief. We cannot support an item which tends to perpetuate a structure that we would like to see abandoned and cease to exist.
For many years the Senate has been nothing more than a haven for political appointees, regardless of what various prime ministers and political leaders have said over the years, even from the time of Sir John A. Macdonald, who I understand wanted to bring about some beneficial changes in the institution at that time. He had some idea that the Senate would be able to give what he called sober second thought to legislation which might be passed by a presumably rash House of Commons. It might be that sort of sober second thought one would give after overindulging in food and drink, a sort of sobriety arising out of sluggishness. This is the type of thing that has existed in the Senate, more an operation out of lethargy than anything else.

In recent years some proposals have been made by two governments with regard to what they have called reform of the Senate. One proposal was presented by the Conservative government to retire senators at age 75, and one was presented by the present government to retire at 75 only those senators appointed subsequent to the passage of a law providing that senators will retire at age 75. This sort of bland, anaemic, reformative approach really will not result in anything worth while in regard to the institution itself. In fact, I do not think it is amenable to reformation. It might even be considered incorrigible or beyond reform. Perhaps we should toss up our hands, admit that there is no possibility of reform and accede to the suggestion of this party that the institution itself be abolished, because in the whole scheme of things it is relatively useless.
Perhaps one could argue that it does perform one service, and I suppose this would depend upon which party one belongs to, in that in recent years the former governor of the Bank of Canada, James Coyne, gained his day in court which I agree was denied him by the Conservative government of the day, and denied him in a most reprehensible fashion. On the other hand, there was a Liberal majority in the Senate who saw fit to reflect the political atmosphere that existed in the House of Commons. If there had been a Conservative majority in the Senate, I do not believe anyone could argue that James Coyne would have had his day in court. The Conservative majority in the Senate, if it had existed at that time, would have carried out the edict of the government of the day and would have refused the governor his democratic rights under our free society. It could not even be argued that the Senate qualify by performing a useful function because it performed a useful function only by reason of the fact there was a Liberal majority who wanted to carry out the political fight that had been conducted in this chamber, incidentally not only by the Liberal party at that time but by the C.C.F. members who numbered some eight or nine on that occasion.
Now, there have been suggestions of alterations in the Senate, as I have stated, dating back to the time when Sir John A. Macdonald was prime minister. This was almost 100 years ago now. For many years, therefore, everybody, particularly prime ministers who have been asked to deal with this question, has said, yes, there needs to be some change in the structure of the Senate. In fact,
Sup p ly-Legis lation
I have a book here I obtained from the library entitled "Senate Reform", and it contains a reprint of a speech delivered by one C. Berkeley Powell, Esq., M.L.A. in the legislative assembly at Toronto, dated March 21, 1899. It is interesting to note that the legislature at that time had presented to it a motion by the attorney general, who incidentally was then a Liberal, with respect to the Senate of Canada. One of the provisions was that the British North America Act should be amended so as to provide that senators should be appointed or chosen for a limited term of years only, and not for life as at present. It is interesting to note that 66 years later we are still toying around with the idea of placing a limit on the term of years a person can serve in the Senate, but we have not got around to it yet.
I was amused also to note that in this book there are 14 pages that deal with the Senate and what it had accomplished at that time, what they thought were some of its worth-while attributes. Then, there are 147 pages that deal with the worth-while aspects of the Senate and the things which make it a commendable institution. Those 147 pages are absolutely blank. There is nothing on them, and to me that is an indication of the value of the Senate itself. It, likewise, has accomplished nothing worthy that could be marked up on the credit balance side. Rather than use my own words, I should like to make a brief quotation from an article written by John N. Turner, who at that time was associated with Stikeman & Elliott, barristers and solicitors in the city of Montreal. On page 57 of this particular book entitled "Essays in Honour of Henry F. Angus", there is an article entitled, "The Senate of Canada-Political Conundrum". I quote- and this pretty well summarizes everything that has been said about the usefulness of the Senate:
Today the debates in the upper house are so dull, dreary, and futile that the press rarely thinks it worth while to give them any coverage. Even more symptomatic of its decay is the political fact that recent governments of the day seem to have abandoned and ignored it. Saddest fact of all, the Senate has become an object of ridicule. Cynics call it the most exclusive club in the country, a haven of old men, retired politicians, and contributors to party funds.

[The Chairman.]

Then the Japanese people use their ingenuity, which we in Canada do not appear to be able to do, and put the coal and iron ore together and turn it into steel, and we in turn buy it back again.
By doing this we perpetuate something which is economically wrong for our nation, by continuing to assist the exploitation of its natural resources in their raw form. It would be much better if we used our money and ingenuity to turn our coal and iron ore into steel.
Even though this program may be helpful to the community at Fernie, and even though the export of Fernie coal and iron ore from mines on the west coast is helpful to those communities, I still raise objection to the fact that it seems to be senseless to continue to export raw materials, pay for part of their shipment, and then re-import the finished product at a much higher price. I wish to heaven somebody in the government would put on his thinking cap and try to devise ways and means to turn the iron ore and coal into steel in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thank my hon. friend for mentioning the fact that I am here. Mr. Chairman, I want to put details of a matter before the minister and assure her that I do this in all sincerity, because this request comes from people who consider this to be a matter of life and death. It is concerned with a drug known as laetrile, alleged to be a controlled drug, used in connection with cancer. The minister is probably aware of this. I think I can do no better in outlining the facts than to read to the committee the contents of a letter written to the right hon. Prime Minister not too long ago. I cannot vouch for and do not accept the accuracy of the statements contained in the letter, but the sincerity with which it

Supply-Health and Welfare and one or two other letters have been written compels me to put this matter before the committee. This letter is addressed to the Prime Minister and reads as follows:
Over a year ago I was told by the experts at the cancer clinic in Edmonton that I had cancer and had but three to six months to live.
Subsequently I was treated for cancer of the lungs in University Hospital here but my condition continued to worsen. In March of this year-nine months ago-I left hospital in a wheel chair- weak, unable to walk, or to care for myself.
By dint of diet and exercise I was able to build up sufficient strength to make the trip by air to Montreal. Perhaps to you an airplane trip is a relatively relaxed affair, but in my condition it was a major ordeal. At Montreal I received treatment for cancer with a drug called laetrile. Within three weeks I was free of pain and in six weeks I was walking a half mile to a mile a day as routine exercise.
On my return to Edmonton I continued taking laetrile and my condition continued to improve.
However, action of the federal food and drug administration has caused my supply of laetrile to be cut off. In the weeks since I have been deprived of medication my health has deteriorated and the pain has begun to return. I am dying again, and I ask you to use your influence and power to persuade food and drug to return my supply of laetrile. I am asking you to save my life.
There are many of us who can attest to the value and effectiveness of the drug which is now banned by this department. We ask that we be allowed to continue treatment. If there are doubts as to the long range effects of laetrile, surely this cannot be a matter of importance to a man who is dying anyway. We who need this drug ask only that its use be permitted in terminal cases or those who have been receiving it in the past.
I consider it a matter of life and death-my life or my death-when I ask your help.
I have another letter here from another person; I will just read one paragraph of it:
I was so ill that I spent the summer in bed. In the fall of 1963 I persuaded my daughter, against the advice of my doctors, to take me to Montreal where I received treatments with the drug laetrile. After five weeks of treatment I returned home under my own steam and in excellent health with no sign of pain. This drug is not a cancer cure. But it does control cancer and my health remained excellent until the recent ban on laetrile imposed by the food and drug administration.
I have one more letter from another person, and this is the last one:
After I took cobalt treatments for cancer the people at the clinic sent me home. They said X would be bed-ridden within three months and there was no hope for me. That was this past May. When I asked them how it was with me they said it was hopeless.
After that I heard about a drug called laetrile and I went to Montreal to get some. When I went down there I was so weak they had to take me off the plane in Winnipeg in a wheel chair. After I took treatments in Montreal the pain went away and I could walk again-
Now they won't let me have any more laetrile and the cancer is getting worse-and the pain

has returned and I can hardly walk again. Can you help me?
I served on the food and drugs committee and understand that following the thalidomide cases the act was amended, the regulations amended and a new schedule was brought into effect. The use of this drug, which under these regulations had been very restricted, was banned entirely until such time as those who are sponsoring it are able to prove effectively to the food and drugs administration that it has some benefits. The onus is upon them.
The food and drugs administration are of course compelled to abide by the law. I suggest to the minister that in the light of these letters written to the Prime Minister by those patients who are regarded as terminal cancer patients, and written with all sincerity, who believe that their prospects for future life are diminished or shortened, she will use her ingenuity to ascertain whether there is some way by which these patients can receive the benefit of this drug.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has raised the question of a drug about which I have received a number of letters, particularly from people in Edmonton. There seems to be sort of a campaign from that area recently. I think my hon. friend knows, as do all those who have written me, that this was a new drug. The McNaughton Foundation put it out in Canada, and neglected or refused to comply with the law which is enacted to protect all Canadians from the use of new drugs that have not been properly tested. Over some two years, beginning before I became minister, increasingly stern warnings were given to the foundation asking them to prove the assertions which they made for the drug and asking them to produce the evidence, if any, which they had. The foundation neglected or refused to do this. Solicitors on its behalf saw me shortly after I became minister, undertook to do certain things but never complied with those undertakings. Accordingly the department thereafter moved in the courts of the province of Quebec, where this drug was being made available, and obtained an injunction against the foundation, closing up their operation until they complied with the Food and Drugs Act. I am as touched as my hon. friend, and as anyone else, by the kind of letter that he has read into the record, but I have an obligation under the law in respect of which I have no discretion.

I do not want to hide behind the law in this particular case, but I think the ethic to which my hon. friend subscribes is a questionable one. He suggests that we should use a drug which is unproven, simply because certain individuals feel that it helps them. My hon. friend is a well read man and knows, I am sure, a great deal about the kind of self-hypnosis which people who are in deep pain can bring about. This is much like faith healing which is believed in by certain people because they feel someone or something is helping them.
I cannot say definitely of my own knowledge whether or not laetrile is useful for anything other than as a placebo. However, I would not be prepared as the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or even as a private individual, to play with the lives of persons who at this moment are characterized as terminal cases.
We know there have been breakthroughs, small admittedly, but what will ultimately be man's knowledge? There will be discoveries about the origin of cancer and the way it spreads. They may be made the day after tomorrow, and it may be possible to stop the spread of cancer. I do not wish to make anything available to these people which may hasten their demise, or which may even appear to lull them into thinking they are getting better, resulting in their denying to themselves the benefits of modern medicine which have been proven. I think what my friend has suggested is close to euthanasia, which is against the law of this country.
I listened with great care to the representations made, and have read many such letters, but this is not the first alleged cancer cure in respect of which the promoters have infringed the law and had to be stopped. I can only say to my hon. friend that the best professional advice I have received is that this compound cannot, or does not have the effect which it is alleged to have, and in any event the promoters have not really attempted to comply with the law.

May I say that I appreciate what the minister has said, and I know that she is under an obligation by her oath as a privy councillor to uphold the law. I hold no brief for this drug or for the people who manufacture it. However, it has been the subject of representations made to me during the last few months and I think I would have been derelict in my duty had I not brought these facts to the attention of the minister at this time. I have already been in touch with
Supply

Health and Welfare the administration, urging that the minister do her best to look into this situation as closely and with as much care as possible, because in the event that this drug is of benefit to terminal cases it should be given some consideration. My duty I believe is to place the facts before the minister, as I have done, and I hope she in turn will look into them.

Mr. Chairman, before the item carries I should like to ask the minister whether she has considered making some changes in the law similar to those made in respect of thalidomide. Those changes were quite radical.
I have also received letters, not only in respect of this drug, but in respect of others which seem to indicate that there is some reluctance on the part of manufacturers to comply with the law or to even consider the regulations. Has the minister considered that the federal government should undertake some research in respect of these drugs which perhaps cannot be done by other firms in their laboratories, in order to speed up the normal proving processes?
What the minister has said is very nice, but it sounded a little bit like a religious sermon. It was similar to that old story that we cannot do anything because it might hurt someone. On the other hand, there might be some value to these things as far as terminal cases are concerned. Usually when an individual is declared to be a terminal case he knows that nothing can be done for him and he completely loses any faith he had. The minister has suggested that perhaps this drug produces the same effect created by faith healing. I suggest that in itself is an advantage to these people.
I hope that the minister is looking for some way of preventing what happened in respect of thalidomide from happening in respect of other drugs. There should be more active participation in the field of drug research. We passed some very stringent regulations in respect of thalidomide and I think this may have had some bearing on the acceptance of new drugs. The department has some obligation to investigate the effects of new drugs, but I hope new drugs will be allowed into Canada under limited conditions in order that they may be tested. It may be unfair to suggest that the regulations adopted in respect of thalidomide were too restricting, because perhaps they were adopted at the time as a result of the terrible circumstances which developed from its use. I hope Canada will adopt less restrictive regulations, similar to

Supply-National Revenue those of other countries which will allow the testing and developing of new drugs.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is one of the items to which the right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred earlier today as being an estimate by which legislation is being achieved. I suggest to the President of the Privy Council that this item should be treated in the same way as the others, and withdrawn. These changes in the legislation should be introduced by way of bills to be considered and passed by the house in the normal manner.
As I read this vote it strikes out the words "December 31, 1964" which appear in section 10(1) of the Excise Tax Act. The vote reads in part:
Vote 3d-To authorize in the current and subsequent fiscal years-
It is not intended that this apply only to this year, but to subsequent fiscal years, so obviously this means a modification to the act. For that reason I suggest that the act should be amended in the normal way rather than by the inclusion of a supplementary estimate. There is another factor to be considered in regard to the question of amendments by means of supplementary estimates. If these amendments are passed by the house they will appear in an Appropriation Act and if a person is searching for amendments to a statute he should not be called upon to look through Appropriation Acts in order to find the amendments to various statutes.
I do not question that there is good reason for the proposal. That is not the subject under consideration so far as I am concerned. I am simply dealing with the method by which once again in this book of supplementary estimates we are asked to amend a statute by means of a supplementary estimate, and I suggest that this item be withdrawn and that the proper course be followed as is going to be done with some of the others to which we have drawn attention.

The purpose of this vote arises from the amendments to the Excise Tax Act which took place in 1963, lifting the exemption on construction materials with regard to the application of the sales tax. At that time it was stated that the government did not wish this action to be retroactive and provision was made in the section quoted by my hon. friend to give the Department of National Revenue the right to make refunds to particular taxpayers in order to alleviate any retroactive effect of the legislation. The date, December 31, 1964, which is the only thing that is being changed by this particular amendment, was put in in order to arrive at some finality with regard to the determination of when these refunds should be made.
Since that time there have been representations to the government indicating that there are some contracts in Canada which were entered into prior to June 13, 1963 and which could not possibly be completed by December 31, 1964. For the information of hon. members I might mention that one of the most important is the Peace river project in British Columbia which has some $54 million still to be expended on it.
The position of the purchaser is fully protected by the fact that he has a fixed price contract. However, the position of the vendor or person who has to perform the service is not protected and therefore he is caught in a squeeze. He must absorb against his business operations any losses arising because of the application of the sales tax on construction materials.
I think it is very important that this item be passed in order that these contractors, who entered into these fixed price contracts in good faith before the enactment of the legislation, may continue to receive the same sort of treatment they have received to date under the legislation as originally enacted. If this were long delayed it would put the particular contractors in a very dangerous position financially in some instances and I commend the vote to the house as an alleviating item to allow us to deal with these contractors in the future in the way we have previously dealt with them.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to protest the passing of this item. I do not question for one moment that it is vital and necessary but this is not the proper way to handle it. I would ask that it be withdrawn and that the necessary changes in the statute be brought in by way of amendment to the act, and not by legislative action through supplementary

*estimates. I do not want to speak at length on this matter again, but when another member of the House of Commons referred tonight to 10 or 11 items he was asked to speak on them individually when they came forward. This one is before us now and I am protesting against its passing as I did at 7.30 tonight with regard to other items, and as I will protest with regard to a few more as we get toward the end of the book. This item should be withdrawn and a legitimate amendment to the act should be passed by the parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr Chairman, I do not want to prolong the discussion but there is a fair amount of endurance over here. The minister made a good explanation of the purpose of the proposed item but, as I said earlier, I am not concerned with the substance of it. I do not question the value of what the minister is attempting to do but I urge that it be done in the normal method, by way of an amending bill.
The minister said it would be unfortunate if the suggested change were too long delayed. I do not anticipate a long delay with regard to this matter. As I mentioned with regard to the other items which will subsequently be introduced in the form of legislation at the next session, why can we not have a small bill with one line in it striking out the words which are to be struck out, and why would such a bill not be passed by the house within minutes? Again I suggest to the President of the Privy Council that when urgent matters have to be considered it is not unusual to interrupt the address in reply to the speech from the throne and deal with matters that should be dealt with quickly.
What I foresee with regard to matters like this, to which we are not offering objection as to substance, is that next week we can take fifteen minutes some day at a quarter to six or a quarter to ten or from ten to 10.15 and pass two or three small bills which have already received discussion in committee today, thus regularizing the amendment of our statutes. That is the point I am making and this is the request I put before the Minister of National Revenue and the President of the Privy Council.
The subject matter that has delayed the passing of the supplementary estimates is the attempt in these estimates to effect changes in legislation by means of the supplementary estimates. It is to that we are objecting. Whether or not it was done in the past is of no concern. I think we should now set our course for the future and see that this does
Supply-National Revenue not happen again. It is for that reason we are emphasizing this point. Let us have supplementary estimates for the purpose for which they were intended, as extensions of the main estimates just as was the case when we were dealing with national defence a few moments ago. The President of the Privy Council said that the $7 million in that case was just an extension of the $400 million voted for tanks and armoured fighting vehicles when the main estimates were before us. There was an underestimating of the cost. That is what supplementary estimates are for and this is clearly understood by the house. Supplementary estimates are not intended for the amending of the statutes of Canada, and this is one item which should be withdrawn.

Mr. Chairman, I agree to some extent with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre when he suggests that major amendments to statutes should not be made by supplementary estimates. However, the minister has explained that the purpose of this item is simply to do justice to certain contractors who had entered into firm contracts for work that could not possibly be completed before the sales tax was applicable. It is simply a case of doing justice to these contractors who were faced with an act of parliament over which they had no control. By that I mean that if the tax were applicable their costs would be substantially increased after they had entered into contracts from which there was no escape. It seems to me that this is not really a major amendment to legislation because if contracts were entered into after the sales tax on building materials was known to the contractors, they could have included that in their estimates.
I would hope, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre would reconsider, because this is not intended as a major amendment to the legislation imposing the sales tax. It is simply giving redress to those who found themselves in a position from which there was no escape.
I recall clearly, so far as some of the contracts in relation to the Peace river dam are concerned, several members of our party suggested to the government that something of this nature should be done because there were contracts in the amount of several millions of dollars for which the materials could not possibly have been purchased. As I said, I think it is just giving simple justice to people who got caught in point of time because of an act of parliament. I hope that we can, in fact, recognize there is some justice that needs to be done.

Supply-National Revenue

In reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I say I believe this is not a major amendment to the act but rather provision for the department to continue expenditures beyond December 31, 1964 in order to assure that no one is affected retroactively by legislation which was introduced in this house on June 13, 1963.

May I ask a question? The minister says these contracts were signed prior to the first introduction of the sales tax. If this is so, why did the department wait until now? Why is it so urgent to have this done now when everybody has known since that time that the 11 per cent was going to become effective in April of this year? Can the minister answer that?

Yes, I have an answer. In answer to the first part of the question, the hon. member is quite correct that over the past 18 months these contracts have come forward. However, only in the recent past have we known how much was involved in this and how many contracts there were. People came forward gradually and indicated their contract was not going to be finished. When the legislation was passed many contractors did not know their contracts could not be finished by December 31, 1964. I think all contractors who could finish by that time made every effort to get their contracts completed. However, the department could not have known the full implications involved.

There must have been some contractors who came to the department after December 31 last year, but you have had January, February and March, three months, to take action. Do you mean to say all these contracts have just come forward before the supplementary estimates were introduced? Surely you had knowledge as to what contractors would not be able to complete these contracts in January or early February?

The Minister of National Revenue has referred to the fact that this is really not of any great importance. Actually, what we have before us is a budget resolution, and not a supplementary estimate at all. While we are not questioning the importance of the action that is proposed under this measure, we do protest the instrumentality for achieving that purpose. When I consider the number of items that have been withdrawn today and compare them to this one which has to do with the remission of taxation, I cannot help but think it is even more important that this item be set aside.

It does not appear as if the minister is willing to go along with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. It would certainly eliminate a lot of questions which we wish to ask him about the 11 per cent sales tax and the manner in which it is being collected at the present time. Earlier, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary the Minister of Labour stated that the 11 per cent sales tax had not affected the construction industry in any way.
There is no better example of just how seriously it affected the construction industry than this item before us. It is an indication of just how seriously it has affected some of the construction companies in this nation. I should like to ask the minister certain questions for verification purposes, because I still get a great many complaints from lumber industries in my constituency about the collection of the 11 per cent sales tax.
I do not know how aware the minister is of the number of complaints relating to the difficulty his officials are having in interpreting the act. I should like to obtain his views on the subject because I had a letter from one constituent who is rather a substantial dealer in lumber for the construction industry. He told me that when the act first went into effect the Department of National Revenue was willing to go along with a $5,000 fidelity bond to permit the dealer to collect the taxes. After some time the officials of the department went over the books of the concern in question with the result that the company has had to purchase a $250,000 fidelity bond at their expense in order to collect this 11 per cent sales tax for the government.
I think this is a serious situation because not only are we asking the lumber dealers to do the government a service, but we are charging them or we are forcing upon them an extra expense in order to do this. The small lumber dealers in my constituency are in the same position. Surely, we should have some explanation as to what the department is going to do to eliminate this irritating situation.
