Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment-to extend the purposes of northern affairs and national resources vote 20 of the main estimates for 1964-65 to include authority to make preliminary expenditures on the proposed new national park in the areas of Kejimkujik lake in Nova Scotia, $1.

The planning of this park was done by the Conservative government and
Supply-Northern Affairs handed to the present administration on a silver platter, but it has taken this government a long time to announce this addition to our national parks.
There is considerable unemployment in the Queens county area of Nova Scotia, particularly in the district where this park is to be established. In view of that I ask when can we hope to see a full scale start made on developing the park in order to provide much needed employment in the area, and to provide necessary facilities for the tourists who will be arriving in Nova Scotia in June? Also, what happened to the sea front that was planned for this park, a section of which was incorporated in the plan drawn up in 1962? We have heard nothing about it from the present administration. There are suitable areas available in Queens county and also in the Crescent beach area in Lunenburg county. I ask the minister to give us some idea of his plans along these lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
We have received complete cooperation from the government of Nova Scotia with respect to this park, co-operation which is required because it has to obtain the property for us and turn it over to us free of encumbrances. This vote is not asking for any new money. We had the money in our estimates, but it is putting a proper allocation to the money. We have spent it on certain roadways within the territory and on surveys in co-operation with the province of Nova Scotia.
We are extremely happy to be making large expenditures during the next three years in this area, because an economic survey indicates the economic situation there is very bad, with high unemployment and extremely low individual family incomes. We think these expenditures will have the effect of raising the nature of its economy perceptibly.
It is our intention to spend something like $650,000 during the current year, on work in the park, $1,375,000 in the following year and $1,850,000 in 1967-68. A great deal of the work will be on roads and certain small improvements within the park. It will be a day park. It is not our intention to build accommodation within the park, but rather to encourage the building of accommodation outside in the economically difficult area.

I thank the minister for his explanation. I should like to take this opportunity to urge upon him the necessity in my view of making a thorough study of the need to add this seashore area to the park. After all, it is hoped this park will serve as

Supply-Northern Affairs a great tourist attraction at the western end of Nova Scotia and no doubt tourists visiting this part of Canada will expect to find a suitable shoreline made available in conjunction with the park. I hope the minister will give this favourable consideration when he begins to plan his estimates for next year.

Item agreed to.
55d. Reimbursement of the northern administration branch stores account for the value of stores which have become obsolete or unserviceable, $53,439.

Reading this item one comes to the conclusion that some materials have deteriorated. What happens to them in such a case? Does the government make a gift of them to somebody, or does it sell them. What about the obsolete part of the material?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
This item pertains largely to northern administration-inaccessible places where deliveries are made about once a year. The most astonishing thing I came across in this department was when I went to Frobisher. I found there were warehouses there stockpiled with materials of all kinds, including two or three carloads of cement which had hardened like stone and a carlot or two of plywood. I asked my officials to bring me an inventory of the contents of those three warehouses and it reached a total value of no less than $665,000.
There had been careless purchasing all along. The government of the day apparently intended to revive the economy by buying goods in southern Canada and shipping them out to the Arctic. There were a dozen or more washing machines. There were items which could not conceivably be used in the northern territories.
Farley Mowat.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
We have arrived at a point where we have to pay attention to this situation and write these things off by means of a bookkeeping entry.
The hon. member has asked what we do with these things. Disposition is statutory, of course. Those things which have any value at all are turned over to surplus assets for disposal. We shall do our best to put them to some use in those particular areas but there are numbers of items which have no utility at all.

This is the type of interesting explanation of bureaucratic bungling which should be provided to parliament in a voluntary way without our having to ask

questions about it. It is well known that over the years people within the administration of the department we are now considering, people in the south as they are called, do not have, generally speaking, the foggiest idea about the situation in the north, but try by means of an ivory tower approach to conceive what should take place in areas with which they are not familiar. This is an example of the loss to the taxpayer which results because of the empire building which has gone on in the hon. gentleman's department in the past. It indicates also, by the very dollar value attached to the material in question, the extent of the benefits which might have accrued to the people who live in the north had there been some sensible consultation with them in the first instance.
One could spend a great deal of time deploring this state of affairs. Suffice it to say, I hope this is a sufficient lesson for those who are handling these things to profit by the mistakes of the past and try to operate this aspect of northern affairs in such a way that it benefits the people in the north. It is a disgraceful and deplorable state of affairs for a minister to have to report that there is such a degree of waste of the taxpayers money-obviously waste which results from ignorance or the desire to build empires within the department or for some other foolish reason. I, for one, hope we will not see any more of it.

The minister referred to materials stored at Frobisher and I think he mentioned the figure of $600,000. He referred to cement and plywood which were no longer useable. I wonder if he would tell us just how long this material had been in storage. To which government was he referring?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I thought the hon. member would have known. The cement went up there in the years 1959, 1960 and 1961 and the plywood went up at the same time. Many thousands of feet of copper piping for the conduct of gas went up at the same time. They do not have much gas around Frobisher. I can only explain supplies of this kind on the basis that the government was determined to revive the economy of southern Canada by buying certain commodities to send north, because they had no utility there at all.

Would it put a strain on the minister's memory to recall millions of dollars worth of similar equipment stored not only in

Frobisher but all round the northern outposts for which the administration previous to that of my right hon. friend was responsible, resulting in a far greater waste than the $600,000 to which the minister just referred?

I am interested in this item and I am not really satisfied with what the minister has said. I think it is safe to say that though an attempt has now been made to say that one government was no worse than another, neither government had a thing to do with this. The administration of the department of northern affairs is in the hands of civil servants. It is they who made the decisions then and it is the same people who make the decisions now. It is my belief that with few exceptions the minister has not yet been able to seize the whole potential of his department.
I think the minister is aware that, in practice, materials declared surplus in the north have always found their way into the Hudson's Bay Company trading posts for resale. The hon. gentleman and his officials have no doubt seen a film, which I also saw a year or so ago, which indicated the waste and extravagance which takes place. I am not prepared to blame any particular government for this. I think it is caused by loose administration. For example, cans of oil were shipped to the north. They were found not suitable for outboard motors, but when this material was declared obsolete the Hudson's Bay Company got hold of it and sold it to the Eskimos in that area. This resulted in the ruin of most of their motors. This oil was bought for very little, and sold at an exorbitant price in places where no alternative oil was available for the motors. The minister is surely aware of this.
I would like to know if the minister-and I am sure he has considered it-has taken precautions to see that the things declared as obsolescent do not find their way back into trade. I think it is wise and advantageous for northern affairs, if they are going to declare some of this stuff surplus, to put it through their own agents and if possible give it as gifts, or in lieu of other kinds of consideration, to the local populations. This has happened not only in northern affairs. Everyone knows that obsolete pork was being sold across the counter in stores throughout Canada when we had paid a near fortune for it. It was not the fault of any particular government, but both governments and their officials were involved.
The fault lies in our inability to handle obsolete goods in many cases. We should give
Supply-Northern Affairs them to the local people or keep them out of the trade, where they work to the detriment of the people. I could name other things that were declared obsolete in the past in the area and were used to the detriment of the people. I would like an assurance from the minister that he has considered this problem, because he is well aware of the fact that this oil was involved because it was brought to his attention by the senior officials of his department. It is something that I think the minister should assure the members of the committee is not being repeated.
If we are going to write it off I believe there is no one in this house who would not agree with our giving it to those who can use it, rather than putting it back into the trade. This has always been a problem, and I think the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will find himself in exactly the same position as anyone else who has been involved in northern commerce, whether it be government or private industry. All he needs to do is travel anywhere in the north and he will find empty gas drums that could be collected and probably put back into some use. These articles are being held in very large caches because it is not possible, feasible or economical to bring them to any place where they can be put back into commerce again. This is a fact. Once you have the cement in northern Canada, what are you to do with it? You cannot bring it back. What are you going to do with the plywood? You cannot bring it back. If it cannot be brought back, it should be given to the people in the area to be used to their advantage. I could cite the example of the rancid butter being sold by Hudson's Bay that was originally purchased for government requirements.
If these things had been declared obsolete before their value deteriorated completely, they would have been useful to the people living in the area. In the case of the butter and oil, they became a liability to the people up there, and a liability that cost them a considerable amount of money and at the same time was detrimental to them. I am always scared when I see something declared obsolete and written off, because there is really no indication as to what happens to it.
Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if I could wish you a good morning.

Along with those good wishes I think a little speed might help.

Supply-Northern Affairs

Mr. Chairman, I am somewhat surprised that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources should come into the chamber at this late hour and start making political charges. Surely if he is interested in concluding the session this morning he will take some advice from the hon. member for Timiskaming, who indicated that no particular government is necessarily at fault for what has occurred, and will admit that the hon. member for Timiskaming might just be in line in pointing out that the administration in the northland might have something to do with what has occurred, which he has indicated as being stupidity or whatever it might be called on the part of the former government. I am sure that if we wanted to argue about this all night we could find there would be a great many examples of the same thing happening in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has advanced an entirely new doctrine. I always thought that the minister, the head of the department, was responsible. If we are going to accept the fact that the minister has no responsibility and are going to blame our civil servants, then we come to an irresponsible situation. The minister must remain responsible, as my hon. friend knows.
I can assure the hon. member for Timiskaming that we are trying to run a tighter ship than has been run in the past, and I think it is tighter already. But it is more difficult to send goods up to the north on once a year delivery, because if you make an error it is a real one. There is new machinery up there costing $3,000 or $4,000, and my hon. friend knows that if we were to bring it back to southern Canada it would only be worth $10; all the rest would be freight. But we are supervising our supplies much more closely than they were watched, and I think we have registered economies already.

Mr. Chairman, could I ask what decision the department has made in the particular cases that I mentioned of the butter and oil? This was brought to the minister's attention, I am quite sure, because he must have known that some inquiry had been made. There is no secret about where the information came from; it came from Bill Eccles who went up into the east side of the area and ran into a great deal of difficulty with the Hudson's Bay Company. He made a film which was seen by the officials of the department and a number of charges were made at that time. If I remember correctly, there was an agreement or a commitment
[The Acting Chairman (Mr. Tardif).]
made by some of the officials that there would be some investigation into the charges that were made. I wonder whether the minister has any knowledge of a report that came from the charges that were made and from the visual picture that the officials got from seeing this film?
Shall vote 55d carry?

I am not interested in just making a statement, Mr. Chairman; I do not know what happened and I want to know, because I was very impressed with the presentation that was made at that time. The minister again falls into a very particular failing that his government is continually falling into. One of his colleagues the other day got up and said, "I have complete faith in my officials", and somebody else gets up and says, "I have complete faith in my officials". If the minister does have this complete faith, he must be either all-knowing or the reverse, because his department is a very extensive one. I have been in parts of the north; it is fairly isolated and I am sure the minister is not completely aware of what happens in every area there. Charges have been made that there has been monkey business between the officials of his department and the factors of Hudson's Bay. Take, for example, the case of this oil selling at 90 cents a quart, as has been mentioned. If you can get the oil for nothing because it is surplus to requirements, and it is sold for 90 cents, there is 45 cents for the local administrator and 45 cents for the factor of the Hudson's Bay Company; and they keep the other oil in the containers until they have unloaded the surplus. To my mind it is a fairly complicated problem and the minister is really stretching the bounds of credulity if he expects us to believe that he can really take responsibility for everybody in his department. It is very nice to hear this, but it does not really mean anything.
Personally I would like to know whether he has received a report on this particular problem. We are not asking him specifically what has been declared obsolete in Fort George or Moosonee, for example, or any of the other particular areas; but it is quite possible that the same situation continues to develop. I suggest that the minister should be able to give us some assurance that he is either looking into this matter or is prepared to look into it. If he does not, then I am not sure we should write this off. Perhaps we should hang on to it because this could

be very detrimental to the operation of good government in the territories. After all, the government here is the government of the territories. There are no representatives of local government in these areas. The real administrator is this government, and I think this could be used in a detrimental way.
Mr. Chairman-
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about the minister coming into this house at midnight and making statements of the kind he has made. When did he learn of these facts-at ten minutes to midnight? Did he feel at that time that he had to come down and give these facts to this committee? When was this information brought to his attention and how long has he been carrying it as a great burden on his soul, keeping it from this house?

As I said earlier, Mr. Chairman, and I will repeat it again, the operations of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the territories is closely allied with the operations carried out in the Soviet union. This involves a communal system in which the state is all powerful, with crushing oppressiveness, and this is the same whether it operates in Canada or the Soviet union. As long as the rules are the same, the results are the same.
The minister enunciated a correct doctrine which applies under our form of government, when he said that the minister must accept responsibility for what takes place within a department under his jurisdiction. We agree with that doctrine. Sometimes there are ministers who are incompetent, or incapable of knowing what does take place, or incapable of accepting responsibility. I do not include the present minister of northern affairs in that category.
Once the minister of northern affairs declares that he is going to accept this responsibility, with which we all agree, or has an obligation to accept this responsibility, there are several results and obligations. The minister has to either accept responsibility for what occurs in his department and correct the abuses, or fire the officials who are responsible for the abuses. In the alternative he must resign. He cannot simply stand up and say that he believes that he should accept responsibility for what has occurred. It is not good enough for him just to make a simple declaration of that kind, unless he is prepared to back it up with some action.
Supply-Northern Affairs
Anyone who has a remote understanding of what has occurred within the department of northern affairs, and the hon. member for Timiskaming only mentioned one or two things which had come to his attention as a result of a film made about a specific area of the territories, knows that there are abuses as a result of incompetent officials, and knows that there are officials who have not even a vague idea of what is taking place, but who try to operate from the sanctity of their offices here in Ottawa. These officials try to transmit their dreams or visions, as they were called at one time, into reality in the north, but they usually turn into nightmares for the people who live there.
I hope the minister will follow through and take his responsibility seriously, and will present evidence to this house at some subsequent date, perhaps during our consideration of the main estimates, to show that he has accepted his responsibility seriously, with the result that these abuses have been terminated by the removal of those individuals who have been responsible or delinquent. If he is not able to do this he should tender his resignation.
There is a motion now on the order paper in respect of a procedure and rules committee which, if passed, will change the committee structure. I hope one of the first items referred to an appropriate committee will be the estimates of the minister's department, so that there may be a complete and thorough examination of its operation at which time we will be able to ferret out those things which have been kept under cover and hidden for so long.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak during the consideration of these supplementary estimates, but having listened to the debate that has taken place, I now want to be very sure that I understood correctly what the minister has said. Has the minister made the charge that there was over $600,000 worth of goods in warehouses at Frobisher which was placed there during the period I was the minister which has now been wasted? speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: When I want the hon. member to put words in my mouth I will tell him, but until that time I will make my own statements. This is a little different now.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The hon. member is not going to make me withdraw my statement to the effect that the situation I found was an example of the worst business inefficiency I have seen in a long time. I can assure this house that goods which have no value in the area of the Arctic will not be sent there under my administration.
The hon. member for Skeena made this point. It is so easy to ship materials or items into the north that have no value to the people of the north. On the other hand, there are some very simple things sent there from southern Canada that have the greatest value to people of the north. We are making changes as rapidly as possible in the direction that has been indicated tonight. There is the old

story of the acres of drums. We are replacing them today with storage tanks in most of the larger settlements. We are getting out of state domination as fast as we can. We are about to let a contract for $350,000 in services to a private individual in one place, involving sewage and water supply as well as other services. In other words, it seems to us that the sooner we can turn over these services to individuals who live there the year round the better for us, and the greater permanence there is for the people there. These are the things we are attempting to do in that area.
I am not grossly critical of the department. I do not agree that there are a great number of employees in the department at Ottawa who care nothing about the north. This is not the case. We have a tremendous number of dedicated servants both in the north and in Ottawa, but I do insist that errors and waste have occurred in the past, which I am going to try to prevent from now on.

The minister has admitted that there was no waste of $600,000 at Frobisher Bay but I think he should give us some precise figures. I will accept the responsibility for some waste because you cannot operate in the north as you would operate a business in the south. But I do not think the impression should be left that the waste is slightly less than $600,000. Would the minister estimate whether it was $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 or $25,000? Do not leave the figure of $600,000 lying around or you will have started a real battle.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I wanted to make it very plain to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and I think he is aware that I stated that the inventory in three warehouses was $660,000. I want to get that straightened out. I do not want to leave anything up in the air. The minister has admitted to less than $600,000 and he said that $25,000 was too low. Would he say $30,000?

Shall
the vote carry?

speechtext: I would be very happy to let the hon. member know as soon as I possibly can what the exact waste was but I have not got the figure with me tonight.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

I figure I am just as good a manager as anybody else and I

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

Could the minister explain the expenditure of $275,000 for mail service by air? What does that cover, and where?

Would the minister take notice of a recent statement made by a highly placed official in the post office, that it is no longer safe to drop first class mail in letter boxes?
Shall the vote carry?
I should like some kind of explanation.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I will give an explanation. I never heard that statement before.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I read the speech made by the president of the C.B.C. which he made to an audience in Montreal recently, and in which he hoped the Fowler commission would recommend that the government give a ten year charter to the corporation. subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton Norlh and Vicloria):
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Would the commission be dealing with matters such as censorship in the C.B.C.?
I refer to an instance where a clergyman, the secretary of the synod of the Presbyterian church in the maritime provinces, was cut off the air in Sydney, Nova Scotia, because he happened to be expressing a particular theological belief. He has forwarded copies of his text. Since I am not a theological student I would be glad to let the minister read this text for himself, but there is nothing in it to be found by me or by others who have read it which appears offensive to other denominations. However, the manager of radio station CBI cut this person off the air during the series known as "Plain Talk" on this radio station.
I have some questions on the order paper at the present time with reference to this series. As yet there has been no chance for an answer to be given, but this is a matter which I think should be brought to the attention of the committee and of the minister. Number 8 in this series of questions asked: "How much plain talk is allowed by the C.B.C. in their series "Plain Talk"? Apparently the manager of CBI does not believe in allowing freedom of speech. It seems that if whoever is speaking does not please the manager of the station he wants to cut them off.
I hold no brief for the Rev. Mr. Bean, who has written to me on this subject, nor do I have an animosity toward Mr. Kenneth Hill, the manager of the station. I do not know either of them. But it is a serious situation in this day and age when a man who speaks on the C.B.C. is not allowed to expound certain philosophies. In question number 9 of the series of questions I placed on the order paper, I asked:
In the past 15 months, apart from news columnist and broadcaster Gordon Sinclair, how many individuals have been allowed by the C.B.C. to expound the philosophy of atheism on their faculties?
Mr. Sinclair is a member of the C.B.C. backscratcher club, and it would seem that at any time he is able to boast on the air that he does not believe in God. Surely, then, we can allow Catholic priests, Presbyterian clergy, rabbis and others to express their philosophy without the manager of a radio station cutting them off on the ground-in this case, at least-that what was said was offensive to other religious denominations.
To be fair to Mr. Hill, I should like to quote from the Cape Breton Post of March 31, 1965:

Meanwhile, CBI manager Kenneth Hill said the decision had been made with respect to Mr. Bean's program on one ground-that the program "Plain Talk" was not designed to be used for airing of theological positions or differences.
I submit it would be difficult for a clergyman of any denomination to express himself on radio or anywhere else unless he is able to talk about his theological position.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me to interrupt him to say this: if there were an item relating to the C.B.C. in the estimates, what the hon. member is saying would no doubt be appropriate. But these are appropriations for the Department of the Secretary of State; they really have nothing whatever to do with the administration of the C.B.C. I wonder whether at this late hour the hon. gentleman would mind if we undertake to see that this matter is brought to the attention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and that he receives his answer in the usual way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for those words. Would he allow me to quote the manager of the radio station in order to be fair to Mr. Hill? Then I will let it go to another occasion. Mr. Hill said:
Personally, whether or not I agree with the views taken by Mr. Bean is of no consequence and has no bearing on this matter. I defend his right to set out his views but in the right place. The program "Plain Talk" was not intended for this use. That was the only question here and it was upon this basis that decisions were made.
According to Mr. Hill the only place where a speaker can express his theological position is in a church. The program, he says, was not intended for this purpose. However, it seems to me we do have a situation here where censorship has been used and I do not think there should be censorship within the C.B.C., despite much of the filth expressed by speakers of television and radios on occasion.

10d. Translation bureau, $48,000.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Looking at the translation booths tonight I am reminded that the translators have been there since eleven o'clock this morning.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: They are inside translators.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
They come under the bureau. We seem to abuse them here. We have had real problems in translation in the house tonight.
After discussing this matter with people who are familiar with the situation in which the government of Canada has responsibility for providing a translation service, it occurs to me it might be advantageous for the government to consider purchasing a machine capable of doing translation work, similar, though possibly on a smaller scale, to the one in use at the United Nations. Information which is placed in that machine is translated into another language. I presume there is a possibility of operating such a machine 24 hours a day, provided sufficient material is available. It occurs to me that much of the translation with which we have to deal involves the translation of reports and documents of a routine nature. I do not know whether Univac or IBM translators would serve this purpose. No doubt there are several types of machine available and we should perhaps think of using something of this nature in the Department of the Secretary of State so as to make translations of at least documents and reports. I wonder whether the minister has considered this matter. Is there some merit in a committee examining the whole problem we have in translation? I

Supply-Secretary of State think it is generally agreed that the work that has been done in this field has been good; it is probably fairly accurate, and it has been done under duress because it has grown from nothing a few years ago to a very large and necessary service.
It seems to me that if the United Nations found it necessary-although it is true that they are translating into five languages rather than just two-to turn to some other means, it is quite possible that the Canadian government would find itself much more able to meet some of the needs, if they did the same, particularly in view of the need that developed not long ago when it looked as though it would be advantageous to fly this stuff to the United Nations and use their machine to speed up the translation. We might find that a machine of this type would be within the scope of the federal government and would probably eliminate some of the problem that appears to be growing, rather than diminishing.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at this stage I can only tell the hon. member that we are very conscious indeed of the problem that exists and we are also considering all ways and means possible to make the service the most efficient that we can have.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I appreciate what the minister has said, Mr. Chairman, and I think it is generally true. I believe it is also true that this is a relatively new field. We may think we are bilingual, but I am sure that when I came here in 1957 this was not the problem that it is today. There were no translation systems even in the house, so the problem has grown very rapidly. For this reason I hope the minister will consider what I think would be a pretty stereotyped translation system, where machines might be able to do this work. I am not suggesting- and I hope it is not conveyed to anybody that I am suggesting this-that we should eliminate the other forms of translation that we use, but for certain fields we might save a lot of our people if we were able to provide that type of service which appears to be working in other areas.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister could just give us a breakdown of these outside translation fees so that we have an idea of what is actually involved?

increase in the volume of work to be translated and the result of this was that we had to get more work done by translators outside the public service. If the hon. member would agree to wait for a few days, I would be very happy to give him any breakdown that he wants; but 1 do not have it available at the moment.

I think it would be discourteous not to receive it.
As long as they do not talk about the reports any more.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Despite the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether I could ask this question: Is there not something which could be done, some way which could be found, whereby we could have a discussion on these two reports, if not tonight, then perhaps on Monday morning? I recognize that the plan is to prorogue this session tonight, but speaking as one of the 15 members of Your Honour's committee, I would remind hon. members that these two reports have the unanimous support of the committee, and I think I can speak for all members of the committee when I say we feel it would be most unfortunate if there were no opportunity for the house to make its decision. The house may reject our work, but surely there should be an opportunity for this decision to be made. We feel that if a decision is not made in this session we shall not have an opportunity to try out in the next session the experiments which we propose. I know this upsets the plan to prorogue tonight, but we do not know how long they will be in the other place and it is almost two o'clock in the morning. What about a short recess to see if we can save the work which the committee has done?
Perhaps I can assist the hon. member. I do think the suggestion that this message should be read is a correct one. Then we could probably adjourn at the call of the Chair.

I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following communication:
Ottawa, April 3, 1965
Sir:
I have the honour to inform you that the Honourable Robert Taschereau, P.C., Chief Justice of Canada, in his capacity as deputy to His Excellency the Governor General will proceed to the Senate chamber at 2,15 a.m. today April 3, 1965 for the purpose of proroguing the second session of the 26th parliament of Canada.
I have the honour to be, sir,
A. G. Cherrier
Assistant Secretary to the Governor General
May I suggest that the sitting be suspended at the call of the Chair?

The house resumed at 2.25 a.m.
A message was delivered by Major C. R. Lamoureux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable house in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the house went up to the Senate chamber.
In the Senate chamber the Deputy Governor General was pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent to the following bills:
An act to amend the Criminal Code (Habeas
Corpus).
An act to incorporate Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada.
An act to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors.
An act to amend the Companies Act.
An act respecting the operation of certain established federal-provincial programs.
An act to incorporate World Mortgage Corporation.
To these bills the royal assent was pronounced by the Clerk of the Senate in the following words:
In Her Majesty's name, the Honourable the Deputy Governor General doth assent to these bills.
Then the Speaker of the House of Commons addressed the Deputy Governor General as follows:
May it please Your Honour:
The Commons of Canada have voted supplies required to enable the government to defray certain expenses of the public service.
Royal Assent
In the name of the Commons I present to Your Honour the following bills:
An Act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending the 31st March, 1966.
An Act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending the 31st March, 1965.
To which bills I humbly request Your Honour's assent.
To these bills the Clerk of the Senate, by command of the Deputy Governor General, did thereupon say:
In Her Majesty's name, the Deputy Governor General thanks her loyal subjects, accepts their benevolence, and assents to these bills.

After which the Deputy Governor General was pleased to close the second session of the twenty sixth parliament of Canada with the following speech:
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
The second session of the twenty sixth parliament opened on February 18, 1964, and you have been in session for a longer time than any other parliament in our history. You have enacted much important legislation and approved many government actions of great significance for Canadians.
Canada was honoured by the presence of Her Majesty The Queen, and of His Royal Highness The Duke of Edinburgh last October, when we commemorated the conferences held a century before which paved the way to confederation.
In the past year there was a very substantial increase in the number of people employed in Canada. Unemployment was reduced to the lowest level for many years. Economic growth has accelerated. The 1964 expansion in the gross national product was the largest percentage increase to be achieved since 1956. The incomes of Canadians have risen to new high levels. Exports have greatly improved, including particularly exports of manufactured products. Interest rates have been held at relatively low levels and monetary conditions have assisted business expansion. The government's budget deficit has been sharply reduced.
The first report of the economic council of Canada, analysing the great potentialities for the expansion of the Canadian economy between now and 1970, has been laid before you. My ministers are assessing the policies required to meet the challenge of these potentialities.
My government has agreed with the governments of all the provinces to recommend a measure whereby all amendments to the constitution of Canada will in future be enacted in Canada.
You have made an important reform by providing that independent commissions shall undertake the redistribution of electoral districts for the House of Commons, on a basis that will rectify many disparities in the representation of the people.
Following the recommendation of a special committee representative of all parties in the House of Commons, you have expressed your approval of a distinctive Canadian flag. By royal proclamation this flag, in the Canadian colours of red and white, and bearing the Canadian emblem of the

Prorogation
maple leal, was Inaugurated on February 15, 1965. My ministers are convinced that, through the years, the flag will constitute an important contribution to Canadian unity and Canadian identity.
With Her Majesty's consent, and in accordance with your recommendation, the royal union flag will be flown on appropriate occasions to symbolize Canada's membership in the commonwealth and our devotion to the crown.
You have enacted legislation authorizing the integration ol Canada's three armed services and have approved a white paper on the reshaping of Canada's defence policy to improve the effectiveness of our contribution to peace keeping and international security.
The preliminary report of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism has been laid before you. My ministers have been gratified to observe the improving understanding of problems arising from the reality and importance of the dual character of our country.
In the spirit of co-operative federalism, my government has held important conferences with the governments of the provinces, and close consultation has greatly improved the co-ordination of federal and provincial policies.
You have enacted legislation whereby the abatement of federal tax on personal incomes, in favour of the provinces, will be increased during the next two fiscal years. You have also enacted legislation whereby my government may make, with provinces which so wish, alternative financial arrangements respecting certain established programs the cost of which is shared by my government.
The federal-provincial conference has established a tax structure committee which is reviewing the fiscal needs and relationships of federal and provincial governments.
You have approved an address to the Queen as a result of which the British North America Act was amended to provide that parliament may legislate concerning benefits, for disabled persons and for survivors, supplementary to old age pensions.
Following this constitutional amendment, you have enacted legislation to establish the Canada pension plan, for the comprehensive provision of retirement pensions which will be fully portable and which will be kept in line with changes in earnings and in the cost of living. In the same legislation you have provided a measure of income maintenance for contributors who become disabled and for the widows and children of contributors who die.
In the same legislation also, you have provided that the old age security pension will in future be paid from age 65 and that the basic amount of the pension will be increased if the cost of living rises.
You have enacted legislation whereby allowances of $10 a month are paid in respect of children aged 16 and 17 who are not working, either because they are unable to do so or because they are receiving full time education.
You have adopted a measure whereby my government may guarantee bank loans to university students and pay the interest on these loans during the years of study; this program is being administered in co-operation with the provinces.
You have enacted a measure to establish a labour code for industries under federal jurisdiction. The code provides for a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour and for standards respecting hours of work and holidays.

The cash income of Canadian farmers rose in 1964 to a record level. Exports of wheat were the largest ever. Revisions in dairy policy were reflected in increased production, especially of cheese, better sales and prices, and the elimination of the butter surplus.
You have enacted a measure establishing a new type of farm credit, so that partnerships of farmers may borrow for the purchase of machinery to be used co-operatively.
You have enacted legislation to double the size of loans which may be made by the Farm Credit Corporation and of loans by chartered banks guaranteed under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
You have adopted a measure whereby my government may provide re-insurance of the major portion of the disaster risk to any province establishing a crop insurance program.
You have approved increased assistance to farmers in eastern Canada and British Columbia purchasing feed grains.
My government is expanding the work of ARDA and has made with the provinces a new agreement respecting programs for the five years beginning 1 April, 1965.
You have approved an increase in Canada s contribution to the world food program.
In 1964 Canada's fisheries established records both in the quantities landed and the value of the catch to fishermen. A federal-provincial conference on fisheries development gave impetus to a widespread program of industrial development in the fisheries.
You have adopted a measure establishing a
12 mile fishing zone.
You have approved increases in veterans pensions and allowances, enabling their recipients to maintain their standards of living and to share in the benefits of a more buoyant economy.
By amending the National Housing Act you have broadened the range of financial assistance available for urban renewal and low rental housing.
My government has concluded an agreement with the United States respecting free trade in automobiles and their components. The agreement makes possible for the industry programs designed to achieve substantial improvements in efficiency, production and employment.
You have approved the payment of subvention assistance on the movement of Canadian coal for a period of five years from 1 April, 1965, and have authorized loans for coal production assistance for a further period of four years.
You have enacted legislation whereby divorce bills can be dealt with more expeditiously.
My government has initiated inquiries directed to the reassessment of immigration policy and procedures.
My ministers have made further progress in the study and implementation of many of the recommendations and suggestions of the royal commission on government organization.
We must note with regret that in the past year there has been little progress in reducing international tensions In recent weeks, some tensions have been heightened. My government has continued to make constructive efforts toward peace and good neighbourliness.
You have approved the participation of Canadian troops in the United Nations force in Cyprus, Though no long term solution to this problem is yet in sight, the United Nations force has been successful in controlling armed conflict.

You have approved the Columbia river treaty and its protocol, which my government subsequently ratified. These arrangements are of mutual benefit to Canada and the United States, providing this country with large supplies of low-cost power and increasing opportunities for employment.
My Prime Minister attended the conference in London of commonwealth prime ministers to discuss matters of common concern, including the establishment of a commonwealth secretariat.
My government convened a conference of experts to exchange experience on the practical and technical problems of peacekeeping. The commonwealth education conference was held in Ottawa.
In the search for international understanding and co-operation, my Prime Minister and his colleagues have visited and received a number of leaders of other countries, including the presidents of Ireland and the United States; the prime ministers of Britain, Japan, Malaysia and Trinidad and
Prorogation
Tobago; the chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany; the foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Britain, France, Germany and Norway; and the secretaries general of the United Nations and of NATO.
Canadians recently joined with the people of Britain, the commonwealth and the world in paying final tribute to Sir Winston Churchill, to whom so much was owed by all free men.
Members of the House of Commons:
I thank you for the provision you have made for the public services in the current fiscal year.
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
May divine Providence continue to bless our country.
This concluded the second session of the twenty sixth parliament.

Reduction of indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement of a settler in respect of a property in his possession, the title of which is held by the director, or such soldier settler loans which are administered by the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. by an amount which will reduce his indebtedness to an amount in keeping with the productive capacity of the property or his ability to repay his indebtedness under regulations approved by the governor in council. $100.
